pools.title: The Problem, and a Second Route
pools.covers: reading §5.0 (the unnumbered Opening), §5.1.1, §5.1.2 · lecture 5.1 slides the_world_changes, modulation_is_not_learning, one_capacity_three_questions, two_ways_a_question_gets_specific, contingency_is_not_new

items.stem: A hungry worm pursues a faint food odor that the same worm ignores once it has been fed. Why does the chapter refuse to call this change learning?

options.text: When the modulator clears, every weight is where it was before, so nothing about what happened has been kept.
options.why: Correct. A neuromodulator changes what the same circuit does with the same input, and that is real flexibility, but the animal afterward is exactly what it was before.

options.text: The change comes from inside the animal rather than from the world, and learning has to be caused by something outside it.
options.why: Hunger is an internal state, but that is not the chapter's reason. What rules modulation out is that nothing is kept once the chemistry clears.

options.text: The change lasts only as long as the hunger does, and learning by definition has to last for days rather than for hours.
options.why: Lasting matters, but the chapter sets no clock. The test is whether anything inside the animal is still different once the modulator is gone.

options.text: The food odor is a signal the worm already responded to, and learning can only be about a stimulus the animal has never met.
options.why: Learning can reweight a familiar stimulus as well as a new one, as when a smell that meant food comes to mean danger.

items.stem: In a model worm, the connection from a copper-sensing cell to the interneuron that drives forward movement carries a weight of −2. What does that number settle?

options.text: How much the copper cell's activity counts toward that interneuron, and that it counts against firing.
options.why: Correct. A weight is the strength of a connection, and it settles which input counts for how much, and with what sign.

options.text: How fast the copper cell's signal travels along its axon to the interneuron, with the minus sign marking a slow connection.
options.why: Conduction speed is a property of the axon, not of the weight. The sign of a weight marks inhibition, not slowness.

options.text: How many times the copper cell must fire before the interneuron responds to it at all, which here is twice.
options.why: That describes something like a threshold on the receiving cell. A weight scales what each input contributes; it is not a count of spikes.

options.text: How strongly a copper molecule binds to the receptor on the sensing cell, with a negative value meaning weak binding.
options.why: Binding happens at the sensory surface, before any connection is involved. The weight belongs to the connection between two cells.

items.stem: Going from "what problem does steering solve?" to "by what procedure is steering done?" is one move. Going from "how is a body coordinated?" to "how is a body coordinated and aimed?" is another. How do the two moves differ?

options.text: The first changes the kind of question with the capacity fixed; the second keeps the kind and adds a constraint.
options.why: Correct. Moving down Marr's levels asks a new kind of question about one capacity. Taking a narrower case asks the same kind of question about fewer situations.

options.text: The first makes the question more general and the second makes it more specific, so the two moves run in opposite directions.
options.why: Both moves make a question more specific; the chapter calls them two different ways of doing so. Neither one generalizes.

options.text: The first moves forward in evolutionary time to a newer animal, while the second stays with the same animal and asks more about it.
options.why: Marr's levels are three questions about one capacity in one animal, not a sequence of animals.

options.text: The two are the same move made at different levels, since each one adds detail that the previous question left out of its answer.
options.why: Both do add detail, which is why they are easy to run together. The chapter separates them because only one of them changes the kind of question being asked.

items.stem: Description A: "the animal must reach warm water". Description B: "the animal must reach warm water that is also low in salt". How should the move from A to B be classified?

options.text: As a narrower case, because both are stated in terms of the animal's world and B only adds a constraint that covers fewer situations.
options.why: Correct. The test is the vocabulary. A move between levels would restate the problem in terms of what is inside the animal or of physical parts.

options.text: As a move down to the algorithmic level, because B is more detailed than A and the algorithmic level is where the detail is supplied.
options.why: More detail is not the test. B is still stated entirely in terms of the world the animal lives in, so it is the same kind of question.

options.text: As a move to a different capacity altogether, because salt is a new kind of stimulus that A never mentioned at all.
options.why: Adding a constraint does not change the capacity. Reaching warm water and reaching warm, fresh water are the same capacity with a narrower target.

options.text: As a move up a level, because B asks more about the world outside the animal and less about what goes on inside it.
options.why: A and B are equally about the world outside the animal. Neither one says anything about what is inside it, which is why they sit at one level.

items.stem: A modeler proposes a special name for "finding food in a dish ten times larger than usual". By the chapter's rule for naming a narrower case, should it get one?

options.text: No, because a bigger dish makes the problem harder without changing what a solution must have.
options.why: Correct. A narrower case earns its own name when it changes what a solution must have, and not when it is merely harder.

options.text: Yes, because any problem that takes an animal measurably longer to solve deserves to be distinguished from the easier version of it.
options.why: Taking longer is being harder, which is exactly what the rule says does not earn a name.

options.text: Yes, because a bigger dish would need more neurons to search, and a change in the machinery always marks a new problem.
options.why: The rule is about what a solution must have, stated at the level of the problem. How many neurons it takes is a question at another level.

options.text: No, because both versions are computational problems, and a narrower case can never be named at the computational level.
options.why: Narrower cases are named at the computational level all the time; coordinating and aiming are both computational, and aiming has its own name.

items.stem: A nerve net coordinates a whole body in time; a bilaterian coordinates a body and aims it. Why is an account of coordinating a body not already an account of aiming one?

options.text: Aiming adds a constraint, that the movement be directed somewhere, so a body can be perfectly coordinated while going nowhere in particular.
options.why: Correct. Both are computational questions, and aiming is coordination with a constraint added, one notch more specific.

options.text: Aiming belongs to a different Marr level from coordination, since it needs a procedure spelled out where coordination needs only a problem stated.
options.why: The chapter places both at the computational level. Each could be asked about at the algorithmic level too.

options.text: Aiming requires kinds of neurons that a nerve net does not have, so the two can only be explained in different physical terms.
options.why: That is a claim about implementation. The point here is about the problems themselves, stated in terms of the animal's world.

options.text: Aiming is a skill an animal has to acquire, while coordinating the body is something the animal is simply born able to do.
options.why: Nothing in the contrast turns on acquisition. Both are problems a body plan can solve, however its wiring came to be.

items.stem: Can a question get more specific by taking a narrower case at the algorithmic or implementational level, or only at the computational level?

options.text: At any level, since a procedure has narrower cases and so does a physical mechanism.
options.why: Correct. The chapter works the move on a computational example first, then says the same move is available at every level.

options.text: At the computational level alone, since procedures and mechanisms are already as specific as a description gets.
options.why: Procedures and mechanisms come in general and narrower forms too; a rule for changing a weight can be narrowed by what it depends on, for instance.

options.text: At the implementational level alone, since a physical mechanism is the one thing with parts that differ from case to case.
options.why: Physical mechanisms do have narrower cases, but so do problems and procedures. Nothing restricts the move to one level.

options.text: At no level, since taking a narrower case is just another name for moving down from one Marr level to the next.
options.why: The chapter's whole point is that these are two different moves, told apart by whether the vocabulary changes.

items.stem: In which vocabulary is an implementational description of steering stated?

options.text: Physical parts.
options.why: Correct. A computational description is stated in terms of the animal's world, an algorithmic one in terms of what is inside the animal, and an implementational one in terms of physical parts.

options.text: The animal's world.
options.why: That is the computational level's vocabulary, the problem as it looks from outside.

options.text: What is inside the animal.
options.why: That is the algorithmic level's vocabulary, stated in terms of internal states and procedures rather than the stuff that realizes them.

options.text: The animal's evolutionary history.
options.why: History explains why a capacity exists, which is part of a computational account, but no level is defined as the vocabulary of history.

items.stem: How does this module's step forward differ from the step most earlier modules took?

options.text: It stays within the same animal and adds a capacity that animal did not have, rather than moving forward in time to a new animal.
options.why: Correct. The module adds a capacity rather than an animal, and several modules after it work the same way.

options.text: It moves forward in evolutionary time to the first vertebrates, whose brains were the first large enough to support learning at all.
options.why: The chapter climbs no animal, and it argues that most of learning is older than the vertebrate.

options.text: It leaves evolution aside altogether, because learning happens within a lifetime and so has no evolutionary history to trace.
options.why: Learning has an evolutionary history the chapter spends time on; what it adds is a within-lifetime route, not an exemption from evolution.

options.text: It jumps directly to humans, since human learning is the case the rest of the course is ultimately trying to explain.
options.why: The animals of this module are the worm and the cnidarians, returning from Module 4 to do new work.

items.stem: The chapter divides the varieties of learning by two questions, what there is to learn and what there is to learn from, and says they cross rather than stack. What does crossing mean here?

options.text: The two are separate axes, so where a learner sits on one does not settle where it sits on the other.
options.why: Correct. The first asks how complicated the relationship is; the second asks what information is available when a connection changes. Treating them as one ladder misreads the chapter.

options.text: The second question is only asked once the first has been answered, so the two form a single sequence from simple to complex.
options.why: That is stacking, which the chapter says they do not do.

options.text: The first question applies to invertebrates and the second to vertebrates, so each divides a different set of animals.
options.why: Both questions apply to any learner. Neither one is sorted by animal group.

options.text: The answer to one question is always the reverse of the answer to the other, so a simple relationship is learned from rich information.
options.why: No such inverse relationship is claimed. Crossing means independence, not a fixed trade between the two.

items.stem: How does the chapter set the weights of this module against the weights Module 4 discussed?

options.text: Module 4 discussed weights set in advance across generations; here weights move within a single lifetime, and the question is what it takes to move one.
options.why: Correct. That framing is the whole module in one line, and it is a contrast between two ways of treating a weight rather than between two kinds of animal.

options.text: Module 4's circuits had no weights at all, while the circuits in this module have weights that start at zero and then grow over time.
options.why: Module 4's circuits had weights and depended on them for everything they did.

options.text: Module 4's weights belonged to invertebrates, while the weights in this module belong to vertebrates with far larger brains.
options.why: The module stays with Module 4's animals and adds a capacity to them. No new animal is introduced.

options.text: Module 4's weights were changed by neuromodulators whenever the animal was hungry or fed, while the weights in this module are changed by experience instead.
options.why: Neuromodulators in Module 4 left every weight where it was, which is why the chapter rules modulation out as learning.

items.stem: Module 4's animal evaluated what reached it, combined signals that disagreed, committed to one action, and held a state that outlasted its cause. What do the chapter's four capacities have in common that makes weights the thing worth changing?

options.text: Every one of them works because of its weights, which settle which input counts for how much and with what sign.
options.why: Correct. Because every arrangement rests on its weights, a change in the weights is a change in what the arrangement does.

options.text: Every one of them depends on a neuromodulator being present, so changing the modulator changes all four at once.
options.why: A modulator changes how an arrangement behaves while it is present, but the arrangements themselves are built out of weights.

options.text: Every one of them runs in a single neuron, so changing that one cell would change all four capacities together.
options.why: These are properties of arrangements of cells, which is exactly why Module 4 was about circuits rather than single neurons.

options.text: Every one of them was already learned, so the weights involved are simply the ones that learning had adjusted before.
options.why: Module 4 treated the weights as set in advance, deliberately. Learning is what this module adds to the story.

items.stem: A model animal with fixed weights is moved to a pond where a plant smell it has always approached now comes from a toxic look-alike. What does the chapter predict it will do?

options.text: Go on approaching the smell and being harmed, the same way every time, because nothing in it can change what the smell counts for.
options.why: Correct. Put an animal with fixed weights into a world whose regularities have shifted and it goes on producing what it was built to produce.

options.text: Approach the smell a little less after each harmful encounter, until after enough encounters it stops approaching altogether.
options.why: A declining response across encounters is exactly what a fixed-weight animal cannot produce. That would be learning.

options.text: Avoid the smell for good after the first harmful encounter, since the harm releases a neuromodulator that reverses the approach permanently.
options.why: A modulator can change behavior while it is present, but when it clears the weights are unchanged and the approach returns.

options.text: Die after the first encounter, after which the rest of its population learns to avoid the smell from what happened to it.
options.why: Nothing about one animal's death changes another animal's weights; the chapter's contrast is between a lineage and a lifetime.

items.stem: A student concludes from Module 4 that worms cannot learn, since every circuit in that module had fixed weights. What does this chapter say?

options.text: It is wrong: fixed weights were a simplification, chosen because a circuit is easier to explain while its numbers are still, and real worms learn.
options.why: Correct. The chapter says outright that fixed weights were a choice about how to teach circuits, not a claim about what the animals can do.

options.text: The conclusion is right, because only animals with a centralized brain have the machinery a lasting change of weight in a circuit requires.
options.why: The chapter argues the reverse: most of learning is older than the vertebrate, and the worm does it.

options.text: The conclusion is right for most of the worm's fixed circuits, but not for its responses to food, which a neuromodulator can change.
options.why: Modulation is not learning, as the chapter insists, so this answer both keeps the mistaken conclusion and misidentifies the exception.

options.text: The conclusion is right about real worms, but the chapter adds learning anyway because a worm that can learn is easier to model than one whose weights hold still.
options.why: The chapter's claim is that real animals learn. It is Module 4's fixed weights, not this module's changing ones, that were the modeling convenience.

items.stem: Module 3 asked the computational question of a cell and Module 4 of an arrangement of cells. What is the computational question when it is asked of a change?

options.text: What problem a change inside an animal solves, and why an animal that could make one left more descendants than one that could not.
options.why: Correct. The computational question is always what problem is solved and why solving it mattered, now asked of a change.

options.text: By what rule a change inside an animal is made, and what information that rule needs to have available when the change happens.
options.why: That is the algorithmic question, about procedure. It is the next lecture's question rather than this one.

options.text: Which molecules at the synapse carry out a change inside an animal, and how much energy the change costs to make and keep.
options.why: That is the implementational question, stated in terms of physical parts and cost.

options.text: How long a change inside an animal lasts once it has been made, and how many times it can be reversed before it becomes permanent for good.
options.why: Duration and reversibility are properties of a change, but neither one is the computational question of what the change is for.

items.stem: The chapter says that the fix for a fixed-weight animal in a shifted world is simple: the weights need to change. Why does it not stop there?

options.text: Naming a fix is not the same as knowing what it requires, and what a changing weight requires is what the rest of the argument works out.
options.why: Correct. The one-line fix is where the section starts, not where it ends.

options.text: The fix turns out to be wrong, because a weight cannot change in a living nervous system, so something other than the weights has to change instead.
options.why: Weights can change; the rest of the module describes how. The fix is right and incomplete, not wrong.

options.text: The fix only applies to model animals, and real animals need a separate account because their weights are not numbers.
options.why: The module applies the same account to model and real animals, down to the synapse.

options.text: The fix applies only to vertebrates, so the argument has to go on to explain how invertebrates manage without one.
options.why: The chapter holds that invertebrates learn too; it does not treat learning as a vertebrate solution.

items.stem: What does contingency mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A reliable relationship between one thing and another, such that the first is a dependable sign of the second.
options.why: Correct. A contingency is a fact about the world, and it can be tracked by a lineage or by a single animal.

options.text: Responding only when two things occur together, and to neither of them alone, as a receptor or a neuron can.
options.why: That is coincidence detection, something a mechanism does. A contingency is a relationship out in the world.

options.text: Learning in which one event comes to be treated as a sign of another, so that a cue that did nothing comes to produce a response.
options.why: That is classical conditioning, one way an animal can come to reflect a contingency within a lifetime.

options.text: An event that produces a response only because it has been paired with something that already produced one.
options.why: That is a conditioned stimulus. It is one side of a relationship an animal has learned, not the relationship itself.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A reliable relationship between one thing and another, such that the first is a dependable sign of the second".

options.text: contingency
options.why: Correct. The chapter introduces the term on the copper-avoiding worm, where the relationship holds in the world whether or not anything in the worm's life taught it.

options.text: conditioned stimulus
options.why: A conditioned stimulus is the cue side of a learned link, not the relationship between two things.

options.text: coincidence detection
options.why: Coincidence detection is responding to two things occurring together, a property of a mechanism rather than of the world.

options.text: reinforcer
options.why: A reinforcer is a consequence that makes a response more likely, one term in a relationship rather than the relationship itself.

items.stem: On one mudflat, a particular shadow passing overhead is reliably followed within seconds by a diving bird. Which description uses contingency as the chapter does?

options.text: The shadow-then-bird relationship is a contingency whether or not any animal on the mudflat has come to respond to it.
options.why: Correct. A contingency is a reliable relationship in the world. An animal's nervous system may come to reflect it, by selection or by learning, but that is a separate matter.

options.text: The relationship only becomes a contingency once some animal on the mudflat has learned to hide when the shadow appears.
options.why: That confuses the relationship with an animal tracking it. The copper contingency held before and without any worm learning it.

options.text: The contingency is the animals' habit of hiding at the shadow, since a contingency is a response that has become reliable.
options.why: The hiding would be a response that reflects the contingency. The contingency itself is the relationship between shadow and bird.

options.text: The relationship is a contingency only if the shadow actually causes the bird to dive, and otherwise it is a coincidence.
options.why: A contingency needs only that the first be a dependable sign of the second. Nothing requires that it be the cause.

items.stem: One worm avoids copper the first time it meets it. Another worm comes to avoid a harmless-smelling chemical after meeting it only in places where it was also harmed. Which sense of adapt from Module 2 fits each?

options.text: The first is adaptation across generations, set by differential survival; the second is adaptation within the second worm's own lifetime.
options.why: Correct. The copper relationship was established in the lineage and nothing in the worm's own life taught it; the second worm changed during its own life.

options.text: Both are adaptation within a lifetime, since each worm is responding to a chemical it can sense in the dish right now, during its own life.
options.why: Responding to something present now is true of both, and does not tell us where the response came from. The first worm's avoidance predates its life.

options.text: Both are adaptation across generations, since every response a worm makes is ultimately built by the wiring it inherits from the worms before it.
options.why: Inherited wiring is where both start, but the second worm's avoidance was changed by what happened to that worm.

options.text: The first is adaptation within a lifetime and the second across generations, because only the second involves any harm.
options.why: That is the pairing reversed. Harm in the lineage's past set the first response; harm in this worm's life set the second.

items.stem: A student writes: "Evolution figured out that copper was dangerous, so it wired the worm to avoid it". What is wrong with this, by the chapter's standard?

options.text: Nothing had to know copper was dangerous: worms whose wiring happened to avoid it left more descendants, and nothing did the fitting.
options.why: Correct. The chapter holds language about selection to the same standard as language about learning. Differential survival has no foresight and knows nothing.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since the sentence is a harmless shorthand for what selection did over many generations of worms.
options.why: The chapter treats this shorthand as the error itself, because it credits selection with knowing something it cannot know.

options.text: The worm learned to avoid copper during its own life, so evolution had nothing to do with the avoidance at all.
options.why: The chapter says the reverse: nothing in the worm's own life established the relationship.

options.text: Copper is not in fact dangerous to worms, so the avoidance is a leftover from an earlier environment rather than a true adaptation to this one.
options.why: The chapter treats copper as a dependable sign of harm in the places the worm's ancestors lived. The problem is the agentic wording.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what is the new capacity this module is about?

options.text: A second route to tracking contingencies, running on a different timescale, inside one animal during one lifetime.
options.why: Correct. Contingency detection is old. What is new is a way of getting there inside a single life.

options.text: Detecting contingencies in the world at all, which animals could not do until they could learn from their own experience.
options.why: Animals were tracking contingencies long before any of them could learn. The worm's copper avoidance is the example.

options.text: Detecting contingencies with a brain, as opposed to the diffuse nerve nets that earlier animals had used for the same job.
options.why: The chapter does not tie the new capacity to brains, and it argues that most of learning is older than the vertebrate.

options.text: Responding to the world at all, as opposed to drifting through it with no response to anything the body encounters.
options.why: Responding to the world is far older than learning; Module 4's animals responded to everything reaching their surface.

items.stem: A researcher finds that a species of snail reliably avoids the scent of a predatory crab. She concludes that the snails learned to avoid it. What would the lecture's test for this kind of claim require?

options.text: Rearing snails that have never met the scent and testing them on first contact, since the avoidance may have been set across generations.
options.why: Correct. The lecture's test is the reared animal: a worm that has never met copper avoids it the first time, so that avoidance was not learned.

options.text: Showing that the snails avoid the scent more strongly than they avoid other smells, since a stronger response is a learned one.
options.why: Response strength does not tell a lineage's adaptation from a lifetime's. An inherited avoidance can be very strong.

options.text: Showing that the snails have a brain large enough to learn, since learning an association needs more neurons than an inherited avoidance does.
options.why: The chapter does not make learning depend on brain size, and the question here is where the avoidance came from.

options.text: Nothing further, since reliable avoidance of a danger is itself the evidence that an animal has learned about that danger.
options.why: That is the misconception the section exists to dispel. Detecting a contingency does not require learning.

items.stem: In the poisoned dish at the end of Lab 4, a person can stop the animal walking into the toxin in a few seconds by moving a slider. What does the lecture take from that?

options.text: The fix is visible and reachable from outside, but nothing in a fixed-weight animal can reach its own numbers, and that gap is the module's problem.
options.why: Correct. The lecture calls the asymmetry between what an observer can see and what the animal can reach the whole problem of the module.

options.text: The animal's wiring was designed badly, and the right response is a better fixed design that would avoid the toxin from the very first encounter onward.
options.why: A better fixed design would fail in the next changed world. The point is that the animal cannot change its own design.

options.text: The animal lacks a sensory cell for the toxin, so it cannot tell the toxin from food and nothing inside it could fix that.
options.why: The animal senses the odor perfectly well. What it cannot do is change what that odor counts for.

options.text: The lab exaggerates the problem, because a real worm would simply stop moving once it had been harmed a few times.
options.why: Stopping after repeated harm would itself be a change produced by experience, which is what the fixed-weight model lacks.

items.stem: The lecture calls the failure in the shifted dish "the limit of a fixed-weight design, not the limit of a worm". What mistake is that distinction meant to prevent?

options.text: Concluding that real nematodes cannot learn, when the limit belongs to a model whose weights were held still on purpose.
options.why: Correct. The lecture makes the same correction the chapter does: Module 4's fixed weights were a simplification, and the nematode learns.

options.text: Concluding that worms cannot steer at all, when the dish shows the model steers well and its limit is simply that it steers toward the wrong thing.
options.why: The model steers perfectly well, which is true, but the distinction is about learning rather than steering.

options.text: Concluding that fixed designs are useless, when most of what any animal does still runs on wiring its lineage established.
options.why: The chapter does agree that much of any animal's behavior is inherited, but that is not what this phrase is correcting.

options.text: Concluding that machines are better than worms, when the slider fix shows that a person is only faster than the animal.
options.why: The contrast drawn is between an observer and the animal being observed, not between machines and worms.

items.stem: A model worm is made hungry and then fed a thousand times over, and each time its pursuit of faint food odor rises and falls with the modulator. By the lecture's account, what is different about the worm at the end?

options.text: Nothing in its weights; each episode changed what the existing wiring made of the odor, and nothing was kept once the chemistry cleared.
options.why: Correct. The lecture's line is that an animal can be modulated a thousand times and be no different at the end of it.

options.text: Its food-odor weight has crept upward, since every hungry episode strengthened the connection a little before the modulator cleared away.
options.why: That would be learning. In the lecture's model, the weights are the same numbers before, during and after each episode.

options.text: It has become sensitized, responding more to every stimulus because so many significant events have happened to it.
options.why: Sensitization is a lasting change in responsiveness, which is exactly what modulation fails to leave behind.

options.text: It pursues faint food odor even when fed, because the thousand episodes have made the hungry state the new default.
options.why: A new default would be a kept change. When the modulator clears, the worm returns to what it was.

items.stem: How does the lecture connect the rule for naming a narrower case to the tiers of learning?

options.text: Each tier is a narrower case of what there is to learn, and each earns a name because it changes what a solution must have.
options.why: Correct. The lecture says the rule will be used four times, because each tier adds something a solution must have.

options.text: Each tier is one of Marr's levels applied to learning, so the tiers are named for the vocabulary each level uses.
options.why: The tiers are all computational, stated in terms of what there is to learn in the animal's world. They are not levels.

options.text: Each tier is named for a harder, narrower version of the same problem, and the naming rule ranks them by how hard each one is.
options.why: The naming rule says the opposite: being harder is not what earns a name.

options.text: Each tier belongs to a different animal, and the naming rule names each after the first animal known to show it.
options.why: The tiers are sorted by the relationship to be learned, and several of them are found in the same animals.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why a hungry worm's pursuit of a faint food odor is not learning, and say what would have to be true of the worm afterward for a change to count as learning.
items.answer: A neuromodulator washing through the tissue changes what the same circuit does with the same input, so a hungry worm pursues a signal a fed worm ignores. That is real flexibility. But when the chemistry clears, the worm is exactly what it was before: every weight is where it was, and nothing that happened has been kept. For the change to count as learning, something inside the worm would have to be different afterward and stay different, because of what it experienced.
rubric: Says the modulator changes what the same circuit does with the same input.
Says that when the modulator clears, the weights are unchanged and the animal is as before.
Says learning requires a lasting internal change that outlasts the episode.
Ties the lasting change to experience rather than to the animal's current state.

items.stem: The chapter says the new capacity in this module is not contingency detection. In a few sentences, using the copper-avoiding worm, explain why not and say what the new capacity is instead.
items.answer: The worm already detects a contingency: copper ahead, and it turns away. Nothing in its own life established that relationship. It was set across generations, because worms whose wiring avoided copper left more descendants, and nothing had to know copper was dangerous for that to happen. So detecting contingencies is old. What is new is a second route to the same result, one that runs inside a single animal during its own lifetime, on a much faster timescale.
rubric: Uses the copper worm as a case of contingency detection without learning.
Attributes the copper response to differential survival across generations.
Avoids crediting selection with knowing or detecting anything.
Names the new capacity as a second route within one lifetime.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, distinguish the two ways a question about a capacity can get more specific. Give the test that tells them apart and the rule for when a narrower case earns a name of its own.
items.answer: Moving down Marr's levels changes the kind of question while holding the capacity fixed: what problem steering solves, by what procedure, by what physical means. Taking a narrower case holds the kind of question fixed and adds a constraint, as aiming adds a direction to coordinating a body. The test is vocabulary. Moving between levels changes it, from the animal's world to what is inside the animal to physical parts, while a narrower case keeps it. A narrower case earns its own name when it changes what a solution must have, not when it is merely harder.
rubric: Describes moving down the levels as changing the kind of question with the capacity fixed.
Describes a narrower case as keeping the kind of question and adding a constraint.
Gives vocabulary as the test that tells the two apart.
States the naming rule: a changed requirement on the solution, not greater difficulty.

pools.title: The Timescale Mismatch, What Learning Requires, and Tier One
pools.covers: reading §5.1.3, §5.1.4, §5.1.5 · lecture 5.1 slides two_routes_and_the_real_problem, what_learning_requires, tier_one

items.stem: The chapter calls selection a slow filter and a coarse one. What makes it so?

options.text: A response becomes common only if its contingency held for a long time and was met by many individuals, so survival differences could add up.
options.why: Correct. That shape is what lets some contingencies slip through: anything brief, local, or new never gives survival differences the time or the numbers to add up.

options.text: Selection acts on one individual at a time, so it can only ever adjust the wiring of an animal after that animal has already died.
options.why: Selection acts on differences across many individuals in a population, which is why it needs numbers as well as time.

options.text: Selection can shape bodies but not nervous systems, so any response that depends on wiring has to be learned during a life rather than inherited.
options.why: The copper-avoiding worm shows wiring shaped by selection. Selection is slow on nervous systems, not blind to them.

options.text: Selection takes a fixed number of generations to act on any trait, however long or briefly the contingency behind that trait has held.
options.why: Nothing fixes the number of generations. The point is that the contingency itself has to hold long enough, and widely enough, to matter.

items.stem: In one lake, a snail is safe grazing on a bright algae mat in spring, but by late summer the same mats shelter a predatory fish. Which kind of contingency is this, in the chapter's terms?

options.text: One that holds for a season and then reverses, so the response that fit in spring no longer fits in summer.
options.why: Correct. A relationship that reverses within a lifetime is one of the three kinds that a response fixed in advance cannot meet.

options.text: One that is true in one patch of territory and false in the next, so that no single wiring fits the whole species.
options.why: That is the second kind. Here the place is the same mat, and what changes is the time of year.

options.text: One that has never occurred in the lineage at all, because the predatory fish is new to the lake and to the snail.
options.why: Nothing says the fish is new. What defeats a fixed response here is that the relationship flips within a single lifetime.

options.text: One that selection has had time to fix, since spring and summer come round every year and the pattern repeats reliably.
options.why: The seasons do repeat, but a single fixed response would be wrong for half of every year. That is why this kind slips through.

items.stem: A berry is harmless in one valley and toxic in the next, because the soils differ. A bird species ranges across both valleys. What does the chapter say about a response to this berry fixed by selection?

options.text: No single wiring fits the whole species, since the relationship is true in one patch of territory and false in the next.
options.why: Correct. Selection shapes one lineage, and a lineage spanning both valleys cannot be wired to fit both.

options.text: Selection will fix avoidance in both valleys in time, since avoiding a berry that is sometimes toxic is always the safer wiring.
options.why: Avoiding a harmless food has a cost too, which is why a blanket response is not a solution to a relationship that varies by place.

options.text: The relationship reverses within each bird's lifetime, so the bird needs a response that can change from month to month.
options.why: Nothing here changes over time; it changes over space. That is the chapter's second kind, not its first.

options.text: The berry is new to the species, so selection has never had any chance at all to act on a response to it.
options.why: Nothing says the berry is new. The trouble is that its meaning depends on where the bird is.

items.stem: A chemical pesticide first sprayed a decade ago now marks fields where insects die. Which kind of contingency does the chapter say this is?

options.text: One that has never occurred in the lineage before, because the chemical is new, so no survival difference could have built up around it.
options.why: Correct. A new flavor, predator or chemical is the third kind of contingency that slips past selection.

options.text: One that holds for a season and then reverses, since the chemical is only sprayed at certain times of the year.
options.why: Spraying may be seasonal, but what defeats a fixed response here is that the chemical has no history in the lineage at all.

options.text: One that differs from place to place, since only some fields are sprayed with the chemical and the fields beside them are left untreated by it.
options.why: Patchiness is real, but the defining trouble is novelty. Even a species living only in sprayed fields would have no inherited response to it.

options.text: One that selection has already fixed, since ten years is many generations for an insect and enough for survival to sort them.
options.why: Selection might eventually act, but it needs the contingency to hold for a long time across many individuals. A decade-old chemical is the chapter's case of something new.

items.stem: What happens in taste aversion, as the chapter describes it?

options.text: A rat eats something with an unfamiliar flavor, is sick several hours later, and will not touch that flavor again.
options.why: Correct. The case carries two of the three kinds of contingency at once, and its delay and its single trial are what make it diagnostic.

options.text: A rat eats a familiar food and is sick within seconds, and so learns across several meals to eat less of that food.
options.why: Familiarity, immediacy and repetition are all the reverse of the case, and each of those features is what the chapter's argument turns on.

options.text: A rat is born avoiding bitter flavors, and continues avoiding them however often they turn out to be harmless.
options.why: That describes an inherited response, like the worm's copper avoidance. Taste aversion is acquired in the animal's own life.

options.text: A rat is made sick on purpose several times until the smell of the room alone makes it refuse to eat anything there.
options.why: A room coming to suppress eating is a different arrangement. Taste aversion links a flavor to a sickness, often after a single meal.

items.stem: The chapter says taste aversion carries two of its three kinds of contingency at once. Which two?

options.text: The flavor may be new to the lineage, and a plant that poisons a rat in one patch may not grow in the next.
options.why: Correct. Novelty and variation from place to place are both present in a single case, which is why the chapter chose it.

options.text: The flavor may reverse its meaning from season to season, and the plant may be new to the rat's lineage.
options.why: Novelty is one of the two, but nothing in the case turns on a seasonal reversal.

options.text: The plant may vary from place to place, and the flavor may reverse its meaning within the rat's own lifetime.
options.why: Variation by place is one of the two, but the case does not depend on a flavor changing its meaning over time.

options.text: All three kinds at once, since a single poisonous meal is new, local, and changeable all together within one case.
options.why: The chapter says two of the three. A reversal within the lifetime is not part of the taste-aversion case.

items.stem: In taste aversion, sickness arrives several hours after the meal. Why does that delay matter to the argument?

options.text: It rules out any moment-by-moment reflex: flavor and sickness never occur together, so something has to carry the flavor forward across hours.
options.why: Correct. The chapter says the delay rules out a reflex, and the lecture draws the consequence, that the flavor must have been carried forward.

options.text: It shows that the rat is slow to learn, since a quicker learner would have linked the flavor to the sickness within minutes rather than hours.
options.why: The delay is a property of the poison, not of the rat. The striking thing is that the link forms at all across that gap.

options.text: It shows that the aversion cannot be learning, since learning needs the two events to occur at the same moment.
options.why: That is the assumption the case refutes. Some learning bridges long gaps, which is exactly what makes this case diagnostic.

options.text: It shows that the sickness was probably caused by something else, since a real poison would act within a few minutes of eating.
options.why: Many toxins act hours later. The chapter takes the delayed sickness as real and asks what the rat must do to link the two.

items.stem: Why does taste aversion hold after a single experience, when many kinds of learning build up over repeated pairings?

options.text: Because the cost of a second experience with a poison can be death, so there may be no second chance to learn from.
options.why: Correct. A rule that waited for more evidence would, in this case, wait for the evidence that kills.

options.text: Because flavors are unusually strong stimuli, so one pairing is enough to push the connection to its maximum strength.
options.why: Strength of the stimulus is not the chapter's reason. The reason is what a second trial would cost.

options.text: Because rats have a separate brain structure dedicated to food, so that food experience is learned faster than any other kind.
options.why: The chapter makes no appeal to a dedicated structure, and systems-level anatomy is deliberately left out of this module.

options.text: Because the sickness lasts for hours, so the rat effectively experiences the pairing many times over before it recovers.
options.why: A long illness is still one experience with the flavor. The single trial is the point, not something explained away.

items.stem: Which statement gives this module's computational problem in the chapter's own terms?

options.text: Detecting contingencies selection could not have fixed a response to: ones that change in a lifetime, differ by place, or are new.
options.why: Correct. It is not contingency detection in general, which Module 4's animals already do; it is the kinds selection's slow, coarse filter lets through.

options.text: Detecting contingencies in the world at all, which an animal must be able to do before it can respond to anything that happens around it.
options.why: Contingency detection long predates learning. The worm's copper avoidance is the chapter's example of detection without it.

options.text: Detecting the contingencies that evolution could not have known about, because they arose far too recently for evolution to have foreseen them coming.
options.why: This phrasing credits selection with knowing and foreseeing, which the chapter refuses. The correct wording says what selection could not have fixed.

options.text: Detecting the contingencies that matter most for an animal's survival, since those are the ones selection works on most weakly.
options.why: Selection works most strongly on what matters for survival. What slips through is a matter of time, place and novelty.

items.stem: One contingency, a flavor followed by sickness, can come to produce avoidance by two routes. What happens to the individual animal on each route?

options.text: Across generations, each individual is unchanged by anything that happens to it; within a lifetime, the animal itself is different afterward.
options.why: Correct. Both routes end in the same behavior, but only on the second is the change inside one animal.

options.text: Across generations, each animal learns a little and passes it on; within a lifetime, one animal learns the whole relationship alone.
options.why: Nothing learned by an individual is passed on in the upper route. What changes there is which wiring is common.

options.text: Across generations, the animal is changed slowly over its life; within a lifetime, it is changed quickly over a few hours.
options.why: The upper route changes no individual at all. It is the makeup of the population that shifts.

options.text: On both routes the individual animal changes in response to what happens to it, and the only real difference is how long the change takes to show.
options.why: Speed is one difference, but the deeper one is where the change happens: in a lineage, or in an animal.

items.stem: A worm reared without ever meeting copper avoids it on first contact. What does that result show?

options.text: The avoidance reflects what happened to the worm's ancestors, not anything that happened to the worm.
options.why: Correct. Whatever the wiring reflects about copper, it reflects because of the lineage's history.

options.text: The worm learned about copper before hatching, from traces of it that were present in the egg it developed in.
options.why: The rearing is what rules this out: the worm has never met copper, in any form, at any stage.

options.text: The worm learned to avoid copper by watching other worms, since worms raised in a group pick up each other's habits.
options.why: Nothing in the case involves other worms. The point of rearing it without copper is that it had no chance to learn.

options.text: Copper is so aversive to every animal that no nervous system of any kind could fail to turn away from it on contact.
options.why: Copper is a relationship in the worm's ancestral world, not a universal repellent. The point is where this worm's response came from.

items.stem: What does an animal need, beyond a fixed-weight nervous system, in order to acquire a new avoidance during its own life?

options.text: A part of itself that changes due to experiences it has, and that thereby comes to reflect something about the world.
options.why: Correct. That is exactly what the fixed-weight picture leaves out, and it is what this module adds.

options.text: More sensory cells, so that it can detect a wider range of stimuli and respond to more of the things that might harm it.
options.why: Detection is not the gap. The fixed-weight worm senses the toxin perfectly well and keeps approaching anyway.

options.text: A neuromodulator for danger, which raises its avoidance of everything whenever it has been harmed recently.
options.why: A modulator changes the circuit's behavior only while it is present. When it clears, nothing has been kept.

options.text: A record of each harmful event it has met, stored with the time and place, so it can look the event up later.
options.why: A record is one thing a lasting change can be, and the module distinguishes it from what learning lays down. The requirement here is simpler: a part that changes and stays changed.

items.stem: What does learning mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A lasting change in what an animal does, produced by experience, and resting on an internal state that experience can modify.
options.why: Correct. The three parts are all needed: the change lasts, experience produces it, and something inside the animal carries it.

options.text: The property of nervous tissue that allows a connection, or a cell, to undergo a lasting change as a consequence of activity.
options.why: That is plasticity, what the tissue can do. Learning is the lasting change in what the animal does.

options.text: A decline in a response to a stimulus that has been repeated without consequence, with the response restored by anything novel.
options.why: That is habituation, one form of learning rather than the definition of the whole category.

options.text: A lasting change whose use is settled at the moment it is laid down, so that the change itself fixes what the animal will now do.
options.why: That is a disposition, the kind of thing learning produces. The definition of learning is about the change in behavior and what carries it.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A lasting change in what an animal does, produced by experience, and resting on an internal state that experience can modify".

options.text: learning
options.why: Correct. The chapter defines it in the section on what an acquired response requires.

options.text: plasticity
options.why: Plasticity is the tissue's capacity for lasting change, what makes learning possible, rather than the change in behavior.

options.text: sensitization
options.why: Sensitization is one form of learning, a general rise in responsiveness after something significant.

options.text: contingency
options.why: A contingency is a relationship in the world. Learning is one way an animal can come to reflect it.

items.stem: What does plasticity mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: The property of nervous tissue that allows a connection, or a cell, to undergo a lasting change as a consequence of activity.
options.why: Correct. Plasticity is what the tissue can do; learning is the lasting change in behavior it makes possible.

options.text: A lasting change in what an animal does, produced by experience and resting on an internal state experience can modify.
options.why: That is learning, the behavioral change. Plasticity is the property of tissue that makes the change possible.

options.text: How readily a cell fires at all, which can itself be lastingly changed so that the same input carries it further than before.
options.why: That is intrinsic excitability, one of the things plasticity can change, rather than the general property.

options.text: The formation of new synapses, which early in life produces far more connections than will eventually survive.
options.why: That is synaptogenesis, one physical process in development, not the general capacity for lasting change.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The property of nervous tissue that allows a connection, or a cell, to undergo a lasting change as a consequence of activity".

options.text: plasticity
options.why: Correct. The chapter defines it alongside learning, as the property that makes learning's internal state possible.

options.text: learning
options.why: Learning is the lasting change in what the animal does, not the property of the tissue.

options.text: synaptic competition
options.why: Synaptic competition is one way plastic synapses interact, when they share a limited resource.

options.text: habituation
options.why: Habituation is a particular form of learning, a declining response to a repeated stimulus.

items.stem: How does the lecture sum up the difference between learning and plasticity?

options.text: Learning is the change in behavior; plasticity is what the tissue can do that makes the change possible.
options.why: Correct. The two words name a behavioral fact and a property of the nervous tissue beneath it.

options.text: Plasticity is the change in behavior; learning is what the tissue can do, at the level of the individual synapse.
options.why: That reverses the two. Learning is defined as a change in what an animal does.

options.text: Learning happens in vertebrates with brains, while plasticity is the simpler form of lasting change found in invertebrates.
options.why: Both terms apply to any animal. The module argues that most of learning is older than the vertebrate.

options.text: They are the same process at two timescales: plasticity over seconds, and learning over days once the change has settled.
options.why: The distinction is between a behavior and a property of tissue, not between two durations of one process.

items.stem: Worms in a pond are wired to approach a smell that, this year, comes from a toxin, and nothing in any worm registers the change. A student says their approach weights are now "wrong". What does the chapter say about that description?

options.text: It is not the right way to put it: the world changed while the connection did not, and nothing in the animal marks the difference.
options.why: Correct. The chapter refuses "wrong" here, and adds that an animal can be learning by any reasonable use of the word without anything in it registering a mismatch.

options.text: It is right, and the weights will correct themselves, since a nervous system always registers when its wiring no longer fits.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite: nothing anywhere in the animal marks the difference. Whether a mismatch can drive its own correction is a further question.

options.text: It is right, since an observer can see what the weights should be, and nothing but the gap between the two is what the word "wrong" names.
options.why: An observer can see a better value, and that is the lecture's point about outside and inside. The chapter still declines to call the animal's state wrong.

options.text: It is not right, because the weights are optimal for the worms' ancestral world, and optimal weights cannot be called wrong.
options.why: The chapter's reason is not that the weights are optimal. It is that nothing in the animal registers any mismatch at all.

items.stem: The lecture says a later rule will make the difference between what happened and what was expected "a real quantity in the mechanism". Why is that language held back while the lecture is defining what learning requires?

options.text: Because nothing yet described computes such a difference, and it is not available to every kind of learning.
options.why: Correct. Error language is licensed only where something in the mechanism plays the part: a represented expectation and a computed difference.

options.text: Because no neuron can compute a difference between two quantities, so the quantity only ever exists in an observer's description.
options.why: Neurons can compute differences, and the next lecture introduces a rule that does. The point is that not every kind of learning has one.

options.text: Because the difference can only be computed after the animal has died, when the outcome of its whole life is known.
options.why: Nothing in the account waits for the end of a life. The difference arrives with a particular kind of rule, moment by moment.

options.text: Because a difference between expected and actual is the same as a neuromodulator, and neuromodulation was already ruled out as learning.
options.why: Modulation was ruled out as learning because it keeps nothing. A computed difference is a different thing altogether.

items.stem: What does habituation mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A decline in a response to a stimulus that has been repeated without consequence, which a novel stimulus restores at once.
options.why: Correct. The restoration is what separates habituation from fatigue.

options.text: A rise in responsiveness to stimuli generally, following something significant that has just happened to the animal.
options.why: That is sensitization, habituation's partner, which moves responsiveness the other way.

options.text: The fading of a learned response when the outcome stops arriving, as new learning that competes with the original.
options.why: That is extinction, which is about a learned link losing its effect, not a response to a repeated stimulus.

options.text: A decline in a response because the cells that produce it have run short of transmitter after firing many times in quick succession.
options.why: That is fatigue, the misreading the chapter rules out. Nothing is used up in habituation.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A decline in a response to a stimulus that has been repeated without consequence".

options.text: habituation
options.why: Correct. It is the chapter's first tier of learning, on the sea anemone touched by a drifting frond.

options.text: extinction
options.why: Extinction is the fading of a learned response when its outcome stops arriving, which presupposes a learned link.

options.text: sensitization
options.why: Sensitization is a rise in responsiveness, the opposite direction.

options.text: blocking
options.why: Blocking is a failure to learn about a cue when another cue already predicts the outcome.

items.stem: What does sensitization mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A rise in responsiveness to stimuli generally, following something significant.
options.why: Correct. An anemone that has just been attacked withdraws from almost anything.

options.text: A decline in a response to a stimulus that has been repeated many times without any consequence following it.
options.why: That is habituation, sensitization's partner.

options.text: Learning in which a cue that previously did nothing comes to produce a response, because it has been paired with another event.
options.why: That is classical conditioning, which needs a link between two events. Sensitization needs none.

options.text: The return of an extinguished response after the outcome has been delivered once on its own, with no cue paired with it.
options.why: That is reinstatement, which concerns a learned response already extinguished.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A rise in responsiveness to stimuli generally, following something significant".

options.text: sensitization
options.why: Correct. It is habituation's partner, and both belong to the first tier.

options.text: habituation
options.why: Habituation is a decline in response to one repeated stimulus, not a general rise.

options.text: spontaneous recovery
options.why: Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response after a delay.

options.text: renewal effect
options.why: The renewal effect is the return of an extinguished response in a new place.

items.stem: A snail stops withdrawing its tentacles after being tapped twenty times in a row. The experimenter then puffs water at it, and it withdraws fully at once. What does the chapter take this pattern to show?

options.text: That the decline was habituation rather than fatigue: nothing had been used up, and something had been adjusted.
options.why: Correct. A novel stimulus restoring the full response immediately is the chapter's test.

options.text: That the snail was fatigued, and that the rest between the last tap and the puff was enough to let it recover.
options.why: Recovery from fatigue would take time. The response came back at once, which is what rules fatigue out.

options.text: That the snail has become sensitized to water, so that any new stimulus now produces a larger response than a tap ever did.
options.why: The response returned to full, not above it. What was shown is that the earlier decline was specific to the repeated taps.

options.text: That the snail has learned that taps are harmless and puffs are harmful, linking each stimulus to its own consequence.
options.why: Tier one needs no link between events. Nothing harmful followed either stimulus.

items.stem: A sea anemone ignores a leaf brushing past it. Minutes after a crab grabs one of its tentacles, the same kind of leaf makes it withdraw. Which tier-one process does this illustrate?

options.text: Sensitization, a general rise in responsiveness after something significant has happened.
options.why: Correct. The crab's attack raised the anemone's responsiveness to stimuli generally, including ones it had been ignoring.

options.text: Habituation, since the anemone had been ignoring the leaf and has now stopped ignoring it after a new stimulus appeared.
options.why: Habituation is the decline. The rise after a significant event is its partner.

options.text: Classical conditioning, since the anemone has learned that leaves predict crabs because the two occurred close together.
options.why: Nothing links the leaf to the crab. The anemone withdraws from almost anything after an attack, which needs no link.

options.text: Fatigue in the opposite direction, since the attack has refilled cells that the repeated leaf touches had run down earlier.
options.why: Neither the decline nor the rise here is a matter of cells running down or refilling.

items.stem: What is the least that tier-one learning requires the animal to keep track of?

options.text: A running count of how often something has occurred, and whether anything ever followed it.
options.why: Correct. There is no link between two events, no outcome to compare against, and no target response.

options.text: A link between two events that occur together, so that one of them can come to stand in for the other.
options.why: A link between two events is what tier two adds.

options.text: An outcome to compare its behavior against, so that it can tell whether a response went well or badly.
options.why: Comparing against an outcome belongs to other kinds of learning, not to the first tier.

options.text: A target response supplied from outside, so that it can adjust its reaction until the reaction matches the target.
options.why: A target is what a teacher supplies. Tier one needs nothing of the kind.

items.stem: Habituation and sensitization form no link between two events. Why do they still count as learning?

options.text: Both are lasting changes in what the animal does, produced by experience, which is what the definition asks for.
options.why: Correct. The definition says nothing about links; it asks for a lasting change, produced by experience, resting on a modifiable state.

options.text: They do not count as learning, because they are reflexes, and a reflex is fixed in advance by the animal's wiring.
options.why: A reflex can be adjusted by experience, and that adjustment is what makes habituation learning.

options.text: They count because they happen in neurons, and any change that happens in a neuron is a kind of learning.
options.why: Plenty of neural changes, like modulation, are not learning. What counts is a lasting change in behavior produced by experience.

options.text: They count because they are found in vertebrates as well as in invertebrates, which shows that they must be genuine learning.
options.why: Where a process is found does not decide whether it is learning. The definition does.

items.stem: What does tier one buy an animal, according to the chapter?

options.text: It stops the animal spending finite attention and energy on a stimulus that is never followed by anything.
options.why: Correct. A response to a non-event is a cost, and habituation stops paying it.

options.text: It lets the animal predict which stimuli will be followed by food, so that it can move toward them in advance.
options.why: Prediction of an outcome needs a link between events, which tier one does not have.

options.text: It protects the animal's cells from fatigue, by stopping them firing before the transmitter they rely on runs out.
options.why: Habituation is not fatigue and does not exist to prevent it. The benefit is about attention and energy.

options.text: It lets the animal learn which of its own actions work, so that it repeats the successful ones in similar situations.
options.why: Linking outcomes to actions is a higher tier. Tier one only changes how strongly a response is made.

items.stem: A cnidarian's stinging cells fire once and are spent. A touch alone does not fire one, and a chemical trace of prey alone does not either, but the two together do. What is sensitization doing here?

options.text: Gating the cell so that independent kinds of evidence for prey must all be present before it fires, which behaves like an AND gate.
options.why: Correct. A single-use cell should not be spent on debris, and requiring two kinds of evidence at once guards against that.

options.text: Gating the cell so that either kind of evidence is enough to fire it on its own, which behaves like an OR gate.
options.why: Under an OR gate, a touch alone would fire the cell, and the case says it does not.

options.text: Letting the cell learn which prey tastes best, so that it fires more readily at prey it has succeeded with before, and is spent less often on the rest.
options.why: Nothing here links prey to outcome. Sensitization only changes how readily the cell fires.

options.text: Making the cell habituate to debris, so that repeated touches from debris stop firing it while prey still does.
options.why: Habituation to repeated touches is a different process, and it would not explain why two kinds of evidence are needed.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why selection alone could not have given a rat a response to taste-aversion contingencies, and say what that tells us about the problem learning solves.
items.answer: Selection is a slow and coarse filter. A response becomes common only if its contingency held for a long time and was met by many individuals. Taste aversion falls outside that. The flavor may be new to the lineage, and a plant that poisons rats in one patch may not grow in the next. The sickness comes hours after the meal, so no moment-by-moment reflex could link the two, and the aversion forms after one meal because a second could kill. So the problem learning solves is not detecting contingencies in general. It is detecting the ones selection could not have fixed a response to.
rubric: Characterizes selection as slow and coarse, needing time and many individuals.
Names at least two of the three kinds of contingency, tied to the taste-aversion case.
Mentions the delay, the single trial, or both, and why each matters.
States the problem as contingencies selection could not have fixed a response to.

items.stem: A classmate says habituation is just fatigue, so it should not count as learning. In a few sentences, give the evidence against the first claim and the reason the second is wrong.
items.answer: If habituation were fatigue, the response should stay down until the cells recover. Instead, a novel stimulus restores the full response immediately, so nothing was used up; something was adjusted. And habituation counts as learning because it meets the definition: a lasting change in what the animal does, produced by experience. The definition does not require a link between two events. Tier one needs only a running count of how often something has happened and whether anything followed.
rubric: Gives the novel-stimulus test and its result.
Concludes that nothing was used up, so it is not fatigue.
Applies the definition of learning: a lasting change produced by experience.
Notes that tier one needs no link, outcome or target.

items.stem: A sea anemone touched again and again by a drifting frond stops withdrawing from it. What has the anemone's experience changed?

options.text: How strongly it responds to something it has met before, the simplest change an animal can make.
options.why: Correct. Tier one changes the strength of a response and nothing more, which is why it sits at the bottom of the four tiers.

options.text: Which of two stimuli it treats as a sign of the other, since the frond has come to stand for something harmless nearby.
options.why: Treating one thing as a sign of another is tier two, which needs a link between two events. The frond is linked to nothing.

options.text: Which of its own actions it repeats, since withdrawing earned it nothing and so the action was dropped.
options.why: Linking an action to its consequence is tier three. The anemone's response simply weakened with repetition.

options.text: How much energy its withdrawal muscles still hold, since repeated contraction has used up what they had stored.
options.why: That is fatigue, which the chapter rules out: a novel stimulus restores the full response at once.

pools.title: Tiers Two, Three and Four
pools.covers: reading §5.1.6, §5.1.7, §5.1.8 · lecture 5.1 slides tier_two, four_terms, tier_three, tier_four

items.stem: What does tier two add to what tier one already asks of an animal?

options.text: A link between two states, rather than a change in the strength of one.
options.why: Correct. Tier one adjusts a single response; tier two ties one thing to another, so that one can come to stand for the other.

options.text: A link between one of the animal's own actions and the consequence that followed that action.
options.why: Linking an action to its consequence is what tier three adds, on top of tier two.

options.text: A record of what was done that persists across a delay until the outcome finally arrives.
options.why: A persisting record across a delay is tier four's new requirement.

options.text: A larger change in the strength of one response, so that a single experience has a bigger effect.
options.why: Tier two is not a bigger version of tier one. It adds a relationship between two things.

items.stem: A ground-nesting bird comes to leave its nest at a particular rustle that has reliably come just before a snake. What has the link bought it?

options.text: The ability to act ahead of the snake's arrival, because something other than the snake has become as meaningful as the snake.
options.why: Correct. Acting before an event rather than waiting for it is one of the two things a link between states makes possible.

options.text: The ability to recognize the snake more accurately when it arrives, because the rustle sharpens the bird's view of the snake itself.
options.why: The rustle does not improve recognition of the snake. It lets the bird respond before there is a snake to recognize.

options.text: The ability to learn which of its own escape routes works best, because the rustle tells it which way the snake will come.
options.why: Choosing among its own actions by their results is a tier-three matter. Here the bird links two events in the world.

options.text: A lower response to the rustle over time, because the rustle has been repeated many times and has come to seem harmless.
options.why: That would be habituation, and it is the opposite of what happened: the rustle came to matter more.

items.stem: A patch of ground is safe only when a particular smell and a particular texture occur together, and neither cue settles anything alone. What must be true of an animal's responses if it has learned the combination as such?

options.text: What it does with both cues together differs from adding up what it does with each cue by itself.
options.why: Correct. The combination has to be distinguishable from its parts. A response that just added the two would treat each cue as carrying half the answer.

options.text: It responds to either cue on its own, since each cue is present whenever the patch happens to be safe.
options.why: Responding to either alone would treat each cue as enough by itself, which the case rules out.

options.text: Its response to the two together is exactly twice its response to either one, since two cues are present instead of one.
options.why: That is precisely the sum of the responses to each, which is what learning the combination has to avoid.

options.text: It carries the smell forward in time until the texture arrives, since the two cues have to be linked across a delay.
options.why: The cues occur together. Nothing has to be carried forward, which is why the chapter calls this the simpler case.

items.stem: Module 4's threshold units and the cnidarian's stinging cell both respond to a combination and not to its parts. What does tier two add that they lack?

options.text: The capacity to acquire a new combination, where theirs were fixed in advance.
options.why: Correct. Distinguishing a combination from its parts is not new; acquiring one within a lifetime is.

options.text: The capacity to respond to a combination at all, since both of those earlier cases respond to one cue at a time.
options.why: Both earlier cases already respond to the combination and not its parts. That is why the chapter cites them.

options.text: The capacity to respond to a combination faster, since a learned link can fire before either cue has finished arriving.
options.why: Speed is not the difference. The difference is whether the combination could be new to the animal.

options.text: The capacity to respond to three or more cues at once, since the earlier cases combined only two cues at a time.
options.why: The number of cues is not what the chapter contrasts. The contrast is fixed in advance against acquired.

items.stem: Why is a link across time harder to form than a link to a combination of cues that occur together?

options.text: Across time, the cue is over when the outcome arrives, so something has to carry the first event forward until the two meet.
options.why: Correct. For a combination, both parts are present at once and nothing has to be carried anywhere.

options.text: Across time, the two events are always of different kinds, so the animal needs two different senses working together to register them both.
options.why: Nothing requires different senses. The difficulty is that the two events are never present at the same moment.

options.text: Across time, the link has to include one of the animal's own actions, which a link to a combination never needs to do.
options.why: A link across time can be between two events in the world, as with the rustle and the predator. Actions are tier three's addition.

options.text: Across time, the outcome has to be good or bad for the animal, while a combination of cues can be neutral about value.
options.why: Neither kind of link requires the outcome to be good or bad. The difficulty is carrying the first event forward.

items.stem: An animal learns about predators from two regularities: a rustle that comes before a predator appears, and a carcass that lies where a predator has already fed. Why must its learning keep track of which event came first?

options.text: The two orders call for different actions, preparing for what is coming or avoiding a feeding ground, so it must tell coming from has-been.
options.why: Correct. Both links are useful and neither does the other's job, which is why an association in time has to record order.

options.text: It need not keep track, since both regularities link a sign to the same predator and so they call for the same response.
options.why: Treating them alike would have the animal preparing for a predator that has already been, or ignoring one that is on its way.

options.text: It need not keep track of the carcass at all, since only a sign that comes before a danger can be of any use to an animal.
options.why: The chapter says the after-link is useful too; it supports avoiding a place where predators like to feed.

options.text: It must keep track because the carcass link is operant, involving what the animal itself did, while the rustle link involves only outside events.
options.why: Neither link involves the animal's own action. Both are links between events in the world, differing in their order.

items.stem: A nematode exposed to a particular food odor together with a chemical that makes it ill afterward steers away from that odor. What does the case show?

options.text: The worm links two things its wiring did not come prepared to relate, needing only reliable dependencies in the world.
options.why: Correct. The worm learns, and what it learns does not need anything about its own actions.
