options.text: The worm has habituated to the odor, since the odor was repeated and the worm's response to it has declined over time.
options.why: The worm's response changed in kind, from approach to avoidance, because of what the odor was paired with. That is a link, not habituation.

options.text: The worm has linked its own act of eating to the illness, so that it now stops eating whenever it smells anything at all like that food.
options.why: The chapter says the worm can learn the odor–illness link without associating either one with eating. Its own actions are not needed.

options.text: The worm's avoidance of the odor was set across generations, exactly like its avoidance of copper, and needed no experience.
options.why: The copper avoidance is present in a worm that never met copper. This avoidance appears only after the pairing.

items.stem: What does classical conditioning mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Learning in which one event comes to be treated as a sign of another, so a cue that did nothing comes to produce a response.
options.why: Correct. Also called Pavlovian conditioning; what changes is which event sets the response off.

options.text: Learning in which what the animal did is one of the linked terms, so that a consequence makes that action more or less likely afterward.
options.why: That is operant conditioning, where the animal's own action is inside the link.

options.text: A decline in a response to a stimulus repeated without consequence, which a novel stimulus restores in full at once.
options.why: That is habituation, a first-tier change with no link between events.

options.text: A rise in responsiveness to stimuli generally, following something significant that has just happened to the animal.
options.why: That is sensitization, which also forms no link between events.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Learning in which one event comes to be treated as a sign of another, so that a cue which previously did nothing comes to produce a response".

options.text: classical conditioning
options.why: Correct. Also called Pavlovian conditioning.

options.text: operant conditioning
options.why: Operant conditioning links an action to its consequence, not one event to another.

options.text: sensitization
options.why: Sensitization raises responsiveness in general, with no link between events.

options.text: unconditioned response
options.why: An unconditioned response is what an untrained stimulus produces, not a kind of learning.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "An event that produces a response without any training".

options.text: unconditioned stimulus
options.why: Correct. The puff of air to the eye is the chapter's example.

options.text: conditioned stimulus
options.why: A conditioned stimulus produces a response only because it has been paired with something that already did.

options.text: unconditioned response
options.why: The unconditioned response is what the event produces, not the event itself.

options.text: reinforcer
options.why: A reinforcer is a consequence that makes an action more likely, a term from operant conditioning.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The response an unconditioned stimulus produces without any training".

options.text: unconditioned response
options.why: Correct. The blink to the puff of air is the chapter's example.

options.text: conditioned response
options.why: A conditioned response is produced by the conditioned stimulus, after pairing.

options.text: unconditioned stimulus
options.why: The unconditioned stimulus is the event, not the response it produces.

options.text: punisher
options.why: A punisher is a consequence that makes an action less likely, from operant conditioning.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "An event that produces a response only because it has been paired with something that already produced one".

options.text: conditioned stimulus
options.why: Correct. The tone sounded just before the puff is the chapter's example.

options.text: unconditioned stimulus
options.why: An unconditioned stimulus produces its response with no training at all.

options.text: conditioned response
options.why: A conditioned response is what the conditioned stimulus comes to produce, not the stimulus itself.

options.text: contingency
options.why: A contingency is the relationship in the world, not one of the events in it.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The response that a conditioned stimulus comes to produce, which is how the link can be seen from outside rather than one of the two things linked".

options.text: conditioned response
options.why: Correct. The blink to the tone alone is the chapter's example.

options.text: unconditioned response
options.why: The unconditioned response is produced by the unconditioned stimulus with no training.

options.text: conditioned stimulus
options.why: The conditioned stimulus is the event that comes to set the response off.

options.text: reinforcer
options.why: A reinforcer is a consequence in operant conditioning, not the response revealing a link.

items.stem: In the chapter's worm case, which part plays the conditioned stimulus?

options.text: The food odor that was paired with the chemical.
options.why: Correct. The odor did nothing in particular before the pairing and comes to set off avoidance afterward.

options.text: The chemical that makes the worm ill.
options.why: The chemical produces illness without any training, so it is the unconditioned stimulus.

options.text: The malaise that the chemical causes in the worm.
options.why: The malaise is produced by the chemical without training, so it is the unconditioned response.

options.text: The worm steering away from the odor.
options.why: Steering away is what the odor comes to produce, the conditioned response.

items.stem: A short jingle has always played just before a vending machine drops a snack, and now a regular customer's mouth waters at the jingle alone. Which pairing of terms is right?

options.text: The jingle is the conditioned stimulus, and mouth-watering at the jingle is the conditioned response.
options.why: Correct. The jingle produces watering only because it has been paired with the snack, which produced watering untrained.

options.text: The snack is the conditioned stimulus, and mouth-watering at the snack is the conditioned response.
options.why: The snack produces watering without any training, so it is the unconditioned stimulus, and that watering is unconditioned.

options.text: The jingle is the unconditioned stimulus, and mouth-watering at the jingle is the unconditioned response.
options.why: A jingle does not make a mouth water without training. It does so only after pairing.

options.text: The jingle is the conditioned stimulus, and buying another snack at the machine is the conditioned response.
options.why: Buying is an action the customer chooses, and nothing in the case says the pairing changed it. The response that reveals the link is the watering.

items.stem: In eyeblink conditioning, the tone comes to make the eye blink. What, according to the chapter, has changed?

options.text: Which event sets the blink off, and nothing about what the animal chooses to do.
options.why: Correct. Classical conditioning changes the trigger of a response, not the animal's choices.

options.text: What the animal chooses to do when it hears the tone, since it has learned that blinking protects its eye.
options.why: That would make the blink an action chosen for its consequence, which is operant conditioning.

options.text: The form of the blink itself, which becomes faster and weaker as the tone takes over from the puff of air.
options.why: The chapter's point is not a change in the response's form, but in what triggers it.

options.text: The puff of air, which gradually loses its power to cause a blink as the tone comes to cause it instead.
options.why: Nothing in the case weakens the puff. The tone gains a power; the puff keeps its own.

items.stem: A worm's steering away from an odor is a movement, while an eyeblink is a reflex. Does that make the worm's odor learning a different kind of learning from eyeblink conditioning?

options.text: No. The difference is worth noticing, but the structure is the same: a link between two events, revealed by a response.
options.why: Correct. The chapter maps the four terms onto both cases and says the movement changes nothing about the structure.

options.text: Yes. Because steering is a movement, the worm's case is operant conditioning, where an action is one of the linked terms.
options.why: The worm's steering is how the link shows, not a term inside it. Operant conditioning needs the action itself to be linked to a consequence.

options.text: Yes. Classical conditioning applies only to reflexes, so the worm's steering cannot be conditioning of any kind at all.
options.why: The chapter uses the worm as its second example of classical conditioning precisely to show that it is not limited to reflexes.

options.text: No. Worms have no reflexes, so every response a worm makes counts as a movement, and all of them are conditioned the same way.
options.why: Whether worms have reflexes is not the chapter's point, and not every response a worm makes is conditioned.

items.stem: A student summarizes eyeblink conditioning as "the tone becomes linked to the blink". What does the lecture single out as wrong with that summary?

options.text: The link is between two events, tone and puff; the blink is the evidence that the link exists, not one of its terms.
options.why: Correct. The lecture calls this the sentence most often mis-stated.

options.text: The link is between the tone and the eye rather than the blink, since the eye is the organ that the tone comes to affect.
options.why: An organ is not an event. The two linked terms are two events: the tone and the puff.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since the tone and the blink occur together after training, and that co-occurrence is all the link ever is.
options.why: They do co-occur after training, which is how the link is seen. The link itself was formed between tone and puff.

options.text: The link is between the puff and the blink, since those are the two events that always occurred together from the start.
options.why: The puff produces the blink with no training at all. Nothing is learned between them.

items.stem: What is the first requirement tier three adds, and why can a purely sensory learner not meet it?

options.text: Telling "this happened" from "this happened after I acted", which a learner registering only events cannot mark.
options.why: Correct. The distinction has no meaning for a purely sensory learner, since its own action is not among the things it registers.

options.text: Telling a cue from the outcome it predicts, which a purely sensory learner cannot do because it registers each event separately.
options.why: Telling cue from outcome is already done in tier two. Tier three's addition concerns the animal's own action.

options.text: Carrying a record across a long delay, which a purely sensory learner cannot do because its senses respond only to the present.
options.why: Bridging a long delay is tier four's requirement, not tier three's.

options.text: Responding to a combination as a whole, which a purely sensory learner cannot do because it adds its responses to each cue.
options.why: Treating a combination as one thing is a tier-two capacity.

items.stem: What does telling "this happened" apart from "this happened after I acted" require of the animal?

options.text: That it can incorporate what it just did as a fact of its own, available to learning alongside the events around it.
options.why: Correct. Its action has to be among the things the learning can link, not just the events around it.

options.text: That it can sense the event more precisely than before, so it can see whether the event was caused by something nearby.
options.why: Sharper sensing of the event does not reveal whether the animal's own action preceded it.

options.text: That it can hold the event in mind for a long delay, so it can tell whether the event came long after the act.
options.why: Holding across long delays is tier four. The distinction here can matter even when the event follows at once.

options.text: That it can predict the event before it happens, so that it can compare the prediction with what actually occurred.
options.why: Prediction is not the requirement named. What is needed is the animal's own action as a fact available to learning.

items.stem: A branch overhead dips and fruit comes down. On one day the wind moved it; on another, the animal had just shaken the trunk. Why can only certain learners tell the two days apart?

options.text: Nothing in the falling fruit differs; only a learner with its own shaking alongside the fruit can separate the days.
options.why: Correct. On the wind day the animal learns about wind; on the shaking day it learns something it can do again.

options.text: The fruit falls differently on the two days, and only a learner whose senses are sharp enough will notice the small difference in how it drops.
options.why: The chapter's point is that nothing in the fruit distinguishes the cases. The difference is available only through the animal's own action.

options.text: The two days differ in how long the fruit takes to fall, and only a learner that can bridge a delay can register that.
options.why: Timing is not the difference, and bridging a delay is a later tier's requirement.

options.text: The two days differ in whether the fruit is ripe, and only a learner that links fruit to its taste can register that.
options.why: Ripeness does not enter the case. What differs is whether the animal's own action came first.

items.stem: An animal facing a log could climb over it, dig under it, or go around it, and each is followed by some consequence. What would a learner that pooled those consequences together come away with?

options.text: The knowledge that logs are an obstruction, and nothing that could guide its choice between the three ways past one.
options.why: Correct. The second tier-three requirement is keeping actions distinct, so that something can change for one action without changing for the others.

options.text: The knowledge of which way past the log is best, since pooling many outcomes gives a more reliable average of each way.
options.why: Pooling mixes the ways together, so there is nothing left to compare. The average belongs to logs, not to any action.

options.text: Nothing at all, since a learner that pools consequences cannot learn anything about logs or about anything else.
options.why: It does learn something: that logs obstruct. What it cannot learn is which of its own actions to choose.

options.text: The knowledge of which way past the log it tried first, since pooled learning keeps the first consequence and drops the rest.
options.why: Pooling does not keep one consequence and drop the others. It merges them, so the order is lost as well.

items.stem: What does operant conditioning mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Learning in which what the animal did is one of the linked terms, so a consequence makes that action more or less likely there afterward.
options.why: Correct. Also called instrumental conditioning; what the animal did is inside the link.

options.text: Learning in which one event comes to be treated as a sign of another, so that a cue which previously did nothing comes to produce a response.
options.why: That is classical conditioning, where two events in the world are linked.

options.text: The problem of working out which of several actions, or which of several connections, was responsible for an outcome that arrived later.
options.why: That is credit assignment, a problem that learning from actions eventually has to solve, not a kind of learning.

options.text: A mapping from situations to what to do in them, adjusted over time so that the animal comes to choose one action in each situation it meets.
options.why: That is a policy, which operant learning can adjust. It is not the name for the kind of learning.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Learning in which what the animal did is one of the linked terms, so that a consequence makes that action more or less likely in that situation afterward".

options.text: operant conditioning
options.why: Correct. Also called instrumental conditioning.

options.text: classical conditioning
options.why: Classical conditioning links two events; the animal's action is not one of the terms.

options.text: habituation
options.why: Habituation is a declining response to a repeated stimulus, with no link at all.

options.text: credit assignment
options.why: Credit assignment is a problem learning faces, not a kind of learning.

items.stem: What does reinforcer mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A consequence that makes the response it followed more likely in that situation afterward.
options.why: Correct. What makes something a reinforcer is its effect on the response, not how pleasant it seems.

options.text: A consequence that makes the response it followed less likely in that situation afterward.
options.why: That is a punisher, the reinforcer's partner.

options.text: An event that produces a response without any training, such as a puff of air to the eye.
options.why: That is an unconditioned stimulus, a term from classical conditioning.

options.text: A signal reporting that an outcome was better or worse than predicted, broadcast widely through the tissue.
options.why: That is a reward prediction error, a signal inside the animal rather than a consequence in the world.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A consequence that makes the response it followed less likely in that situation afterward".

options.text: punisher
options.why: Correct. It is defined by its effect on the response.

options.text: reinforcer
options.why: A reinforcer makes the response more likely, not less.

options.text: unconditioned stimulus
options.why: An unconditioned stimulus produces a response without training; it is not defined by an effect on a prior action.

options.text: extinction
options.why: Extinction is the fading of a learned response when its outcome stops, not a consequence.

items.stem: A child who whines at a store's checkout is given candy, and afterward whines more often at that checkout. In the operant vocabulary, what is the candy?

options.text: A reinforcer, the consequence that followed the whining and made it more likely in that situation from then on.
options.why: Correct. The checkout is the discriminative stimulus, the whining is the response, and the candy is a consequence that reinforced it.

options.text: A punisher, since candy given to stop the whining is meant to end the whining and so makes whining less likely there.
options.why: What the candy was meant to do does not matter. It made whining more likely, which makes it a reinforcer.

options.text: The discriminative stimulus, since the sight of candy at the checkout is what sets the whining off in the first place.
options.why: The discriminative stimulus is the situation, here the checkout. The candy came after the response.

options.text: An unconditioned stimulus, since candy produces a pleasant response in any child without any training at all.
options.why: That describes the candy in classical terms. In this case what matters is that the candy followed an action and changed its likelihood.

items.stem: What distinguishes operant conditioning from classical conditioning?

options.text: In operant conditioning the animal's action is a linked term; in classical, two events are linked and the response reveals the link.
options.why: Correct. That is why Skinner's word fits: what the animal did is now inside the link.

options.text: Operant conditioning is found only in vertebrates, while classical conditioning is found in every animal with a nervous system.
options.why: The chapter sorts these by what is linked, not by animal group.

options.text: Classical conditioning works only on reflexes such as a blink, while operant conditioning works on movements such as steering or climbing.
options.why: The worm's steering is the chapter's second example of classical conditioning, which rules this out.

options.text: Operant conditioning needs a pleasant consequence, while classical conditioning needs an unpleasant one such as a puff of air.
options.why: Both can involve pleasant or unpleasant events. The difference is whether an action is one of the linked terms.

items.stem: Why does the chapter call tier four the hardest of the four tiers?

options.text: The outcome arrives long after the actions that produced it, and many irrelevant actions happen in between.
options.why: Correct. Cooking a meal, studying across a semester and practicing an instrument all have that shape.

options.text: The outcome depends on two cues occurring together, and neither cue on its own is enough to settle anything.
options.why: That is the combination case of tier two, which the chapter calls the simpler kind of link.

options.text: The outcome arrives at the same moment as the action, so the animal cannot tell its action apart from the outcome.
options.why: Tier four's difficulty is the reverse: the outcome arrives long afterward.

options.text: The outcome is always punishing rather than rewarding, so the animal is slow to repeat anything that led to it.
options.why: Nothing about tier four depends on the outcome being bad. Its difficulty is the delay.

items.stem: What is the new requirement in tier four?

options.text: Something marking what was done, persisting until the outcome arrives, or there is nothing left to modify when it does.
options.why: Correct. The chapter calls it a record of what was done, and without it the outcome arrives to find nothing it can change.

options.text: A link between two events in the world, so that a cue can come to stand for an outcome that follows it closely in time.
options.why: That is tier two's requirement. Tier four adds persistence across a long delay.

options.text: A way to tell "this happened" from "this happened after I acted", so that the animal can tell its own actions from events in the world.
options.why: That is tier three's first requirement, about whose doing an event was rather than about a delay.

options.text: A running count of how often a stimulus has occurred, so that the animal can stop responding to one that leads nowhere.
options.why: That is all tier one requires, and it asks for no persistence across a delay between an action and an outcome.

items.stem: Suppose a cook kept a perfect mark of every action taken while making a meal: chopping, stirring, waiting, scratching an itch. The meal turns out well. What problem remains that the record alone cannot solve?

options.text: Apportioning credit: every action on the record preceded the meal, and the record does not say which ones produced it.
options.why: Correct. The lecture puts it as the record alone cannot tell us which arrow to draw. That is credit assignment.

options.text: Carrying the record forward, since the actions happened long before the meal and the record will fade before it arrives.
options.why: The case assumes the record persists. What remains is deciding what each action on it deserves.

options.text: Linking the meal to the kitchen, since the cook has to learn which place the good outcome was associated with.
options.why: That would be a link between two events. The problem here is apportioning an outcome across actions.

options.text: Nothing remains, since a complete record of every action is all that an animal needs to learn from a delayed outcome.
options.why: The chapter says the second half of the problem is just as hard as the first, even given the record.

items.stem: What does credit assignment mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: The problem of working out which of several actions, or several connections, was responsible for an outcome that arrived later.
options.why: Correct. The chapter says it bedeviled the first machines built to learn.

options.text: The finding that a cue perfectly paired with an outcome is not learned about, when some other cue already predicts that outcome.
options.why: That is blocking, a result about what gets learned, not the problem of apportioning an outcome.

options.text: Using one of a system's own estimates as the target for another, rather than waiting for the true outcome to arrive.
options.why: That is bootstrapping, one way a learner can make headway on delayed outcomes.

options.text: Counting an outcome for less the further in the future it lies, by applying a factor below one for every step of delay.
options.why: That is discounting, a way of weighting future outcomes, not the problem of finding which action earned one.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The problem of working out which of several actions, or which of several connections, was responsible for an outcome that arrived later".

options.text: credit assignment
options.why: Correct. It is the second half of tier four's problem.

options.text: eligibility trace
options.why: An eligibility trace is a proposed mark that helps credit find connections, not the name of the problem itself.

options.text: bootstrapping
options.why: Bootstrapping is using one estimate as another's target.

options.text: discounting
options.why: Discounting weights future outcomes by their delay.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe the two requirements tier three adds to tier two. Use the dipping branch for one and the log across the path for the other.
items.answer: First, the animal has to tell "this happened" from "this happened after I acted". When a branch dips and fruit falls, nothing in the fruit shows whether the wind moved the branch or the animal shook the trunk; only an animal that has its own shaking alongside the fruit learns something it can do again. Second, the animal has to keep its different actions distinct, so that something inside it can change for one action without changing for the others. A learner that pooled the outcomes of climbing over, digging under and going around a log would learn only that logs obstruct, and nothing about which way past one to choose.
rubric: States the first requirement: distinguishing an event from an event after one's own action.
Uses the branch to show that the outcome alone does not distinguish the cases.
States the second requirement: keeping actions distinct so one can change without the others.
Uses the log to show what a pooling learner fails to learn.

items.stem: In a few sentences, map the four terms of classical conditioning onto the worm that learns to avoid an odor paired with an illness-causing chemical, and say what is actually linked.
items.answer: The chemical is the unconditioned stimulus, since it causes illness without training, and the malaise is the unconditioned response. The odor is the conditioned stimulus, and steering away from it is the conditioned response. Steering is a movement rather than a reflex, but the structure is the same as in eyeblink conditioning. What is linked is the odor and the chemical, two events; the steering is the evidence that the link exists, not one of the linked terms.
rubric: Identifies the chemical as the unconditioned stimulus and the malaise as the unconditioned response.
Identifies the odor as the conditioned stimulus and steering away as the conditioned response.
States that the link is between two events, odor and chemical.
States that the response is evidence of the link rather than one of its terms.

items.stem: Tier two's link across time and tier four both involve a gap between two things. In a short paragraph, explain what each asks the animal to carry across its gap, and what extra problem tier four has even once the gap is bridged.
items.answer: In tier two, a cue arrives and the thing it predicts has not happened yet; when the outcome arrives, the cue is over. So something in the animal has to carry the first event forward until the two can meet. In tier four, what has to persist is a record of what the animal did, lasting until the outcome arrives, which may be long afterward and after many irrelevant actions. Even with that record, tier four has a second problem: the credit has to be apportioned among all the actions on it, since stirring mattered to the meal and scratching an itch did not. That is credit assignment.
rubric: Says tier two must carry the first event forward until the second arrives.
Says tier four must carry a record of the animal's own actions across a long delay.
Names credit assignment as the further problem in tier four.
Illustrates that preceding the outcome is not the same as producing it.

pools.title: What There Is to Learn From, Who Learns, and What Learning Costs
pools.covers: reading §5.1.9, §5.1.10, §5.1.11, §5.1.12 · lecture 5.1 slides do_brainless_animals_learn, what_the_dispute_teaches, older_than_the_vertebrate, problems_learning_brings, what_there_is_to_learn_from

items.stem: The four tiers say what information has to be in a link and how far apart its terms can lie. What do they leave unsettled?
tags: what there is to learn from

options.text: What the animal's situation makes available to go on at the moment something has to change.
options.why: Correct. That is the second of the two crossed questions: what there is to learn from, rather than what there is to learn.

options.text: How many neurons an animal needs before it can manage each tier, since the tiers say nothing at all about anatomy.
options.why: The tiers indeed say nothing about anatomy, but that is not the gap the chapter names. The gap is about available information.

options.text: Which animals have each tier, since the tiers are defined without reference to any particular group of animals.
options.why: The chapter goes on to place the tiers on the animal tree. What the tiers themselves leave open is the information available for learning.

options.text: How the four tiers are ordered relative to each other, since each tier could in principle come before or after any other.
options.why: The tiers are ordered, each adding a requirement to the one before. It is the things to learn from that are not.

items.stem: At the moment a connection changes, all a learner has to go on is a report of how things went: well or badly. Which of the four things an animal can learn from is that?
tags: what there is to learn from

options.text: A verdict on whether the outcome was good or bad.
options.why: Correct. One number about how things went, with nothing about what the right response would have been.

options.text: Nothing but what occurred together.
options.why: Co-occurrence carries no judgment of good or bad; it only says which things happened at once.

options.text: The next thing that happened.
options.why: The next event is information the world supplies unasked, and it need not be good or bad at all.

options.text: The way the animal should have responded, from a source that knew the answer.
options.why: That is a teacher's kind of information, which says what the response should have been, not merely how things went.

items.stem: A learner changes a connection using only the sound that comes next, which the world supplies without being asked. Which of the four things to learn from is it using?
tags: what there is to learn from

options.text: The next thing that happened.
options.why: Correct. The world provides the next input whether or not anything asked for it.

options.text: A verdict on whether the outcome was good or bad.
options.why: The sound need carry no judgment at all. The learner is using what came next, not how well things went.

options.text: The way the animal should have responded, from a source that knew the answer.
options.why: Nothing here knows the right response. The world simply goes on to its next event.

options.text: Nothing but what occurred together.
options.why: What occurred together is a matter of the same moment. The case uses what followed.

items.stem: A student ranks the four things an animal can learn from as a ladder, with a verdict on good or bad at the top because it builds on having a teacher. What does the chapter say?

options.text: The four are not ordered: a teacher does not bring a verdict on good or bad with it, and a verdict does not bring a teacher.
options.why: Correct. The tiers are ordered; the things to learn from are not. Running the two together is the misreading the chapter warns against.

options.text: The ranking is right, since a verdict on good or bad is the most informative signal an animal can get and so has to be built on top of the others.
options.why: A verdict is in some ways the least informative of the four. More to the point, none of the four is built on another.

options.text: The ranking is right that they are ordered, but has it upside down, since a teacher is the most advanced and belongs at the top.
options.why: Putting the teacher on top keeps the ladder, which is the mistake. No column is a more advanced version of another.

options.text: The ranking confuses the things to learn from with the tiers, which are the same four items listed under a different set of names.
options.why: The student has confused ordering, but the tiers and the things to learn from are two different lists answering two different questions.

items.stem: Of the two ways the chapter divides learning, which one is ordered?

options.text: The tiers of what there is to learn, each adding a requirement to the one before.
options.why: Correct. The four things there are to learn from are not ordered, which is why the two questions cross rather than stack.

options.text: The four things there are to learn from, each adding more information than the one before it.
options.why: These are the ones the chapter says are not ordered.

options.text: The tiers and the things to learn from alike, since each list runs from the simplest case to the most demanding case in it.
options.why: Only the tiers form a sequence. Treating the second list as a ladder too is the mistake the chapter warns about.

options.text: The two lists equally lack an order, since each simply names different kinds of learning in no particular sequence.
options.why: The tiers are ordered, one on top of another. Only the things to learn from lack an order.

items.stem: An animal learns that turning left in its burrow is followed by a draft of cold air. Does learning that require any verdict on whether turning left was good or bad?
tags: what there is to learn from

options.text: No. The relationship can be learned with none of it being good or bad; learning that turning left went well is a different thing.
options.why: Correct. Good and bad are not what any tier adds.

options.text: Yes, since cold air is unpleasant for any animal, so the animal must be learning that turning left was a bad thing to do.
options.why: The draft might matter to the animal, but nothing in the relationship requires it to. The case is chosen to be neutral.

options.text: Yes, since the animal's own action is involved, and learning about one's own actions always depends on a reward or on a punishment.
options.why: Linking an action to what followed it is tier three, and it can be done without any verdict on how things went.

options.text: No, since this is tier-one learning, and tier one is the only tier that can be learned without good or bad being involved.
options.why: Linking an action to what followed is tier three, not tier one. And no tier requires good or bad.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say that good and bad are not what any of the four tiers of learning add?

options.text: Module 4's animals already tag the affect of what reaches them, so valence is not new with learning.
options.why: Correct. Tagging things as good or bad came first. What learning can add is a change that depends on how things went, which is a separate matter.

options.text: Good and bad first appear with vertebrates, which arrive after all four tiers are already in place in other animals.
options.why: Module 4 gives good and bad to the worm. They are neither vertebrate nor recent.

options.text: Good and bad first appear in the fourth tier, where the delayed outcome finally gives the animal something to judge.
options.why: No tier adds good and bad; that is the chapter's claim. Tier four adds bridging a delay.

options.text: Good and bad are human categories that do not apply to animals, so no kind of animal learning can involve them.
options.why: The course applies good and bad to worms without apology. The point is that they come before learning, not that they do not apply.

items.stem: What is the adaptive argument that non-bilaterians need only tier-one learning?

options.text: A sessile filter-feeder neither chooses patches nor pursues, and can act ahead on little that happens to it, so associations would serve it poorly.
options.why: Correct. The chapter calls it a good argument and gives it its due before testing it.

options.text: A non-bilaterian has too few neurons to form an association, so whatever its way of life, only tier one is within its reach.
options.why: The argument is about what learning would be useful for, not about how many neurons it takes.

options.text: A non-bilaterian has had too little evolutionary time to acquire anything more, since it appeared shortly before the bilaterians did.
options.why: The argument concedes hundreds of millions of years, and says the animals should still have stopped at tier one.

options.text: A non-bilaterian has no centralized brain, and learning of any kind beyond habituation and sensitization is a function that a brain is needed to perform.
options.why: The argument makes no claim about brains. It rests on the animal's way of life.

items.stem: The chapter calls the cnidarian case an adaptive argument "tested rather than admired". What made the argument testable, and what does the lecture add about who the warning applies to?

options.text: It predicted an absence research could look for, and the absence is not holding up; the lecture adds that good arguments are not exempt.
options.why: Correct. An adaptive story that predicts something can fail, and this one is failing. Being well formed did not protect it.

options.text: It was stated with confidence, and a confident claim is testable where a hedged one is not; the lecture adds that confidence is a warning sign.
options.why: Confidence does not make a claim testable. A prediction does, here the predicted absence of tier two and three.

options.text: It relied on anatomy that can be examined directly; the lecture adds that anatomy is more reliable than behavioral evidence for questions like this.
options.why: The argument rests on the animals' way of life, not their anatomy, and the evidence against it is behavioral.

options.text: It was written after the results were known, so it could be checked against them; the lecture adds that only careless arguments are affected.
options.why: The chapter suggests it was written before its author could have known the results. And the lecture says the reverse about careless arguments.

items.stem: Which part of the question about learning in cnidarians is not in dispute at all?

options.text: Tier one: habituation is amply shown in hydras, jellyfish and anemones, and sensitization has been studied in detail in anemones.
options.why: Correct. The dispute is about tiers two and three.

options.text: Tier two: classical conditioning is amply shown in all three groups, and only operant conditioning is still debated.
options.why: Classical conditioning rests on two demonstrations in anemones and has not been studied in the other groups.

options.text: Tier three: operant conditioning is well established, since it was shown in an isolated cluster of cells in a dish.
options.why: The operant result is a single 2023 demonstration. It is the newest and least settled part of the picture.

options.text: Not one part of it, since every claim about cnidarian learning, habituation included, depends on studies that critics have rejected.
options.why: Tier one is the settled part. The chapter is explicit that it is not in dispute.

items.stem: In the 2023 study of Nematostella, anemones given light paired with shock retracted considerably more to light alone than anemones given only light or only shock. What do those two comparison groups rule out?

options.text: That the extra retraction came from exposure to the light itself, or from being shocked, rather than from the pairing of the two.
options.why: Correct. Only the pairing group learned the relationship, so the effect of the pairing is separated from the effects of each stimulus alone.

options.text: That the anemones could detect light at all, since an animal that could not detect it would respond the same way in every one of the groups.
options.why: Detection of light is assumed in every group. The comparisons are there to isolate the effect of pairing.

options.text: That the shock was painful to the anemones, since only a painful shock would change their response to anything else.
options.why: Whether the shock is painful is not what the controls address. They address what caused the extra retraction.

options.text: That the result would hold in other species, since three groups make the finding general enough to cover other animals.
options.why: More groups in one species do not generalize across species. What would settle that is replication elsewhere.

items.stem: Box jellyfish in a 2023 study learned to stop bumping into obstacles. The effect vanished when the obstacles were made easy to see, and again when the visual cue was removed. Why does the lecture say those two results make it a controlled result rather than an anecdote?

options.text: They tie the improvement to the conditions a learning account predicts, not to a general change such as the animals slowing down.
options.why: Correct. An animal that merely tired or slowed would bump less under every condition. The effect appears only where learning would be needed and possible.

options.text: They show that the jellyfish can see obstacles clearly, which proves that its eyes are as good as those of a vertebrate.
options.why: Visual acuity is not what the controls test. They test whether the improvement depends on the conditions learning predicts.

options.text: They show that the jellyfish improves under every condition tested, which is what a well-controlled experiment on learning has to demonstrate first.
options.why: The reverse: the improvement disappears under two conditions, and that is what makes it informative.

options.text: They show that bumping into obstacles is harmful to the jellyfish, which is needed before an avoidance can count as operant.
options.why: Whether bumping hurts does not separate learning from other explanations. The two vanishing conditions do.

items.stem: What did the 2023 box jellyfish study show about a cluster of about a thousand of the animal's neurons?

options.text: Cut away from the rest of the animal, the cluster was conditioned on its own in a dish.
options.why: Correct. A small isolated set of neurons, outside any body, showed conditioning.

options.text: Cut away from the rest of the animal, the cluster stopped responding altogether until it was reconnected.
options.why: The result is the opposite: the isolated cluster responded, and was conditioned.

options.text: The cluster grew new neurons in the dish until it reached the size of a small insect brain and began to learn.
options.why: Nothing about growth is reported. The cluster was conditioned at the size it was.

options.text: The cluster was the only part of the animal to habituate, while the rest of the body showed no tier-one learning at all.
options.why: The finding is about operant conditioning in an isolated cluster, not about which parts habituate.

items.stem: Before 2023, what did the case for classical conditioning in a sea anemone rest on?

options.text: One well-controlled study from 1975 and two weaker ones, all of them now decades old.
options.why: Correct. The 2023 study made it two well-controlled demonstrations.

options.text: Dozens of studies across several laboratories, which is why the question had long been considered settled.
options.why: The evidence was thin, which is part of why the adaptive argument could be stated so confidently.

options.text: No studies at all, since nobody had thought to look for conditioning in an animal without a brain until 2023.
options.why: One well-controlled study dates to 1975, so the question had been asked long before.

options.text: Studies of hydras and jellyfish, from which anemone learning was inferred because the three groups are close relatives.
options.why: Classical conditioning has not been studied in hydras or jellyfish at all.

items.stem: The chapter says Morgan's Canon has been applied asymmetrically to cnidarian learning. What does it mean?

options.text: The same controls would convince anyone in an insect; here a prior assumption about brainless animals is doing work the data should do.
options.why: Correct. The canon asks for the simplest explanation the evidence allows, but it is being held to a stricter standard for one group because of an expectation, not because of the evidence.

options.text: The canon has been applied more strictly to insects than to cnidarians, so that insect learning is doubted and cnidarian learning believed.
options.why: That is the asymmetry reversed. The stricter standard is being applied to the cnidarians.

options.text: The canon cannot be applied to cnidarians at all, because it only applies to animals whose brains can be compared with our own.
options.why: The canon applies to any animal. The complaint is that it is being applied unevenly.

options.text: The canon has been applied correctly, since the simplest explanation of anything a brainless animal does is that it cannot learn from experience at all.
options.why: The simplest explanation depends on the evidence and controls, which are the same as those that would convince in an insect.

items.stem: Cnidaria is the sister group to Bilateria. If cnidarians do learn by association, what question does that open?

options.text: Whether the capacity is ancestral to all nervous systems, and so homologous, or arose twice, by convergent evolution.
options.why: Correct. It is the pair from Module 2, applied to learning itself.

options.text: Whether bilaterians inherited their learning from cnidarians, since cnidarians are the more primitive of the two groups.
options.why: Neither group descends from the other; they are sister groups. Calling one primitive is the ladder reading.

options.text: Whether any nervous system at all is needed for learning, since cnidarians show that learning can happen without neurons.
options.why: Cnidarians have neurons, and the box jellyfish result came from a cluster of them. The question is about ancestry.

options.text: Whether vertebrates learned from cnidarians or from other bilaterians, since both groups are older than the vertebrates.
options.why: Learning is not handed from group to group. The question is whether shared learning reflects shared ancestry.

items.stem: The chapter extends a point of fairness to the author of the confident adaptive argument. What is it, and how does the lecture widen it?

options.text: It was likely written before the contradicting results could be known; the lecture adds that this holds for the course's own chapter too.
options.why: Correct. A field moving faster than publication will leave confident claims behind, and that is a caution about all of them.

options.text: The argument was right when it was published and only the later evidence is wrong; the lecture adds that newer results are usually the less reliable ones.
options.why: The chapter treats the new evidence as positive. Its point is about timing, not about which results to trust.

options.text: The argument's author later withdrew it; the lecture adds that withdrawing a confident claim is the mark of a good chapter or paper.
options.why: Nothing is said about a withdrawal. The point is that the author could not have known the results in time.

options.text: The argument was stated about a different group of animals; the lecture adds that it was misapplied to cnidarians by later readers.
options.why: The argument was about cnidarians and similar animals. The fairness concerns when it was written.

items.stem: What is the chapter's current verdict on whether non-bilaterians have tier-two and tier-three learning?

options.text: The evidence is positive and the burden now sits with the skeptics, but the question is still open.
options.why: Correct. A shifted burden, not a finding. Items about the dispute test the reasoning and what would settle it, not a verdict.

options.text: The question is settled: cnidarians have been shown to learn by association and by consequence, and the matter is closed.
options.why: The chapter declines to call it settled. Two demonstrations, neither replicated, move the burden without closing the question.

options.text: The question is settled the other way: the adaptive argument is right, and the reported results are not true learning.
options.why: The chapter says the adaptive argument's prediction appears to be failing, and puts the burden on the skeptics.

options.text: There is no evidence either way, so the burden sits with whoever claims that cnidarians can learn anything beyond tier one.
options.why: There is positive evidence, and the chapter says the burden has moved to the skeptics.

items.stem: Classical conditioning in sea anemones rests on two well-controlled demonstrations. What would settle the question, according to the chapter's summary of the evidence?

options.text: Independent replication in a second laboratory, and a retention test lasting beyond ten minutes.
options.why: Correct. Both address the weaknesses that remain: the result has not been repeated elsewhere, and it has not been shown to last.

options.text: A demonstration of classical conditioning in hydras, since hydras are the simplest of the three groups.
options.why: That would open a new cell rather than settle this one. The anemone result itself needs replication and a longer test.

options.text: A demonstration that sea anemones have a centralized brain, since conditioning requires one.
options.why: Anemones have no centralized brain, and the chapter does not treat one as necessary.

options.text: A demonstration of habituation in sea anemones, since that would confirm they can learn anything at all.
options.why: Habituation in anemones is already amply shown. It does not bear on whether they condition.

items.stem: Operant conditioning in jellyfish rests on one 2023 demonstration. What would settle it, according to the chapter's summary of the evidence?

options.text: Replication in a second species, together with an acquisition curve and an extinction test.
options.why: Correct. One species and one study leave open whether the result is general and whether it behaves like learning over time.

options.text: A second demonstration in an isolated cluster of cells, since the whole animal cannot be trusted to show learning cleanly.
options.why: The isolated-cluster result is already part of the evidence. What is missing is breadth and the time course.

options.text: A study showing that box jellyfish have more neurons than other jellyfish, since that would explain why only they can learn.
options.why: Neuron counts would not settle whether the effect is operant learning. Replication and time-course tests would.

options.text: A study showing that bumping into obstacles harms jellyfish, since operant learning needs a punishing consequence.
options.why: Whether bumping hurts is not what the evidence lacks. Replication and the shape of acquisition and extinction are.

items.stem: Which tiers of learning does the chapter call old and widespread?

options.text: Tiers one and two, found in animals with a few hundred neurons and throughout the bilaterians, tier one even below them.
options.why: Correct. The early tiers are the ancient ones.

options.text: Tiers three and four, found in nearly every animal with a nervous system and extending below the bilaterians.
options.why: Tier three thins out below the bilaterians and tier four arrives with vertebrates.

options.text: Tier four alone, since bridging a delay is the most basic problem any animal that moves has to solve.
options.why: Tier four arrives late, with vertebrates, so it is the one tier that is not old and widespread.

options.text: Only whichever tiers vertebrates have, since all four tiers appeared together with the first vertebrates about five hundred million years ago.
options.why: The chapter's headline is the reverse: most of learning is older than the vertebrate.

items.stem: Where does the chapter place tier three and tier four on the animal tree?

options.text: Tier three is documented across the bilaterians, with one result below them; tier four arrives with vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. Tier four is the one that arrives late.

options.text: Tier three arrives with vertebrates and tier four with mammals, since each tier needs a larger brain than the one before.
options.why: Tier three is documented across invertebrate bilaterians, and tier four with vertebrates in general.

options.text: Both are found throughout the bilaterians and below them, so neither can be tied to any particular group of animals.
options.why: Tier three thins below the bilaterians and tier four is tied to vertebrates.

options.text: Tier three is found only in cnidarians and tier four only in bilaterians, so each tier belongs to one branch of the tree.
options.why: Tier three is widespread among bilaterians, with only one result below them.

items.stem: Is learning a vertebrate invention, on the chapter's account?

options.text: No. Most of learning is far older than the vertebrate, and what the vertebrate adds is bridging a delay.
options.why: Correct. The headline is the opposite of the expected one.

options.text: Yes. Invertebrates have reflexes that look like learning, but only a vertebrate brain can change a connection.
options.why: The worm changes connections, and so do the invertebrates in which tiers two and three are documented.

options.text: Yes, in part. Classical conditioning is found in invertebrates, but operant conditioning is a vertebrate invention.
options.why: Tier three is documented across the bilaterians, including invertebrates.

options.text: No. Learning is older than the vertebrate, and vertebrates add nothing new to what invertebrates can already learn.
options.why: Vertebrates do add something: tier four, bridging a delay.

items.stem: A student looks at the tiers placed against the animal tree and concludes that cnidarians are an early draft of the vertebrate. What do the chapter and the lecture say?

options.text: It says when capacities appear, not how to rank animals; cnidarians are a lineage that has been succeeding alongside ours.
options.why: Correct. Module 2's warning about reading the tree as a ladder applies here, and the lecture puts it in exactly those terms.

options.text: The conclusion is right, since cnidarians show fewer tiers and so represent an earlier stage of the same design.
options.why: Fewer tiers on current evidence is not an earlier stage of anything. Every surviving lineage has been evolving for the same length of time.

options.text: The conclusion is right about capacities but wrong about time, since cnidarians appeared only after the first vertebrates did.
options.why: Cnidarians are far older than vertebrates. The error is the draft reading, not the dates.

options.text: The conclusion cannot be judged, since the placement of every tier is contested and no conclusion follows from it.
options.why: Some placements are contested, but the chapter draws a firm conclusion: this is about when, not about rank.

items.stem: How settled is the timing of when tiers three and four first appear on the animal tree?

options.text: Contested for both, with tier three's the most uncertain of all, so neither can be pinned to a single date.
options.why: Correct. That is why both are marked as ranges rather than points, and why tier three's range is the widest.

options.text: Settled for both, since each tier's first appearance can be read directly from the fossil record.
options.why: Behavior does not fossilize, and the chapter treats both timings as contested.

options.text: Settled for tier three and contested for tier four, since tier three is the older of the two capacities.
options.why: Tier three's timing is the most contested, which is why it is the widest range.

options.text: Contested for tier three and settled for tier four, since vertebrates are the only animals studied for tier four.
options.why: Tier four's timing is contested too, though less than tier three's.

items.stem: Of the three problems that come with learning, which one belongs to every learner, whatever it is learning?

options.text: Stability versus plasticity.
options.why: Correct. The other two belong to a learner working out which of its actions lead to good outcomes.

options.text: Exploration versus exploitation.
options.why: Exploration versus exploitation belongs to a learner choosing among actions by their outcomes.

options.text: How far ahead to care about outcomes.
options.why: How far ahead to care belongs to a learner weighing outcomes of its actions over time.

options.text: Credit assignment across a delay.
options.why: Credit assignment is tier four's problem, not one of these three.

items.stem: What does exploration versus exploitation mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: The trade-off between taking an option already known to be decent and sampling one that might be better and might be worse.
options.why: Correct. Every attempt at one is an attempt not made at the other.

options.text: The trade-off between changing enough to learn something new and changing little enough to keep what was learned before.
options.why: That is stability versus plasticity, which belongs to every learner.

options.text: Counting an outcome for less the further in the future it lies, by applying a factor slightly below one for every step of delay.
options.why: That is discounting, the answer to how far ahead to care.

options.text: The problem of working out which of several actions was responsible for an outcome that arrived later on.
options.why: That is credit assignment, tier four's second problem.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The trade-off between taking an option already known to be decent and sampling one that might be better and might be worse".

options.text: exploration versus exploitation
options.why: Correct. It is the first of the three problems that come with learning.

options.text: stability versus plasticity
options.why: Stability versus plasticity is about how much a connection changes, not which option to take.

options.text: credit assignment
options.why: Credit assignment is about which action earned an outcome.

options.text: temporal-difference learning
options.why: Temporal-difference learning is a family of rules for learning from successive estimates, not a trade-off between options.

items.stem: A bee always returns to the first flower patch it found that gave a decent amount of nectar, and never tries another. What does the chapter say about this strategy?

options.text: It is stuck with the first adequate option it met, and no setting between exploring and exploiting is right in general.
options.why: Correct. Never sampling the uncertain option has a cost, and so does sampling it too much.

options.text: It is the right strategy in general, since a known decent option always beats an unknown one on average.
options.why: An unknown option might be much better. There is no setting that is right in general.

options.text: It is the wrong strategy in general, since an animal should always sample new options before settling on one.
options.why: Always sampling has its own cost: every attempt at the uncertain option is one not made at the reliable one.

options.text: It is not a learning problem at all, since the bee is simply following an inherited preference for the first patch it meets.
options.why: Choosing between a known and an unknown option by past outcomes is one of the problems the chapter says comes with learning.

items.stem: Why can an outcome arriving in ten seconds and an identical outcome arriving in ten days not count equally?

options.text: If they did, nothing would favor acting now over later, so some rate at which distant outcomes count for less is unavoidable.
options.why: Correct. The chapter gives this rate a name and a number later.

options.text: Because a later outcome is less certain to arrive, and an animal ought to count an uncertain outcome for less than a sure one.
options.why: Uncertainty is a reason people often give, but the chapter's argument is more basic: equal counting would leave no reason to act now.

options.text: Because an animal cannot remember an action for ten days, so the later outcome cannot be linked to anything it did.
options.why: That is a mechanism problem about bridging delays. The chapter's point here is about how outcomes should be weighed.

options.text: Because the later outcome will be smaller when it arrives, since outcomes shrink the longer they are delayed.
options.why: The outcomes are stipulated to be identical. Only how much they count differs.

items.stem: What does stability versus plasticity mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: The trade-off between changing enough to learn something new and changing little enough to keep what was learned before.
options.why: Correct. Every learner faces it, whatever it is learning.

options.text: The trade-off between taking an option already known to be decent and sampling one that might be better or worse.
options.why: That is exploration versus exploitation, which belongs to learners choosing among actions.

options.text: Mechanisms that hold total activity and total synaptic strength within a range, bounding what plasticity would drive to an extreme.
options.why: That is homeostatic plasticity, one mechanism that manages the problem rather than the problem itself.

options.text: A window during which experience has an outsized and lasting effect on how part of a nervous system ends up wired.
options.why: That is a critical period, one way a schedule of plasticity is carried out.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The trade-off between changing enough to learn something new and changing little enough to keep what was learned before".

options.text: stability versus plasticity
options.why: Correct. It is the one of the three problems that belongs to every learner.

options.text: exploration versus exploitation
options.why: That is the trade-off between a known option and an uncertain one.

options.text: homeostatic plasticity
options.why: Homeostatic plasticity is a set of mechanisms, not the trade-off itself.

options.text: critical period
options.why: A critical period is a window of heightened plasticity, one part of a schedule.

items.stem: One model's connections change completely with every experience; another's never change at all. What does the chapter conclude a real learner needs instead?

options.text: A setting between the two, probably on a schedule over a lifetime: plastic early and more fixed later.
options.why: Correct. The first model keeps nothing from yesterday; the second never learns.

options.text: The first model's setting, since a learner that changes completely with each experience is always fully up to date.
options.why: Always up to date means nothing from yesterday survives into this afternoon.

options.text: The second model's setting, since a learner that never changes can never forget anything it once knew.
options.why: A learner that never changes also never learns anything.

options.text: A setting halfway between the two, fixed for life, since any single compromise is as good as any other.
options.why: The chapter suggests the setting should move, being more plastic early and more fixed later.

items.stem: In what sense is stability versus plasticity a genuine trade-off?

options.text: In the Module 4 sense: two properties that cannot both be had at once, so gaining more of one costs some of the other.
options.why: Correct. A connection cannot at the same moment change freely and hold still.

options.text: In the sense that one of the two is always the better choice, and the trade-off is just a matter of discovering which.
options.why: A genuine trade-off has no answer that wins in general. That is what makes it one.

options.text: In the sense that a learner can have both at once, as long as it has enough synapses to split between the two jobs.
options.why: Having both at once is exactly what a genuine trade-off rules out.

options.text: In the sense that it only arises for vertebrates, since invertebrates never keep anything long enough to lose it.
options.why: It arises for every learner, whatever it is learning.

items.stem: Once the problems learning brings have been laid out, what mechanical question remains, and what mainly separates the candidate answers?
tags: what there is to learn from

options.text: What rule could move a weight so as to meet any of this; the candidates differ mainly in what they make the change depend on.
options.why: Correct. That is why the next step divides learning by what there is to learn from rather than by the tiers.

options.text: Which brain structure carries out each tier; the candidates differ mainly in which region of the brain they place each tier in.
options.why: Structures are deliberately left to a later module. The question here is about rules for changing a weight.

options.text: How many tiers an animal can learn at once; the candidates differ mainly in how many connections each one uses.
options.why: The number of tiers is not the open question. The rule that moves a weight is.

options.text: When in evolution each tier appeared; the candidates differ mainly in which animal they take to be the first learner.
options.why: That question has already been taken up. What remains is mechanical.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what the chapter means by saying Morgan's Canon has been applied asymmetrically to cnidarian learning, state the chapter's current verdict, and name one result that would help settle the question for classical conditioning in sea anemones.
items.answer: Morgan's Canon asks for the simplest explanation the evidence allows. The same controls that were run in the 2023 anemone and box jellyfish studies would convince anyone if they were run in an insect or a tardigrade. What makes people hesitate with cnidarians is a prior assumption about what a brainless animal ought to be able to do, which is doing work the data are supposed to do. The chapter's verdict is that the evidence is positive and the burden now sits with the skeptics, but the question is still open. For anemone conditioning, an independent replication in a second laboratory, or a retention test beyond ten minutes, would help settle it.
rubric: Explains that the same controls would be accepted in another animal group.
Identifies a prior assumption about brainless animals as what resists the conclusion.
States the verdict without closing the question: positive evidence, shifted burden, still open.
Names replication in a second lab or a longer retention test.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain the difference between the tiers of learning and the four things an animal can learn from, and why one list is ordered and the other is not.
items.answer: The tiers answer what there is to learn: one thing that keeps happening, two things that go together, an action and what followed, and terms separated by a long delay. Each adds a requirement to the one before, so they are ordered. The four things to learn from answer a different question: what the animal has to go on when a connection changes, which may be co-occurrence, the next thing that happened, a teacher's answer, or a verdict on how things went. These are not ordered. An animal with a teacher does not thereby have a verdict on good or bad, and one with a verdict does not thereby have a teacher.
rubric: Says the tiers concern what there is to learn and the four sources concern what there is to learn from.
Says the tiers are ordered because each adds a requirement.
Says the four sources are not ordered.
Gives the teacher and verdict example, or another showing neither source implies the other.

pools.title: Hebb's Rule, and What Coincidence Cannot Do
pools.covers: reading §5.2.1, §5.2.2, §5.2.3 · lecture 5.2 slides title, hebbs_rule, hebb_only_grows, coincidence_without_a_goal, three_things_coincidence_cannot_do · lab (Parts 1 and the learning-rate step)

items.stem: What constraint does the chapter say does most of the work in sorting the rules that can change a weight?

options.text: Whatever changes a weight can use only what is at the connection at that moment, so anything else has to be delivered.
options.why: Correct. A rule that needs only the two cells a connection joins is one kind of answer; one that needs a report from elsewhere is another, and much harder to arrange.

options.text: Whatever changes a weight has to act within a few milliseconds, so the rule that wins is whichever one runs fastest in real tissue.
options.why: Speed matters to the physical story, but it is not the constraint the chapter says does the sorting.

options.text: Whatever changes a weight has to be able to make it negative, so any rule that only adds can be discarded at once.
options.why: The basic Hebbian rule only adds and is still a real answer. The sorting constraint is about where information comes from.

options.text: Whatever changes a weight has to be present in every animal that learns, so a rule found only in vertebrates is ruled out.
options.why: Where a rule is found is a later question. The chapter's constraint is about what information is available at the connection.

items.stem: The lecture calls locality the property that makes Hebb's rule so attractive for a nervous system. Why is it attractive?

options.text: Everything the rule uses is already at the connection, so nothing has to be delivered to it from anywhere else in the animal.
options.why: Correct. The sending cell's activity is arriving there and the receiving cell's activity is right there. Nothing else is consulted.

options.text: It lets a weight change in either direction, so the connection can become excitatory or inhibitory as the animal's experience requires.
options.why: A basic Hebbian weight can only grow. Locality is attractive despite that, not because of it.

options.text: It guarantees that only useful pairings are strengthened, since a local rule cannot be fooled by coincidences.
options.why: Hebb's rule strengthens useful and useless pairings alike. Being local is exactly why it cannot tell them apart.

options.text: It lets the rule bridge long delays, since each connection can hold its own record until an outcome arrives.
options.why: Hebb's rule cannot bridge a delay at all. It works on simultaneity.

items.stem: What did Donald Hebb propose in 1949, often shorthanded as "neurons that fire together, wire together"?

options.text: When one cell repeatedly takes part in firing another, some growth process makes the first more effective at firing the second.
options.why: Correct. The shorthand captures it: correlated firing strengthens the connection between the cells.

options.text: When one cell repeatedly fires just after another, the connection between them weakens, so the second stops depending on the first.
options.why: Timing-dependent weakening is a later refinement, not what Hebb proposed. His proposal only strengthens.

options.text: When a cell fires and something good follows, a signal from elsewhere strengthens every connection that cell has made.
options.why: A signal from elsewhere about good outcomes is exactly what Hebb's proposal does not use.

options.text: When a cell repeatedly fails to fire another, the first cell grows new branches until it succeeds in triggering the second.
options.why: Hebb's proposal concerns cells that do succeed in firing each other together, not repeated failures.

items.stem: What does Hebb's rule mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A rule changing the weight between two neurons in proportion to how active both were at once, needing nothing beyond those two cells.
options.why: Correct. It is the simplest rule in the chapter, and its locality is both its strength and its limit.

options.text: A learning rule that changes a weight in proportion to the difference between a target output and the output produced.
options.why: That is the delta rule, which needs a target and computes a difference.

options.text: A rule in which the two cells' activity makes a synapse eligible to change, and a third signal from elsewhere settles whether it does.
options.why: That is the three-factor rule, which adds a signal from outside the two cells.

options.text: A lasting strengthening of a synapse, produced when the two cells it joins are repeatedly active together.
options.why: That is long-term potentiation, a physical change at a synapse rather than a rule stated at the algorithmic level.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A learning rule that changes the weight between two neurons in proportion to how active both were at the same time, and that needs nothing beyond the two cells the connection joins".

options.text: Hebb's rule
options.why: Correct. Written as Δb₁ = ηx₁y, it uses only what is at the connection.

options.text: delta rule
options.why: The delta rule needs a target output, which is not available at the connection.

options.text: three-factor rule
options.why: The three-factor rule needs a third signal delivered from elsewhere in the animal.

options.text: long-term potentiation
options.why: Long-term potentiation is a physical strengthening at a synapse, not a rule stated algorithmically.

items.stem: In Hebb's rule, written Δb₁ = ηx₁y, what does y stand for?

options.text: The receiving cell's own firing rate.
options.why: Correct. x₁ is the input cell's rate, b₁ the weight, and η the learning rate.

options.text: The input cell's firing rate as it arrives.
options.why: That is x₁, the sending cell's rate arriving at the connection.

options.text: The learning rate that scales the change.
options.why: That is η, a small number set for the rule.

options.text: The weight of the connection being changed.
options.why: That is b₁, the quantity whose change is written Δb₁.

items.stem: Under Hebb's rule with a learning rate of 1, an input cell fires at 10 and the receiving cell at 5 at the same time. By how much does the weight change?

options.text: It rises by 50, the product of the two rates.
options.why: Correct. The rule multiplies the two rates and the learning rate: 1 × 10 × 5 = 50.

options.text: It rises by 15, the sum of the two rates.
options.why: The rule multiplies the rates rather than adding them, which is what makes co-activity matter.

options.text: It rises by 2, the ratio of the two rates.
options.why: Nothing in the rule divides one rate by the other; it multiplies them.

options.text: It falls by 5, the difference between the two rates.
options.why: Hebb's rule never subtracts, and it does not take a difference.

items.stem: Under Hebb's rule with a learning rate of 0.1, an input cell fires at 20 and the receiving cell at 30 at the same time. By how much does the weight change?

options.text: It rises by 60.
options.why: Correct. The product of the rates is 600, and the learning rate takes a tenth of it.

options.text: It rises by 600.
options.why: That is the product of the rates with the learning rate left out.

options.text: It rises by 5.
options.why: That applies the learning rate to the sum of the rates, and the rule multiplies them.

options.text: It rises by 6,000.
options.why: That multiplies by ten rather than by a tenth.

items.stem: With a learning rate of 1, an input rate of 40 and a receiving rate of 2 raise a Hebbian weight by 80. What would an input rate of 2 and a receiving rate of 40 do, and what does that show?

options.text: Also raise it by 80, since only joint activity matters, not which cell fired harder.
options.why: Correct. The product is symmetric, so all that matters is joint activity.

options.text: Raise it by 42, since the rule adds the two rates once the input cell is the quieter of the two.
options.why: The rule multiplies the rates in every case. Nothing switches it to addition.

options.text: Raise it by 20, since the receiving cell's rate counts for less than the input cell's in the rule.
options.why: The two rates enter the product on equal terms.

options.text: Leave it unchanged, since a weight only grows when the input cell fires faster than the receiving cell.
options.why: The rule has no such condition. Any joint activity produces a positive change.

items.stem: What does learning rate mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A small number setting how much of the available change a rule takes on any one occasion.
options.why: Correct. A high rate follows the most recent occasion; a low rate averages over many.

options.text: A factor slightly below one applied for every step of delay, so that a distant outcome counts for less.
options.why: That is discounting, which weights outcomes by delay rather than scaling each change.

options.text: A fading mark left on whatever was recently active, so a later signal can find the connections involved.
options.why: That is an eligibility trace, a mark on a connection rather than a scaling factor.

options.text: An estimate of how well things will go from a given situation onward.
options.why: That is value, an estimate a learner can hold, not a number setting how far one occasion moves a weight.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A small number setting how much of the available change a rule takes on any one occasion. A high rate follows the most recent occasion; a low rate averages over many".

options.text: learning rate
options.why: Correct. Written η in the chapter's equations.

options.text: discounting
options.why: Discounting weights future outcomes by their delay.

options.text: plasticity
options.why: Plasticity is the tissue's capacity for lasting change, not a number in a rule.

options.text: prediction error
options.why: A prediction error is a gap between expected and actual, not a scaling factor.

items.stem: Why does a low learning rate ignore coincidences, while a high one is liable to treat an accident as a rule?

options.text: At a high rate one chance co-firing moves a weight as far as a hundred ordinary occasions at a low rate, where only repetition builds it.
options.why: Correct. How much a single occasion is allowed to matter is the whole job of the learning rate.
