options.text: At a high rate, the rule starts to subtract as well as add, and subtraction is what lets it tell an accident from a real relationship in the world.
options.why: Changing the learning rate changes the size of each step, not its sign. Hebb's rule never subtracts at any rate.

options.text: At a low rate, the rule compares each occasion with a prediction, and a prediction is what lets it discount a coincidence.
options.why: Hebb's rule makes no prediction and no comparison at any learning rate.

options.text: At a low rate, the firing rates of the two cells are themselves slower, so a single occasion produces less activity to multiply.
options.why: The learning rate leaves the firing rates untouched. The chapter's example keeps both rates at forty.

items.stem: For a rule like Hebb's, what does the stability-versus-plasticity trade-off turn out to be?

options.text: A single number, the learning rate.
options.why: Correct. How far one occasion may move a weight is exactly the choice between keeping the old and taking in the new.

options.text: A single number, the weight's upper limit.
options.why: A ceiling on a weight bounds how large it gets, but it does not set how much one occasion changes it.

options.text: The count of synapses each cell has.
options.why: Having more synapses does not set how much one occasion changes each of them.

options.text: It vanishes, since Hebb's rule never forgets.
options.why: Hebb's rule has the trade-off like any learner; its learning rate sets where it sits.

items.stem: Why is the change in a weight under Hebb's rule never negative?

options.text: Firing rates are never negative, and neither is the learning rate, so their product never can be.
options.why: Correct. Every occasion makes the weight grow, by a small amount or a large one.

options.text: Weights in a nervous system are never negative, so the rule was written to keep every weight above zero.
options.why: Module 3's model neuron already had a weight of −3. Negative weights exist; the rule just cannot reach one.

options.text: The rule includes a floor that stops any change from going below zero, so weights are protected from shrinking.
options.why: No floor is written into the rule. The sign follows from the arithmetic of three non-negative numbers.

options.text: Neurons in the chapter are all excitatory, so a connection between any two of them has to be strengthening.
options.why: Inhibitory connections exist in the course's models. The rule's arithmetic is what keeps the change positive.

items.stem: Module 3's model neuron had an inhibitory weight of −3. What difficulty does a weight like that pose for Hebb's rule?

options.text: Not that negative weights cannot exist, but that the rule cannot learn its way to one, since it only adds.
options.why: Correct. Module 3 already had a negative weight. What the basic rule cannot do is learn its way there.

options.text: That negative weights cannot exist in real neurons, so the rule has to be adjusted to keep them all positive.
options.why: Inhibitory connections are real. The chapter's point is about how one could be learned, not whether one can exist.

options.text: That a connection starting at −3 would flip to a positive weight on its first co-activation and then run away.
options.why: A connection with a negative weight rarely drives its target, so there is little co-activity for the rule to act on. Nothing flips it on the first occasion.

options.text: That a negative weight makes the rule subtract, so the connection would shrink without limit instead of growing.
options.why: The rule's change is set by the firing rates and the learning rate, all non-negative. The weight's own sign does not enter.

items.stem: What information does Hebb's rule consult when it changes a weight?

options.text: Only the sending cell's arriving activity and the receiving cell's own activity, both present at the connection.
options.why: Correct. No signal reports whether anything good happened, and none says what the receiving cell should have done.

options.text: The two cells' activity and a report of whether anything good happened, delivered from elsewhere in the animal.
options.why: A report of how things went is exactly what Hebb's rule lacks.

options.text: The two cells' activity and what the receiving cell should have done, supplied by some source that already knew the answer.
options.why: What the cell should have done is a teacher's information, which Hebb's rule never uses.

options.text: The two cells' activity and the animal's current state, such as whether it is hungry or has just been fed.
options.why: A modulator can change what a circuit does, but Hebb's rule itself consults only the two cells' activity.

items.stem: A rat hears a tone a moment before food arrives, over and over. Under Hebb's rule, what happens to the connection between tone-responsive and food-responsive cells, and what guided it?

options.text: It strengthens until the tone alone sends the rat to the tray, guided by nothing but the tone and food co-occurring.
options.why: Correct. No teacher labeled anything. A rule that responds to co-occurrence did the rest.

options.text: It strengthens until the tone alone sends the rat to the tray, guided by a signal that reports each meal as a good outcome.
options.why: No such signal is in Hebb's rule. The outcome did not guide it; the co-occurrence did.

options.text: It weakens until the rat ignores the tone, because the tone has been repeated many times without anything bad following.
options.why: The tone was always followed by food. The connection grows because the cells fire together.

options.text: It stays the same until the rat makes a mistake at the tray, after which it is corrected by the size of the mistake.
options.why: Correction by the size of a mistake is error-driven learning. Hebb's rule has no mistake to measure.

items.stem: A student writes: "The rat's neurons figured out that the tone means food". What is wrong with that, under Hebb's rule?

options.text: Nothing in the rule represents a goal or registers right or wrong; the fit is simply left over from co-activity.
options.why: Correct. The wiring ends up fitted to the world, which is what makes the agentic description tempting.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since the rat now behaves exactly as it would if it had figured out what the tone means.
options.why: The behavior may look the same, but the description credits the neurons with a goal and a verdict the rule does not contain.

options.text: The rat figured it out, but its neurons did not, since only a whole animal can understand a relationship like that.
options.why: The chapter's objection is to crediting any part of the process with working anything out, the rat included.

options.text: The neurons learned the relationship, but only after a teacher told them which pairing mattered, so they did not figure it out alone.
options.why: No teacher is involved. The link formed because the tone and food kept co-occurring.

items.stem: The chapter says Hebbian learning has the same structure as adaptation by selection, one level down and on a far shorter timescale. What is the shared structure?

options.text: A process with no foresight leaves a fit that looks like foresight: after differential survival, or after repeated co-activity.
options.why: Correct. The regularity in the wiring is what is left over, not what anything was aiming at.

options.text: Both are driven by a goal the organism holds, so each ends up fitting the world because the organism was trying hard to fit it.
options.why: Neither process contains a goal. That absence is the whole parallel.

options.text: Both work by eliminating the unfit, so Hebbian learning is selection among neurons, with the unhelpful ones dying off.
options.why: Hebb's rule strengthens connections; it does not kill cells. The parallel is about structure, not about death.

options.text: Both are driven by prediction error, so each corrects itself toward the world by measuring how wrong it has been.
options.why: Neither selection nor Hebb's rule computes an error. Error-driven learning comes later and is a different thing.

items.stem: Hebb's rule has no term for good or bad. How can an animal that does distinguish good from bad still make use of it?

options.text: When a cue and a good outcome co-occur a Hebbian link forms, making the animal likelier to repeat what it did at that cue.
options.why: Correct. The rule forms the link; the good outcome only has to be present for the co-occurrence.

options.text: It cannot, since an animal with good and bad has to replace Hebb's rule with a rule that includes a term for outcomes.
options.why: An animal can use a rule without a good-or-bad term; the good outcome simply has to co-occur with the cue.

options.text: The rule reads the animal's verdict on each outcome directly and strengthens only the links that were followed by good ones.
options.why: The rule reads no verdict. It strengthens whatever co-occurred, good or not.

options.text: The animal adds a negative term to the rule whenever the outcome is bad, so that bad pairings are unlearned.
options.why: The basic rule has no negative term, and the animal cannot add one to it.

items.stem: The chapter separates two jobs that learning with good and bad involves. What are they, and which one do the later rules mainly differ on?

options.text: Forming the link, and biasing which links count as good and by how much; the rules that follow differ mainly on the second.
options.why: Correct. Hebb's rule does the first job and leaves the second to something else.

options.text: Detecting the cue, and detecting the outcome; the rules that follow differ mainly in which of the two senses each one relies on.
options.why: Detection is done by sensory cells. The two jobs named are forming a link and biasing which links count.

options.text: Strengthening connections, and weakening them; the rules that follow differ mainly in whether they can do the first.
options.why: Every rule can strengthen. The separation the chapter draws is between forming a link and weighting it by good or bad.

options.text: Learning fast, and learning slowly; the rules that follow differ mainly in which learning rate they use.
options.why: Learning rate is one number any rule can have. The two jobs are forming a link and biasing it.

items.stem: What are the three limitations of Hebb's rule that the chapter names?

options.text: It is indifferent to outcomes, it cannot bridge a delay, and it cannot apportion credit across a sequence.
options.why: Correct. Each blocks something a learner was said to need.

options.text: It is indifferent to outcomes, it cannot respond to combinations, and it cannot work in an animal without a brain.
options.why: Responding to combinations and working without a brain are not among the three.

options.text: It needs a teacher, it cannot bridge a delay, and it cannot work unless the learning rate is set exactly right.
options.why: Hebb's rule needs no teacher at all, which is one of its attractions for a nervous system.

options.text: It is too slow for a nervous system, it forgets everything overnight, and it cannot apportion credit across a sequence.
options.why: Slowness and overnight forgetting are not the chapter's complaints. Only credit assignment matches.

items.stem: A rat hears a tone just before food, and over several hundred meals it also hears the ventilation fan just before food. Under Hebb's rule, what happens?

options.text: Both links form, and nothing marks either as the useful one, since no term in the rule refers to how things turned out.
options.why: Correct. Whatever was active together is wired together, whether the pairing mattered or merely happened.

options.text: Only the tone link forms, since the tone is the more informative cue and Hebb's rule strengthens whichever cue is most informative.
options.why: Hebb's rule has no measure of informativeness. It strengthens whatever co-occurs.

options.text: Only a weak fan link forms, since the fan hums all the time and a constant stimulus cannot be linked to anything.
options.why: The chapter's case has the fan occurring before food several hundred times, and that link forms too.

options.text: The tone link wins and the fan link fades, since the two compete for a fixed amount of strength at the food cells.
options.why: Competition for a limited resource is a separate mechanism that basic Hebb's rule does not include.

items.stem: Food is moved to arrive ten seconds after the tone. Why does Hebb's rule then fail to link them?

options.text: The two sets of cells are never active at once, so the product of their activity is near zero at every instant.
options.why: Correct. There is nothing for the rule to multiply, so nothing to strengthen.

options.text: The ten-second gap lets the tone's weight decay back to zero before the food arrives to strengthen it.
options.why: The rule has no decay term in its basic form. It fails because nothing is active at once.

options.text: The rat habituates to the tone during the ten-second gap, so the tone no longer drives any of its cells by the time food arrives.
options.why: Habituation is a separate process. The failure here is arithmetical: nothing coincides.

options.text: The food arriving late is treated as a punisher, so the rule subtracts from the tone's weight instead.
options.why: Hebb's rule never subtracts and has no notion of a punisher.

items.stem: The lecture calls Hebb's failure at delay the pivot of the whole lecture. Why does that failure carry so much weight?

options.text: Hebb's rule works on simultaneity, yet much of what an animal must learn is not simultaneous; the rules that follow exist to handle that.
options.why: Correct. The delay failure is what motivates the move to rules that can carry something forward.

options.text: It is the one limitation that cannot be fixed at all, so it marks the point where the lecture gives up on rules and turns to anatomy.
options.why: The lecture goes on to rules that do bridge delays. Nothing is given up.

options.text: It shows that Hebb's rule is wrong about how neurons work, so the lecture drops Hebb's rule entirely from that point on.
options.why: Hebb's rule remains in play; its failure at delay motivates additions, not abandonment.

options.text: It is the only one of the three limitations that applies to real animals, while the other two apply only to the machines people built to learn.
options.why: All three limitations apply to animals. The delay one is singled out because it drives what comes next.

items.stem: In a chamber, pressing a lever drops a pellet a moment later, and the rat then crosses to the food opening and noses in. Why can neither simple version of a coincidence rule credit the lever press properly?

options.text: Crediting only what was active at the meal misses the finished press; crediting the whole last minute credits grooming equally.
options.why: Correct. One version misses what mattered, and the other cannot tell it from what merely happened along the way.

options.text: Strengthening only what was active at the meal credits the press correctly, since the press is what caused the pellet to drop into the opening.
options.why: The press was over when food arrived. Causing the meal does not make it active at the meal.

options.text: Strengthening all of the last minute credits the press correctly, since the press happened within that minute.
options.why: It does credit the press, but it credits grooming and sniffing just as much.

options.text: Neither version can strengthen anything, since a rat's lever press is an action and coincidence rules can only link events.
options.why: Coincidence rules strengthen whatever is active together, actions included. The trouble is apportioning.

items.stem: The lever chamber shows Hebb's rule failing on which general problem of learning?

options.text: Credit assignment, working out which action was responsible for an outcome that arrived later.
options.why: Correct. It arises here as a problem for Hebb's rule in particular.

options.text: Exploration versus exploitation, choosing between a known option and an uncertain one.
options.why: The rat is not choosing between a known and an unknown option here.

options.text: Stability versus plasticity, changing enough to learn without losing what had been learned before.
options.why: That trade-off concerns the learning rate, not which action earned the food.

options.text: Habituation, the declining response to a stimulus that has been repeated without consequence.
options.why: Habituation is a kind of learning, not the problem the lever case exposes.

items.stem: The lecture sets a rule that needs only the two cells a connection joins against a rule that needs a report from elsewhere, and says the distinction will sort every rule it meets. What is being sorted?

options.text: Where a weight change's information comes from: already present at the synapse, or delivered by a signal from outside it.
options.why: Correct. That is the through-line of the lecture and the module: what a weight change depends on, and how far away that information is.

options.text: How fast each rule changes a weight: all at once on a single occasion, or gradually and in small steps over a great many occasions.
options.why: Speed is set by the learning rate, which any rule can have. The sorting is about where information comes from.

options.text: Which animals each rule is found in: those with a centralized brain, or those with a diffuse nerve net.
options.why: The distinction is about the information a rule uses, not the animals it is found in.

options.text: Whether each rule strengthens or weakens a weight: upward alone, or in both directions.
options.why: Direction of change matters, but it is not what this distinction sorts.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why Hebb's rule cannot arrive at an inhibitory weight by learning, and why the existence of negative weights is not itself the problem.
items.answer: Under Hebb's rule the change is the learning rate times the two firing rates. None of those can be negative, so the change is never negative: every occasion makes the weight grow. So a connection running the rule can grow without limit and can never shrink, and it cannot reach an inhibitory value. Negative weights do exist, since Module 3's model neuron already had one of −3. The difficulty is only that the basic rule cannot get there by learning.
rubric: Says the change is a product of the learning rate and two firing rates.
Says none of these is negative, so the change is never negative.
Concludes the weight can only grow and cannot learn its way to an inhibitory value.
Notes that negative weights exist, so the problem is reaching one by learning.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the parallel the chapter draws between Hebbian learning and adaptation by natural selection, and say why it makes agentic language wrong in both cases.
items.answer: Adaptation makes organisms look designed without anyone designing them, because adaptive fit is what is left over after differential survival. Hebbian learning has the same structure one level down and on a far shorter timescale: the regularity in the wiring is what is left over after repeated co-activity. In both, a process with no foresight leaves a result that looks like foresight. Because nothing in either process represents a goal or registers being right or wrong, saying that evolution figured something out, or that neurons learned what a tone means, credits the process with something it does not contain.
rubric: Describes adaptive fit as what is left over after differential survival.
Describes Hebbian wiring as what is left over after repeated co-activity.
States the shared structure: no foresight, a result that looks like foresight.
Explains that agentic language credits a goal or verdict neither process contains.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, name the three limitations of Hebb's rule and give a one-sentence example of each.
items.answer: First, it is indifferent to outcomes: a rat forms a link between a tone and food, and equally between the ventilation fan and food, and nothing marks one as useful. Second, it cannot bridge a delay: if food comes ten seconds after the tone, the two sets of cells are never active together, so there is nothing to multiply. Third, it cannot apportion credit across a sequence: if a lever press drops a pellet that the rat eats later, strengthening only what was active at the meal misses the press, and strengthening everything recent credits grooming just as much.
rubric: Names indifference to outcomes, with an example such as the fan.
Names failure to bridge a delay, with the reason nothing coincides.
Names failure to apportion credit, with an example such as the lever.
Each example fits the limitation it is given for.

items.stem: In the lab's poisoned dish, the food odor comes from a toxin and the rule on the Learning tab is Coincidence. Over four minutes, what did the food-odor weight and the harm counter do, compared with a run with learning switched off?

options.text: The weight climbed and never came down, and harm kept arriving at about the same rate as with nothing able to change.
options.why: Correct. Letting the weight change under a coincidence rule strengthened approach to the toxin and saved the animal nothing.

options.text: The weight fell toward zero after the first few poisoned meals, and harm stopped arriving once it had fallen far enough.
options.why: That is what a rule sensitive to outcomes would do. The coincidence rule has no term for how things went, so it never falls.

options.text: The weight climbed at first and then fell back once harm built up, so harm slowed but did not stop.
options.why: Under this rule the weight never goes down. There is nothing in it that harm could act on.

options.text: The weight did not move at all, since the rule changes a weight only when the animal is rewarded.
options.why: The rule moved the weight on every approach; it just moved it the wrong way for the animal.

items.stem: In the same poisoned dish under the Coincidence rule, the Chemistry tab's dopamine plot was watched while the animal ate poisoned meals. What did the plot do, and what effect did that have on the food-odor weight?

options.text: It dipped below zero at each bad meal, and the weight ignored it, since this rule listens to the receiving cell's own output.
options.why: Correct. Something in the animal registered that things went badly, and the rule was not listening to it.

options.text: It rose above zero at each meal, since eating anything at all counts as better than expected, and that rise is what drove the weight up.
options.why: The plot dipped at poisoned meals. And under this rule the dopamine signal plays no part in the change.

options.text: It stayed flat at zero, since dopamine only responds to food and the toxin is not food.
options.why: The plot did respond: it dipped below zero at each poisoned meal.

options.text: It dipped below zero at each meal, and each dip pushed the weight down a little, though not enough to save the animal.
options.why: The weight never came down under this rule. The dips were registered and unused.

items.stem: In the lab's dish where salt sites turn into food a moment after they are touched, the salt weight started at zero under the Coincidence rule. How did it grow?

options.text: Slowly at first, then much faster once salt alone could make the interneuron fire, until it reached the ceiling.
options.why: Correct. Once the receiving cell fires to salt, every salt touch is a coincidence, and the growth feeds itself.

options.text: Steadily by the same amount at every meal, from the first meal until it reached the ceiling.
options.why: The growth was not steady. It sped up once salt alone could fire the interneuron.

options.text: Quickly at first, then more and more slowly, leveling off well below the ceiling.
options.why: That is the shape of an error-driven rule approaching its target, not of this coincidence rule.

options.text: Not at all, since salt was a cue the animal ignored at the start, and an ignored cue can never gain any weight however often it is touched.
options.why: Salt was ignored at the start, but touching salt just before food paired it with the food.

items.stem: In the salt dish under the Coincidence rule, a second cue, almond odor, was added at every site alongside the salt. After three minutes, what did the weight trace show?

options.text: The salt and almond-odor weights were identical, lying on top of each other as a single line.
options.why: Correct. The rule had no way to tell which cue mattered; both co-occurred with food equally.

options.text: The salt weight grew and the almond weight stayed at zero, since salt had been paired with food first.
options.why: That would look like blocking. The coincidence rule does not block; it strengthens both.

options.text: The almond weight grew and the salt weight fell, since the newer cue replaced the older one.
options.why: Nothing in this rule makes one cue replace another.

options.text: Both weights stayed at zero, since two cues arriving together cancel each other out under this rule.
options.why: Both weights grew. The trace showed them exactly on top of each other.

items.stem: In the salt dish under the Coincidence rule, the interval between touching salt and the food's arrival was set to 10 seconds. After about five minutes, what had the salt weight done, and why?

options.text: It had barely moved from zero, because the salt was gone before the food arrived, so the salt term was zero at every meal.
options.why: Correct. The animal still ate, and salt still came before every meal, but nothing coincided.

options.text: It had reached the ceiling as usual, since salt still came before every meal and the rule rewards anything at all that precedes food.
options.why: The rule rewards what co-occurs, not what precedes. With a gap, there is nothing to multiply.

options.text: It had gone negative, since salt without food at the same moment is treated as a sign that food is absent.
options.why: This rule never subtracts. It simply had nothing to strengthen.

options.text: It had grown halfway, since a delayed pairing counts for half as much as a simultaneous one.
options.why: There is no partial credit for delay under this rule. The product is near zero at every instant.

items.stem: In the poisoned dish, the food-odor weight was set by hand to about −2, and the run was skipped ahead three minutes under the Coincidence rule. What did the rule do to that weight, and why?

options.text: Nothing: the receiving cell never fired, so the product the rule multiplies stayed at zero.
options.why: Correct. The animal avoided the toxin because a person set the weight, and the rule could neither reach nor move it.

options.text: It raised the weight back toward the positive values the rule prefers, undoing the hand setting.
options.why: With the receiving cell silent, there were no coincidences to strengthen anything.

options.text: It pushed the weight further negative, since avoiding the toxin went well for the animal.
options.why: This rule has no term for how things went, and it never subtracts.

options.text: It set the weight to zero, since the rule only allows weights between zero and the ceiling.
options.why: The weight stayed where it was set; nothing in the rule clips it to a range.

pools.title: Blocking, and Error-Driven Learning Discovered Twice
pools.covers: reading §5.2.4, §5.2.5 · lecture 5.2 slides blocking, error_driven, discovered_twice, when_error_language_is_earned · lab (blocking)

items.stem: A rat learns that a tone predicts food. Then a light is added, so tone and light arrive together and food still follows, for many trials. Tested on the light alone, what does the rat do?

options.text: Almost nothing, even though every light was followed by food and no food ever came without the light.
options.why: Correct. Every light was followed by food and no food came without one, and still the rat never learned that the light signaled food.

options.text: Respond strongly, since the light was followed by food on every trial and no food ever arrived without the light being present.
options.why: That is what a coincidence rule would predict, and it is exactly what the experiment shows does not happen.

options.text: Respond exactly as strongly as to the tone, since the two cues were presented together and so ended up with equal strength.
options.why: Equal treatment of the two cues is the naive expectation. The earlier training on the tone made the difference.

options.text: Respond about half as strongly as to the tone, since the two cues shared the food between them on every compound trial.
options.why: Sharing the outcome evenly is not the result. The light gains almost nothing at all.

items.stem: Why can a coincidence rule like Hebb's not explain the blocking result?

options.text: Light and food co-occurred as reliably as anything in the experiment, so a coincidence rule would have linked them.
options.why: Correct. Blocking is the case where the prediction of a coincidence rule fails outright.

options.text: Light and food never occurred at the same moment, so a coincidence rule would have had nothing to strengthen in the first place.
options.why: They did occur together, on every compound trial. That is what makes the result a problem for coincidence rules.

options.text: The light was too weak a stimulus to drive its cells, so a coincidence rule could not have strengthened anything from it.
options.why: Nothing in the design makes the light weak. The rat can plainly see it.

options.text: A coincidence rule would have linked the tone to the light instead, since those two were the cues that occurred together.
options.why: A coincidence rule would link those too, but that does not explain why the light fails to predict food.

items.stem: What kept the rat from learning that the light signaled food?

options.text: The food was already predicted by the tone when the light arrived, so nothing about the light was news.
options.why: Correct. The outcome held no surprise, and the chapter's explanation turns on that.

options.text: The light came too late on each trial, after the tone had already finished and the food was about to arrive.
options.why: Tone and light arrived together. The timing within a trial is not the explanation.

options.text: The rat had habituated to the light, having seen it many times with no consequence of its own following.
options.why: The light was followed by food every time, so it was never repeated without consequence.

options.text: The rat decided the light was redundant, and chose to pay attention to the tone that had predicted food first.
options.why: The chapter rejects the idea of a decision. There was simply almost nothing left to learn.

items.stem: What does blocking mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: The finding that a cue perfectly paired with an outcome goes unlearned when another cue already predicts it.
options.why: Correct. What gets learned tracks what was not already predicted.

options.text: The fading of a learned response when the outcome stops arriving, as new learning competes with the original association.
options.why: That is extinction, which concerns a response that was learned and is now losing its effect.

options.text: A decline in a response to a stimulus that has been repeated without consequence, restored at once by a novel stimulus.
options.why: That is habituation, a first-tier change with no second cue involved.

options.text: Competition among the synapses onto one cell for a limited shared resource, so that strengthening some weakens others.
options.why: That is synaptic competition, a physical mechanism rather than the behavioral finding.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The finding that a cue perfectly paired with an outcome is not learned about, when some other cue already predicts that outcome".

options.text: blocking
options.why: Correct. Learning tracks what was not already predicted.

options.text: extinction
options.why: Extinction is the fading of a learned response when the outcome stops.

options.text: habituation
options.why: Habituation is a declining response to one repeated stimulus.

options.text: renewal effect
options.why: The renewal effect is the return of an extinguished response in a new place.

items.stem: A dog has long known that its owner's car door slamming means a walk is coming. The owner starts jingling keys at the same moment as every slam, and walks still follow. Later the keys are jingled alone. What does the blocking result predict?

options.text: Little response to the keys, because the walk was already predicted by the slam whenever the keys were heard.
options.why: Correct. Pairing is not the point; the keys never carried news about the walk.

options.text: A strong response to the keys, since they were followed by a walk on every occasion they were heard.
options.why: That is the prediction of a coincidence rule, which blocking contradicts.

options.text: A strong response to the keys but none to the slam any longer, since the newer cue replaces the older one.
options.why: Adding a redundant cue does not undo what the first cue predicts. The slam keeps its strength.

options.text: A response to the keys whenever they are louder than the car door, since the rule favors the stronger stimulus.
options.why: Stimulus intensity is not what blocking turns on. Prior prediction is.

items.stem: What does the chapter say about whether blocking occurs outside mammals?

options.text: It is well documented in mammals; a honeybee case failed to replicate, so for invertebrates it is an open question.
options.why: Correct. As the lecture puts it, not a known yes and not a known no.

options.text: It is well documented in mammals and in honeybees, which shows that error-driven learning is shared across the bilaterians.
options.why: The honeybee result did not survive a replication attempt, so it cannot be cited as a demonstration.

options.text: It is known to be absent in all invertebrates, which shows that prediction error is a vertebrate invention.
options.why: Absence has not been shown either. The chapter's claim is that the question is unsettled.

options.text: It is well documented in the nematode, which is why the chapter chose that animal for its account of learning.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim of blocking in the nematode.

items.stem: What did Rescorla and Wagner's 1972 rule set out to explain?

options.text: Blocking: why a cue perfectly paired with an outcome can go unlearned.
options.why: Correct. Explaining blocking was a major challenge, and their rule met it.

options.text: Habituation: why a response declines to a stimulus repeated without consequence.
options.why: Habituation needs no link between events, and it was not the problem their rule addressed.

options.text: Credit assignment: which of a sequence of actions earned an outcome that came much later.
options.why: Their rule works trial by trial and does not address sequences of actions.

options.text: Extinction: why a response that fades after the outcome stops can later return.
options.why: Their rule was built for blocking. Extinction's return is a separate story in the chapter.

items.stem: In Rescorla and Wagner's rule, ΔV = αβ(λ − V), what do V and λ stand for?

options.text: V is how strongly the cue now predicts the outcome; λ is the strength this outcome would eventually support.
options.why: Correct. A large food delivery supports a large λ, and no food supports none.

options.text: V is the value of the outcome to the animal; λ is how long the animal has been trained on the cue so far.
options.why: V is the association's current strength, and λ is set by the outcome, not by the length of training.

options.text: V is the size of the food delivered on this trial; λ is the size the animal expected before the trial began.
options.why: The roles are reversed: λ stands for what the outcome supports, and V for what the animal already expects.

options.text: V is the learning rate for the cue; λ is the learning rate for the outcome that follows the cue on each trial.
options.why: The rate terms are α and β. V and λ are strengths.

items.stem: In Rescorla and Wagner's rule, what job do the rate terms α and β do?

options.text: They belong to the cue and the outcome and together do the job the learning rate did for Hebb.
options.why: Correct. They scale how much of the gap is taken on one trial.

options.text: They measure the gap between what the animal expected and what the outcome actually supported.
options.why: The gap is λ − V. The rate terms scale it.

options.text: They record whether the cue was present on the trial, one when it was and zero when it was not.
options.why: That role belongs to the input term, which drops out of the animal version.

options.text: They set the strength the association would eventually reach if the animal were trained without end.
options.why: That is λ, the strength the outcome supports.

items.stem: What does prediction error mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: The gap between what was expected and what occurred; in Rescorla and Wagner's rule, λ minus V.
options.why: Correct. When the two match, nothing changes.

options.text: A signal reporting that an outcome was better or worse than predicted, broadcast widely rather than to particular cells.
options.why: That is a reward prediction error, a broadcast signal carrying a prediction error about how things went.

options.text: A small number setting how much of the available change a rule takes on any one occasion it is applied.
options.why: That is the learning rate, which scales the change rather than measuring a gap.

options.text: An estimate of how well things will go from a given situation onward, held by a learner and updated.
options.why: That is value, an estimate rather than a gap between expected and actual.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The gap between what was expected and what occurred".

options.text: prediction error
options.why: Correct. In Rescorla and Wagner's rule it is λ − V.

options.text: reward prediction error
options.why: A reward prediction error is a broadcast signal about how things went, one particular carrier of a prediction error.

options.text: learning rate
options.why: The learning rate scales a change; it does not measure a gap.

options.text: value
options.why: Value is an estimate of how well things will go, not a gap.

items.stem: Why does it make sense to subtract V from λ and call the result a prediction error?

options.text: λ describes the outcome that arrived and V what was expected, on one scale, so the difference is arrived minus expected.
options.why: Correct. Two numbers on the same scale can be subtracted, and that particular difference is what a prediction error is.

options.text: λ and V are both rates of firing in the same cell, so their difference is how much the cell's activity changed on the trial.
options.why: Neither term is a firing rate. They are association strengths, one delivered and one expected.

options.text: λ is the largest value V can ever take, so the difference is simply how far the animal still has to go before it stops learning.
options.why: That is true as far as it goes, but it misses why the gap is an error: λ is what arrived and V what was expected.

options.text: λ and V come from two different animals, so the difference measures how much one animal knows that the other does not.
options.why: Both terms belong to one animal on one trial.

items.stem: On a trial where λ = 1, the cue's strength is already V = 0.6, and αβ = 0.5, how much does V change?

options.text: It rises by 0.2.
options.why: Correct. The gap is 1 − 0.6 = 0.4, and half of it is taken: 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2.

options.text: It rises by 0.4.
options.why: That is the whole gap, with the rate terms left out.

options.text: It rises by 0.3.
options.why: That multiplies the rate terms by V rather than by the gap between λ and V.

options.text: It rises by 0.08.
options.why: That takes a fifth of the gap rather than half of it. The rate terms here multiply to 0.5.

items.stem: After many tone trials, V for the tone has reached about 0.95 with λ = 1. A light is now added to the tone. How much change is available on that trial, and to which cues?

options.text: Roughly a twentieth of what the tone's first pairing allowed, and the same small amount for every cue present, the light included.
options.why: Correct. The gap is 0.05 against the first trial's 1, and it is the same gap for any cue on that trial.

options.text: The full amount for the light, since the light is new and its own strength still starts at zero, and just a twentieth for the tone.
options.why: The gap is set by the outcome and the total prediction, not by each cue's own history. Newness does not reopen it.

options.text: None at all for either cue, since the rule stops completely once V has come within a tenth of λ.
options.why: The rule does not switch off; a small gap still allows a small change.

options.text: A twentieth for the tone and nothing for the light, since only a cue that was present from the start can gain strength.
options.why: The rule applies to every cue present on the trial. The light gets the same small gap the tone does.

items.stem: A student explains blocking by saying the rat "decided the light was redundant and chose to ignore it". What does the chapter say instead?

options.text: No choice was involved; there was almost nothing left to learn while the outcome was already predicted.
options.why: Correct. The small gap falls out of the arithmetic, not out of a choice.

options.text: The rat did decide, but it did so without awareness, as an unconscious judgment that the light added nothing new.
options.why: Calling the decision unconscious keeps the decision. The chapter's point is that no decision is needed.

options.text: The rat failed to notice the light at all, since its attention was taken up entirely by the tone it already knew.
options.why: Nothing says the rat failed to see the light. The light was simply not news about the food.

options.text: The rat's light cells were exhausted by the tone training, so they could not fire strongly enough to learn.
options.why: Nothing exhausted the light cells. The explanation is the size of the prediction error.

items.stem: Under Rescorla and Wagner's rule, what happens on a trial where V already equals λ?

options.text: Nothing changes, since the animal got exactly what it expected.
options.why: Correct. With no gap there is no error and nothing to learn.

options.text: The change is as large as the rate terms allow, since the prediction has been fully confirmed.
options.why: The largest change comes when the gap is largest, on the first trial, not when it has closed.

options.text: V starts to decrease, since the rule always pulls a strong association back toward zero.
options.why: The rule pulls V toward λ, not toward zero. With V at λ it stays.

options.text: V keeps rising past λ, since each confirming trial adds a little more strength.
options.why: The rule changes V in proportion to the gap, and there is none.

items.stem: A cue's strength is V = 0.8. On the next trial the food is withheld, so the outcome supports λ = 0. What does Rescorla and Wagner's rule do, and what ability does that show which Hebb's rule lacks?

options.text: V decreases, since the gap is negative; unlike Hebb's rule, it subtracts when an outcome falls short.
options.why: Correct. No food supports no association, so λ − V is −0.8 and the change is downward.

options.text: V stays at 0.8, since the rule only acts on trials where an outcome arrives and there is nothing to learn from.
options.why: A missing outcome is information too. The gap between zero and 0.8 is large.

options.text: V increases a little, since the cue was still present and every presentation of a cue adds some strength.
options.why: That is how a coincidence rule would behave. This rule follows the gap.

options.text: V drops straight to zero, since a single omission cancels everything the cue had come to predict.
options.why: The change is scaled by the rate terms, so V moves part of the way toward zero, not all of it.

items.stem: What were Widrow and Hoff trying to do when they wrote their rule?

options.text: Build an adaptive electronic circuit whose output would come to match a desired one.
options.why: Correct. They called the desired output t, for target, and the actual output o.

options.text: Explain why a rat trained on a tone fails to learn about a light added to it.
options.why: That was Rescorla and Wagner's problem, which they took up twelve years later with a rat rather than a circuit.

options.text: Model how two neurons that fire together come to strengthen their connection.
options.why: That is Hebb's proposal, from 1949, which uses no target and no difference.

options.text: Program a machine to play checkers against itself and improve with practice over thousands of games.
options.why: That describes a later game-playing program, a different piece of history that used a different rule.

items.stem: What does delta rule mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A rule changing a weight in proportion to target minus actual output, scaled by that weight's input.
options.why: Correct. Delta is for the difference, which is what drives each change.

options.text: A rule that changes the weight between two neurons in proportion to how active both were at the same time.
options.why: That is Hebb's rule, which multiplies activities rather than using a difference.

options.text: A family of rules comparing each estimate against the next estimate the system itself produces.
options.why: That is temporal-difference learning, which uses the system's own next estimate as its target instead of a supplied one.

options.text: A rule where the two cells' activity makes a synapse eligible and a third signal from elsewhere settles the change.
options.why: That is the three-factor rule, which needs a signal from elsewhere rather than a target output.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A learning rule that changes a weight in proportion to the difference between a target output and the output actually produced, scaled by the input that weight carries".

options.text: delta rule
options.why: Correct. Widrow and Hoff named it for the difference.

options.text: Hebb's rule
options.why: Hebb's rule uses the receiving cell's activity, not a difference from a target.

options.text: temporal-difference learning
options.why: Temporal-difference learning compares estimates across time, not output against a supplied target.

options.text: three-factor rule
options.why: The three-factor rule gates eligible synapses with a third signal.

items.stem: The chapter says the delta rule differs from Hebb's rule in exactly one place. What is it?

options.text: Hebb multiplies the input by the receiving cell's activity; the delta rule multiplies it by how wrong that cell was.
options.why: Correct. Everything else — the learning rate, the input term — is shared.

options.text: Hebb uses a learning rate and the delta rule does not, so each step of the delta rule takes the whole of the error.
options.why: Both rules have a learning rate, η, scaling each change.

options.text: Hebb ignores the input rate and the delta rule includes it, so only the delta rule depends on the sending cell at all.
options.why: Both rules include the input rate x₁ as a factor.

options.text: Hebb changes weights only upward and the delta rule only downward, which is why the two are used together.
options.why: The delta rule can move a weight either way, depending on the sign of the difference.

items.stem: Under the delta rule with η = 0.5, a unit's target is t = 1, its output is o = 0.2, and its input is x₁ = 1. How much does the weight change?

options.text: It rises by 0.4.
options.why: Correct. (1 − 0.2) × 1 = 0.8, and half of that is 0.4.

options.text: It rises by 0.8.
options.why: That is the difference before the learning rate is applied.

options.text: It rises by 0.1.
options.why: That multiplies the learning rate by the output rather than by the error.

options.text: It rises by 0.04.
options.why: That takes a twentieth of the error rather than half of it.

items.stem: Set Rescorla and Wagner's rule beside Widrow and Hoff's delta rule. Which pairing of terms is correct?

options.text: λ matches the target t, V matches the output o, and α and β together match η.
options.why: Correct. What the world delivered is the target, and what the animal already expects is its output.

options.text: λ matches the output o, V matches the target t, and α and β together match η.
options.why: That swaps target and output. The outcome that arrived is the target, not the output.

options.text: λ matches the learning rate η, V matches the input x₁, and α and β together match the target t.
options.why: λ and V are strengths, not a rate and an input.

options.text: λ matches the input x₁, V matches the output o, and α and β together match the target t.
options.why: The input term has no counterpart in the animal version. λ is the target.

items.stem: The delta rule includes an input term, x₁, that does not appear in Rescorla and Wagner's rule. Why does it drop out of the animal version?

options.text: On a conditioning trial the input is one if the cue was present and zero if not, so it only selects which cues change.
options.why: Correct. Multiplying by one changes nothing, and multiplying by zero means that cue does not change.

options.text: Animals have no inputs in the relevant sense, since their cues arrive through senses rather than through weighted connections.
options.why: Cues do arrive as inputs; on a conditioning trial the input simply takes one of two values.

options.text: Rescorla and Wagner forgot to include it, and later versions of their rule put it back in its proper place.
options.why: The omission is principled. With a present-or-absent cue, the term does no work beyond selecting cues.

options.text: The input is folded into λ, since the strength the outcome supports already includes the cue's intensity.
options.why: λ is set by the outcome, not by the cue. The input term vanishes for a different reason.

items.stem: Two groups, one explaining a rat and one building a circuit, wrote down the same algorithm without knowing of each other. Which idea from Module 1 does the chapter say this makes checkable term by term?

options.text: Multiple realizability: one procedure, whether run in a rat or in wires, described at a level that mentions neither.
options.why: Correct. The algorithmic description is the same object in both, and it names no tissue and no wires.

options.text: Convergent evolution: two lineages that arrived at the same solution because they faced the same problem in their surroundings.
options.why: Two groups arriving at one answer independently does resemble convergence. What the chapter draws from it is that one procedure runs in either medium.

options.text: Reverse inference: reading the procedure off which part of a rat's brain is active when the rat learns about a cue.
options.why: Reverse inference is a move from brain activity to process. Nothing here involves brain imaging.

options.text: Homology: the rule is shared because rats and circuits inherited it from a common origin in earlier learning systems.
options.why: A rat and a circuit share no ancestry. The point is about levels of description.

items.stem: Why is "the system was wrong and corrected itself" a literal description of the delta rule, but not of Hebb's rule?

options.text: The delta rule holds an expectation and computes the difference driving the change; Hebb's rule registers no miss.
options.why: Correct. For the delta rule the error language describes the mechanism rather than being laid over it.

options.text: The delta rule changes weights much faster than Hebb's rule, so its changes look like corrections to an outside observer.
options.why: Speed has nothing to do with it. What matters is whether an expectation and a difference are in the mechanism.

options.text: The delta rule is used in machines and Hebb's rule in animals, and only machines can literally be said to be wrong.
options.why: Both rules can run in either medium. The chapter's test is what the mechanism contains.

options.text: Both rules are equally wrong and equally corrected; the phrase is simply more common in the engineering literature.
options.why: The chapter draws exactly this distinction and denies that the two rules are alike in it.

items.stem: The chapter says language about goals and errors earns its place only where something in the mechanism involves them. Which description earns it?

options.text: A heater that compares a set temperature with the room's and adjusts by the difference "corrects its error".
options.why: Correct. There is a represented target and a computed difference, which is what the rule asks for.

options.text: A Hebbian synapse that has strengthened after repeated co-activity has "fixed its earlier mistake" about the two cells it joins.
options.why: Nothing in a Hebbian synapse holds an expectation or computes a miss.

options.text: A population of insects that has become resistant to a pesticide has "corrected the error" in its ancestors' wiring.
options.why: Nothing in a population computes anything. The resistance is what differential survival left behind.

options.text: A sea anemone that has stopped withdrawing from a frond has "realized its mistake" about the frond being dangerous.
options.why: Habituation involves no expectation and no comparison, so there is no mistake to realize.

items.stem: What does gradient descent mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Measuring how wrong an output is, finding which way each weight must move to reduce it, and stepping a little that way.
options.why: Correct. It is the general method behind the delta rule.

options.text: Using one of a system's own estimates as the target for another, rather than waiting for the true outcome to arrive.
options.why: That is bootstrapping, which supplies a target but says nothing about stepping down a slope.

options.text: Counting an outcome for less the further in the future it lies, by applying a factor below one for every step of delay.
options.why: That is discounting, a way of weighting outcomes rather than of reducing an error.

options.text: Cutting back an early overabundance of connections, with activity deciding which of them survive to adulthood.
options.why: That is pruning, a developmental process rather than a method of reducing error.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A general method for reducing error: measure how wrong an output is, work out which direction each weight would have to move to make it less wrong, and take a small step in that direction".

options.text: gradient descent
options.why: Correct. For a single unit it is precisely the delta rule.

options.text: bootstrapping
options.why: Bootstrapping uses one estimate as another's target.

options.text: temporal-difference learning
options.why: Temporal-difference learning compares successive estimates of value.

options.text: discounting
options.why: Discounting weights outcomes by their delay.

items.stem: Plot one weight's value against how wrong the output is. What does the gradient at a point on that curve tell a learner?

options.text: How steeply the line rises or falls there: which way is downhill, and how big a step is worth taking.
options.why: Correct. Gradient means slope, and the slope gives both the direction and a sense of the step.

options.text: How far the output is from the target at that point, which is the same thing as the prediction error on that trial.
options.why: The height of the curve is how wrong the output is. The gradient is its slope.

options.text: How many steps remain before the lowest point is reached, counting from the current value of the weight.
options.why: The slope does not count steps. It gives the direction and a sense of step size.

options.text: Which of several weights matters most for the output, since the steepest weight is the one to change first.
options.why: On a one-weight plot there is only one weight. The gradient says how that weight should move.

items.stem: For a single unit, what is gradient descent the same thing as?

options.text: The delta rule.
options.why: Correct. Widrow and Hoff's rule is gradient descent's one-unit case.

options.text: Hebb's rule.
options.why: Hebb's rule computes no error, so there is no slope for it to descend.

options.text: Temporal-difference learning.
options.why: Temporal-difference learning compares successive estimates. It is not the one-unit case of gradient descent.

options.text: The three-factor rule.
options.why: The three-factor rule is a physical arrangement at a synapse, not the one-unit gradient method.

items.stem: Biologists draw an adaptive landscape for natural selection, with populations climbing toward greater fitness. What makes the delta rule different from that picture?

options.text: The delta rule computes a slope and moves along it; nothing in a population computes anything at all.
options.why: Correct. The landscape is in the biologist's description, not in the population.

options.text: The delta rule descends while selection climbs, so the two are really the same computing process run in opposite directions.
options.why: Up and down is a drawing convention. The difference is whether anything computes the slope.

options.text: The delta rule can only be drawn for machines, while an adaptive landscape can only be drawn for living populations.
options.why: A picture of this kind can be drawn over any process that extremizes something. Drawing it is not the difference.

options.text: The delta rule reaches the lowest point in one step, while a population needs many generations to reach the top.
options.why: The delta rule also takes small steps. The difference is not speed.

items.stem: The lecture sums up Rescorla and Wagner's rule as "learn in proportion to the surprise". In the rule's terms, what is the surprise?

options.text: The prediction error, λ minus V: what arrived minus what was expected.
options.why: Correct. A large surprise drives a large change, and no surprise drives none.

options.text: The outcome itself, λ: the bigger the food delivery, the bigger the surprise.
options.why: A big outcome that was fully expected produces no surprise and no change.

options.text: The rate terms, α and β: the faster the learning, the bigger the surprise.
options.why: The rate terms scale the change. The surprise is the gap they scale.

options.text: The association strength, V: the stronger the prediction, the bigger the surprise.
options.why: A strong prediction that is met leaves no surprise at all.

items.stem: Using Rescorla and Wagner's rule and the chapter's numbers, explain in a short paragraph why a light added to a well-trained tone gains almost no strength, even though it is perfectly paired with food.
items.answer: The rule changes an association in proportion to λ − V, what the outcome supports minus what is already predicted. With λ = 1, the first tone trial has V = 0, so the whole of λ is available to learn. After many trials the tone has driven V to about 0.95, leaving a gap of 0.05, a twentieth of the first trial's. That small gap is the same for every cue present, so when the light is added it can gain only a little. Nothing decided to ignore the light. The food was already predicted, so there was almost nothing left to learn.
rubric: States the rule's change as proportional to λ − V.
Uses numbers showing the gap shrinking from 1 to about 0.05.
Says the same small gap applies to every cue present, including the light.
Rejects a decision or attention story in favor of the arithmetic.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, map the terms of Rescorla and Wagner's rule onto the delta rule, and say what the correspondence shows about levels of description.
items.answer: The outcome the world delivered, λ, corresponds to the delta rule's target t. The strength already present, V, corresponds to the circuit's output o, what the animal currently produces by way of expectation. The rate terms α and β do the work of the learning rate η, and the input x₁ is one or zero on a conditioning trial, so it drops out of the animal version. One group was explaining a rat and the other building a circuit, and they wrote the same algorithm without knowing of each other. That is multiple realizability checked term by term: the procedure is the same whether run in a rat or a circuit, and its algorithmic description mentions neither.
rubric: Maps λ to t and V to o.
Maps α and β to η, and explains why x₁ drops out.
Notes the two groups worked independently.
Connects the correspondence to multiple realizability at the algorithmic level.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, state the chapter's rule for when error language is earned, apply it to the delta rule and to Hebb's rule, and explain why drawing an adaptive landscape does not earn it for natural selection.
items.answer: Language about goals and errors earns its place exactly where something in the mechanism involves them. The delta rule holds an expectation and a delivered outcome, and the computed difference drives the change, so "it was wrong and corrected itself" describes the mechanism. Hebb's rule holds no expectation and registers no miss, so the same words would be a story laid over it. An adaptive landscape looks like gradient descent turned upside down, but drawing the picture is not what matters. The delta rule computes a slope and moves along it; nothing in a population computes anything, and the climb is what differential survival leaves behind.
rubric: States the rule: error language only where the mechanism holds an expectation and computes a difference.
Applies it positively to the delta rule.
Applies it negatively to Hebb's rule.
Explains that the landscape is in the description, since a population computes no slope.

items.stem: In the lab's blocking dish, salt marks the food first, then almond odor is added at every site, and finally almond odor marks places on its own with nothing there. Under the Prediction rule, what did the almond weight and the animal do?

options.text: The almond weight barely moved, and in the last phase the animal ignored almond odor, as a rat ignores the light.
options.why: Correct. Food was already predicted by salt, so almond odor carried no news.

options.text: The almond weight grew to match salt, and in the last phase the animal sought out almond odor sites.
options.why: That is what happened under the Coincidence rule, which cannot block.

options.text: The almond weight grew and the salt weight fell, so in the last phase the animal sought out almond odor instead of salt.
options.why: Under Prediction, salt kept its strength and almond gained almost nothing.

options.text: Both weights fell to zero, since the compound of two cues predicted more food than arrived.
options.why: Salt held its level; only almond failed to gain.

items.stem: In the blocking dish's first phase, the salt weight stopped climbing near 1 under the Prediction rule, but ran to its ceiling under the Coincidence rule. What explains the difference?

options.text: Under Prediction, once salt fully predicted the food no error was left to learn from; Coincidence has no such stopping point.
options.why: Correct. The error term closes as the prediction catches up. A coincidence rule keeps multiplying.

options.text: Under Prediction the learning rate is lower, so the weight simply ran out of time before it could climb all the way to the ceiling.
options.why: The weight did not run out of time; it stopped because what arrived and what was predicted matched.

options.text: Under Coincidence the animal ate more food, and more meals always push a weight higher.
options.why: The animal's meals are not what separates the two. The rules' arithmetic is.

options.text: Under Prediction the weight was bounded by competition, which is always on under that rule.
options.why: The bounds were not what stopped it. The prediction error reaching zero did.

pools.title: Where the Target Comes From, and Four Kinds of Learning
pools.covers: reading §5.2.6, §5.2.7 · lecture 5.2 slides where_the_target_comes_from, four_kinds, the_ranking_is_backward · lab (four signals, one problem)

items.stem: What does the delta rule need that Hebb's rule does not?

options.text: A target: a statement of what the output should have been, on this occasion, for this input.
options.why: Correct. That is a nontrivial piece of information to have lying around.

options.text: A learning rate: a small number setting how much of the possible change is made on any one occasion.
options.why: Both rules have a learning rate. The target is what the delta rule adds.

options.text: An input rate: the activity of the sending cell arriving at the connection at the moment of change.
options.why: Both rules use the input rate. It is already at the connection.

options.text: A decay term: a steady weakening of every connection that keeps the weights from growing without any limit at all.
options.why: Neither rule, as written, has a decay term. The delta rule's addition is a target to compare against.

items.stem: The obvious source of a target is a teacher. Why is that a poor bet for a nervous system?

options.text: Animals are not well supplied with teachers; very little an animal must get right arrives with its answer attached.
options.why: Correct. A teacher is something that already holds the right answer and can hand it over, and that is rare inside an animal.

options.text: A teacher's answers arrive too slowly to be of use, since by the time they come the connection has already changed.
options.why: Speed is not the problem. The problem is that the answer rarely exists to be handed over at all.

options.text: A teacher can only correct weights that are already negative, so it would do nothing for the connections that most need it.
options.why: Nothing restricts a teacher to one sign of weight. The difficulty is having one.

options.text: A teacher would make every animal learn the same thing, so no individual could ever adapt to its own particular surroundings.
options.why: Uniformity is not the chapter's objection. Scarcity of anything that holds the answer is.

items.stem: A system predicts its upcoming input, holds that prediction until the input arrives, and compares the two. Where has its target come from?

options.text: From the world itself: the next thing that occurred served for comparison, and nothing had to know the answer in advance.
options.why: Correct. It manufactured its own target out of the world, and the rule is the same rule with a different supplier.

options.text: From a teacher inside the system, which stored the correct input in advance and released it at the very moment of comparison.
options.why: Nothing held the answer in advance. The world supplied it by going on to its next moment.

options.text: From the system's own weights, which already contain the right answer and simply confirm it when the input arrives.
options.why: The weights produced the prediction. The target is what then arrived.

options.text: From a verdict on how things went, a single number reporting whether the prediction had turned out good or bad.
options.why: A verdict says only how things went. Here the target is a specific input.

items.stem: What does prediction learning mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Error-driven learning whose target is the next input, supplied by the world unasked, so a prediction must be made beforehand and held.
options.why: Correct. The holding is what earns it a name of its own.

options.text: Error-driven learning whose target is the correct output, supplied by a source that already holds the answer and hands it over to the learner.
options.why: That is supervised learning, the teacher case.

options.text: Learning in which the weight between two cells changes in proportion to how active both were at the same moment.
options.why: That is Hebbian learning, which holds nothing and compares nothing.

options.text: Learning driven by one number reporting how things went, attached to no particular output and naming no better response.
options.why: That is reinforcement learning, the verdict case.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Error-driven learning in which the target is the next input, supplied by the world unasked, which requires that a prediction be generated before that input arrives and held until it does".

options.text: prediction learning
options.why: Correct. Machine learning calls it self-supervised.

options.text: reward prediction error
options.why: A reward prediction error is a broadcast signal about how things went, not a kind of learning whose target is the next input.

options.text: bootstrapping
options.why: Bootstrapping uses one of the system's own estimates as a target, not the world's next input.

options.text: temporal-difference learning
options.why: Temporal-difference learning compares successive estimates of value, a related but different thing.

items.stem: Prediction learning uses the same rule as learning from a teacher and differs only in where the target comes from. Why does it still earn a name of its own?

options.text: Its source changes what a solution must have: an expectation formed before the input arrives and held until it does.
options.why: Correct. That is the Opening's naming rule applied, since none of the other rules require anything to be held.

options.text: Its source makes the rule harder to run, and any version of a rule that is harder to run is given a name of its own.
options.why: Being harder is exactly what the naming rule says does not earn a name.

options.text: Its source is found only in vertebrates, and every kind of learning restricted to one group of animals is named separately.
options.why: Nothing restricts prediction learning to vertebrates, and animal group is not the naming rule's test.

options.text: Its source works at a different Marr level from a teacher, since the world is physical and a teacher is algorithmic.
options.why: Both are sources of a target at the same level. The difference is what must be held.

items.stem: A student argues that Hebb's rule is prediction learning, since a strong weight b₁ amounts to a prediction that the receiving cell will fire. What does the chapter say?

options.text: Nothing in Hebb's rule is generated in advance, held or compared, so calling b₁ a prediction is our description, not the mechanism's.
options.why: Correct. It is our description in the same way the adaptive landscape is the biologist's.

options.text: The student is right, since any weight that makes one cell likely to fire another is a prediction, whatever rule happened to produce it.
options.why: The chapter declines this reading, because nothing in the rule plays the part of a held prediction.

options.text: The student is right only at a high learning rate, since a large weight change is a prediction and a small one is not.
options.why: The learning rate does not create a held prediction. The rule's arithmetic stays a product of two present quantities.

options.text: The student is wrong because Hebb's rule changes weights only downward, and predictions have to be able to grow.
options.why: Hebb's rule only grows weights. The student is wrong for a different reason.

items.stem: Where does Rescorla and Wagner's rule fall among the kinds of learning?

options.text: It has been prediction learning all along: the association predicts food, a moment passes, and the world supplies the answer.
options.why: Correct. The target is the outcome the world delivers, so no teacher was ever involved.

options.text: It is supervised learning, since an experimenter decides on every trial whether food is delivered and so acts as the teacher.
options.why: The experimenter arranges the world, but what supplies the target is the outcome itself, arriving a moment later.

options.text: It is Hebbian learning, since the cue and the food occur close together and the rule strengthens what occurs together.
options.why: Blocking is exactly where Rescorla and Wagner's rule departs from a coincidence rule.

options.text: It is reinforcement learning, since food is a good outcome and the rule is driven by how good the outcome was.
options.why: The rule compares a specific predicted strength with a specific delivered one, not one verdict about how things went.

items.stem: A visual system predicts where a moving edge will be a moment from now, then adjusts using where the edge actually turns up. What kind of learning is this, in the chapter's terms?

options.text: Prediction learning, with no teacher and no labels: the edge's actual position is the target.
options.why: Correct. The chapter uses exactly this example of the same shape away from conditioning.

options.text: Supervised learning, since the true position of the edge is the correct answer that a teacher inside the eye supplies.
options.why: The true position is supplied by the world a moment later, not by anything that held the answer in advance.

options.text: Reinforcement learning, since getting the edge's position right is a good outcome that the system is rewarded for.
options.why: The system compares a specific predicted position with a specific actual one, not a verdict about how things went.

options.text: Hebbian learning, since the cells for neighboring positions fire close together and so wire together.
options.why: That describes a coincidence, but the case has a held prediction and a compared outcome.

items.stem: Why can a large language model be trained on huge amounts of text that nobody has labeled?

options.text: Its target is the next word, which the text supplies about itself, so no one has to annotate anything.
options.why: Correct. It is prediction learning, and the target is manufactured from the input stream.

options.text: Its target is a verdict on whether each sentence was good, which the text supplies through its punctuation.
options.why: A single verdict per sentence is not what the training uses. The target is the specific next word.

options.text: Its weights are set by Hebb's rule, which needs no target, so labels would never have been of any use to it.
options.why: Language models are trained against a target, the next word. That is what makes them prediction learners.

options.text: Its labels are added automatically by a second model that already knows the right answer for every sentence.
options.why: Nothing needs to know the answer in advance. The next word in the text is the answer.

items.stem: The rules in the chapter differ from one another in exactly one respect. Which?

options.text: What information has to be present, at the moment of change, for a weight to move at all.
options.why: Correct. That is the second of the two crossed questions, what there is to learn from.

options.text: How large a change each rule makes to a weight on any one occasion, and how quickly it settles.
options.why: That is set by a learning rate, which any rule can have.

options.text: Which animals each rule is found in, from the earliest nervous systems to vertebrates with large brains.
options.why: The four kinds are sorted by information, not by animal group.

options.text: Which Marr level each rule belongs to, from the computational down to the implementational one.
options.why: All four are rules stated at the algorithmic level.

items.stem: Which kind of learning needs only one number reporting how things went, attached to no particular output and carrying no indication of what would have worked instead?

options.text: reinforcement learning
options.why: Correct. It is the verdict case, and a body can supply such a number easily.

options.text: supervised learning
options.why: Supervised learning needs the specific correct output from a teacher, not one number about how things went.

options.text: prediction learning
options.why: Prediction learning needs the next input, a specific target.

options.text: Hebbian learning
options.why: Hebbian learning needs only the two cells a connection joins, and no report at all.

items.stem: Which kind of learning needs a statement of what the output should have been, from a source that already holds it?

options.text: supervised learning
options.why: Correct. It is the teacher case, the hardest of the four for a nervous system to arrange.

options.text: reinforcement learning
options.why: Reinforcement learning needs only a verdict on how things went, not the correct output.

options.text: prediction learning
options.why: Prediction learning's target is supplied by the world a moment later, not by a source that already holds it.

options.text: Hebbian learning
options.why: Hebbian learning needs no target of any kind.

items.stem: Which of these is reinforcement learning in the chapter's sense?

options.text: A young animal tries an unfamiliar food, and its only feedback is how full and well it feels afterward.
options.why: Correct. One number about how things went, attached to no particular output and naming no better choice.

options.text: A robot arm is told after each reach exactly where its hand should have ended up, and adjusts toward that spot.
options.why: Being told the correct output is supervised learning.

options.text: A system predicts the next frame of a video, then adjusts using the frame that actually appears after it.
options.why: The next frame is a target the world supplies, which makes this prediction learning.

options.text: Two cells that are often active together at the same moment come to strengthen the connection between them.
options.why: Strengthening by co-activity is Hebbian learning.

items.stem: How are the four kinds of learning related to one another, according to the chapter?

options.text: They are four different situations an animal can be in, and nothing makes them a sequence.
options.why: Correct. A teacher does not bring a verdict with it, and a verdict does not bring a teacher.

options.text: They are four stages each learner passes through in order, starting from Hebbian learning and ending with supervised learning.
options.why: Nothing makes them stages. They are situations defined by what information is available.

options.text: They are four levels of intelligence, with reinforcement learning at the top because it needs the least information.
options.why: The chapter declines any ranking of this kind, and needing little information is not being more intelligent.

options.text: They are four names for one process, which differ only in the vocabulary of the fields that studied it.
options.why: They differ in what a weight change depends on, which is a real difference in the mechanism.

items.stem: What does the chapter mean when it calls prediction learning self-supervised?

options.text: The target is manufactured out of the input stream itself, so no separate teacher is needed.
options.why: Correct. The world's next input plays the part a teacher would otherwise play.
