options.text: The learner supervises its own behavior by judging each action good or bad as it happens.
options.why: Judging actions good or bad is the verdict case, reinforcement learning.

options.text: The learner has no target at all and learns only which inputs tend to occur together.
options.why: That describes unsupervised Hebbian learning.

options.text: The learner writes its own labels using a stored copy of the right answers learned from a teacher earlier in life.
options.why: No stored answers are involved. The next input supplies the target.

items.stem: Why is Hebbian learning called unsupervised?

options.text: There is no teacher because there is no target at all, only the picking up of correlated structure in the input.
options.why: Correct. It differs from the other three in having no target of any kind.

options.text: There is a target, but it is supplied by the world rather than by a teacher, one moment after the input arrives.
options.why: That describes prediction learning, which is self-supervised.

options.text: There is a teacher, but it only reports how things went rather than what the right output would have been.
options.why: That describes reinforcement learning, where a verdict takes the place of a teacher.

options.text: There is a target, but the learner ignores it until enough co-activity has built up to make the target worth using.
options.why: Hebbian learning has no target to ignore; it only multiplies activities.

items.stem: Supervised, prediction and reinforcement learning are often grouped as learning from a teaching signal. When is that grouping fair, according to the chapter?

options.text: As long as it stays clear how different the three signals are from one another.
options.why: Correct. A correct output, the next input and a verdict are very different things to have available.

options.text: When all three are run by the same kind of cell, so that one teaching signal can serve each of them in turn.
options.why: The grouping is about the presence of a signal, not the cells that carry it.

options.text: When Hebbian learning is included as a fourth, since it too learns from a signal delivered by the world.
options.why: Hebbian learning is excluded precisely because it has no teaching signal at all.

options.text: Never, since the three kinds share nothing and the term hides the fact that none of them uses a target.
options.why: Two of the three do use a target. The chapter allows the grouping with a caution.

items.stem: Ranked from easiest to hardest for a body to arrange the information it needs, how do the four kinds of learning come out?

options.text: Hebbian, then prediction, then reinforcement, then supervised.
options.why: Correct. The order comes out backward from the one most readers expect.

options.text: Supervised, then prediction, then reinforcement, then Hebbian.
options.why: That is roughly the expected order, and the chapter says the real one runs the other way.

options.text: Hebbian, then supervised, then prediction, then reinforcement.
options.why: Supervised learning is the hardest by a wide margin, not the second easiest.

options.text: Reinforcement, then Hebbian, then supervised, then prediction.
options.why: Hebbian learning needs nothing beyond the connection, so it is the easiest of all.

items.stem: Why is the information reinforcement learning needs easy for a body to supply?

options.text: It needs one number, and bodies generate such numbers readily: a full stomach, a rise in blood sugar, a pain signal.
options.why: Correct. One broadcast quantity is enough.

options.text: It needs the correct output, and a body stores the correct output for every action in its genes from birth onward.
options.why: Reinforcement needs no correct output. That would be a teacher, which is the hard case.

options.text: It needs nothing beyond the two cells a connection joins, so nothing has to be generated anywhere else in the animal's body.
options.why: That describes Hebbian learning. Reinforcement needs a report from elsewhere, if only one number.

options.text: It needs the next input, which the world delivers a moment later whether or not anything asks for it to arrive.
options.why: That describes prediction learning, whose target is a specific next input.

items.stem: Why is a teacher the hardest of the four kinds of information for a nervous system to arrange?

options.text: Something inside the animal would already have to hold the right output and deliver it to the connections that erred.
options.why: Correct. Both the answer and its delivery to the right connections have to exist.

options.text: A teacher's signal is a single number, and single numbers are hard for a body to generate reliably at the right moment.
options.why: One number is the reinforcement case, and the chapter calls that easy.

options.text: A teacher's signal has to be predicted in advance and held until it arrives, which no other kind of learning needs.
options.why: Holding a prediction is prediction learning's requirement, which the chapter calls easy.

options.text: A teacher's signal only works at the implementational level, so it cannot be described by a rule at all.
options.why: Supervised learning is a rule like the others, stated at the algorithmic level.

items.stem: Someone who learned machine learning first expects supervised learning to be the simple case. Why, according to the lecture, is that expectation natural but wrong for a nervous system?

options.text: On a computer we already have the labels and simply hand them over; inside an animal the answer rarely exists.
options.why: Correct. The lecture calls this inversion the most transferable single fact in the module.

options.text: Supervised learning really is simplest for both, and the lecture only claims that it is less often studied in animals.
options.why: The lecture says the order flips: in a nervous system supervised learning is the exotic case.

options.text: Supervised learning is hardest on a computer too, and the expectation comes from textbooks listing it first by accident.
options.why: On a computer it is simple, because the labels exist. That is why the expectation is natural.

options.text: Supervised learning is simple for a nervous system, and only reinforcement learning is harder in animals than in machines.
options.why: The lecture places supervised learning at the hard end for animals, not reinforcement.

items.stem: What can Hebbian learning and prediction learning each NOT learn, according to the chapter's comparison of the four kinds?

options.text: Hebbian learning cannot learn whether a result was good; prediction learning cannot learn what the world never reveals.
options.why: Correct. Each is limited by the information it has.

options.text: Hebbian learning cannot learn which things go together; prediction learning cannot learn how one moment follows the next.
options.why: Those are exactly what each of them can learn.

options.text: Hebbian learning cannot learn anything quickly; prediction learning cannot learn anything without a teacher first.
options.why: Speed is set by a learning rate, and prediction learning needs no teacher.

options.text: Hebbian learning cannot learn in invertebrates; prediction learning cannot learn in any animal without a large brain.
options.why: The comparison is about information, not animal groups.

items.stem: An animal's only feedback after a failed leap between branches is a sharp pain. What can it NOT learn directly from that feedback alone?

options.text: What it should have done instead.
options.why: Correct. A verdict says how things went and names no better response.

options.text: That the leap it just made led to a bad outcome.
options.why: That is exactly what a verdict can teach: which actions lead to good or bad outcomes.

options.text: That leaps of this kind are worth doing less often in the future.
options.why: Making a punished action less likely is what a verdict can do.

options.text: That the pain came after its own action rather than just happening.
options.why: Linking an outcome to its own action is a tier-three matter, and the verdict can support it.

items.stem: What does supervised learning offer that the other kinds lack, and what is its limit?

options.text: It learns any mapping a teacher can specify, quickly and precisely, and nothing for which no answer exists.
options.why: Correct. Its power and its limit both come from the teacher.

options.text: It learns which things go together without any target at all, and nothing about whether the result was any good.
options.why: That is Hebbian learning's profile, which has no teacher at all.

options.text: It learns how one moment follows another, and nothing the world never eventually reveals to the learner.
options.why: That is prediction learning's profile, with the world as its teacher.

options.text: It learns which actions lead to good outcomes, and not directly what should have been done instead.
options.why: That is reinforcement learning's profile, where only a verdict is available.

items.stem: The lecture reads one axis through the four kinds of learning: how far away the information a weight change depends on has to come from. Where does each fall?

options.text: At the connection for Hebb; a specific target per output for prediction and supervision; one broadcast number for reinforcement.
options.why: Correct. The axis is the module's through-line: what a weight change depends on, and how far away that is.

options.text: At the connection for supervision; a target from the world for prediction; a broadcast number for Hebb and for reinforcement.
options.why: Supervision's target comes from a source that holds the answer, and Hebb needs nothing broadcast.

options.text: At the connection for all four, since every rule in the end changes a weight using only what the synapse itself can register locally.
options.why: Only Hebb's rule manages with what is at the connection. The others need something delivered.

options.text: Far away for Hebb, since its correlations span the whole brain; close by for the other three, which use a nearby target.
options.why: Hebb's rule is the local one. The others reach further.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, rank the four kinds of learning by how hard their required information is for a body to arrange, and explain why the ranking surprises people who know machine learning.
items.answer: Hebbian learning is easiest, since it needs nothing that is not already at the connection. Prediction learning needs nothing the world is not already delivering. Reinforcement learning needs one number about how things went, and a body generates such numbers easily, from a full stomach or a pain signal. Supervised learning is hardest by a wide margin, because something inside the animal would already have to hold the correct output and deliver it to the connections that produced the wrong one. People who meet supervised learning first in machine learning expect it to be simple, because on a computer the labels exist and are handed over. In a nervous system it is the exotic case.
rubric: Gives the order Hebbian, prediction, reinforcement, supervised.
Justifies reinforcement as easy because one number is enough.
Justifies supervised as hardest because the answer must already exist and be delivered.
Explains the surprise: on a computer the labels already exist.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how prediction learning differs from learning with a teacher, why that difference earns it a name of its own, and why Hebb's rule is not a case of it.
items.answer: Prediction learning uses the same error-driven rule as learning with a teacher. It differs only in where the target comes from: the next input, which the world supplies unasked, rather than a source that already holds the answer. That difference earns a name because it changes what a solution must have. The prediction has to be generated before the input arrives and held until it does, and no other rule needs anything held. Hebb's rule is not a case of it. Nothing in Hebb's rule is generated in advance, held, or compared, so calling a Hebbian weight a prediction is our description rather than the mechanism's.
rubric: Says prediction and supervised learning share a rule and differ in the target's source.
Says the prediction must be generated beforehand and held, which no other rule needs.
Ties the name to the naming rule: a changed requirement on the solution.
Explains that Hebb's rule generates, holds and compares nothing.

items.stem: In the lab's dish with two salt sites and two almond sites, one kind holding food, the rule was set to Teacher. Where did the weights settle, and where did the target come from, according to the panel?

options.text: They stopped short of 1, and the target was supplied by the scenario; nothing inside the animal held it.
options.why: Correct. The lab could supply a teacher only from outside, which is the point about how hard a teacher is to arrange.

options.text: They ran to the ceiling, and the target was supplied by the animal's own dopamine cells.
options.why: The Teacher setting's target does not come from dopamine; the panel says the scenario supplies it.

options.text: They stayed at zero, since a teacher only corrects a weight after the animal has already made a clear mistake of some kind.
options.why: The weights did move, toward the target the scenario supplied.

options.text: They stopped short of 1, and the target was supplied by the next input the world delivered.
options.why: That would be Prediction, whose target is the next input. Teacher's comes from the scenario.

items.stem: In the same two-cue dish, the rule was set to Coincidence, and after three minutes a switch flipped which cue marks the food. What did the two weights do?

options.text: Both had run to the ceiling, and both stayed there after the flip.
options.why: Correct. The rule could not tell the food cue from the empty one, and could not let go of either.

options.text: The food cue's weight rose and the empty cue's stayed at zero, and they swapped after the flip.
options.why: That tracking belongs to rules that use outcomes, such as Prediction or Verdict.

options.text: Both stayed at zero, since neither cue was paired with food often enough to strengthen.
options.why: Both cues were touched near food often enough for coincidences to build them up.

options.text: Both rose, then both fell back to zero after the flip, since the flip changed what the world does.
options.why: This rule never lowers a weight, so the flip changed nothing.

pools.title: Bridging the Delay, and Assigning the Credit
pools.covers: reading §5.2.8 · lecture 5.2 slides bridging_the_delay, actor_critic_and_the_trace · lab (the corridor)

items.stem: Error-driven learning repairs one of Hebb's three limitations. Which one, and what do the other two have in common?

options.text: Indifference to outcomes; the other two, bridging a delay and apportioning credit, are both problems about time.
options.why: Correct. An error term on its own has no way to reach across time.

options.text: Failure to bridge a delay; the other two, indifference to outcomes and apportioning credit, are both problems about value.
options.why: Error-driven learning does not by itself bridge a delay. It fixes indifference to outcomes.

options.text: Failure to apportion credit; the other two, indifference to outcomes and bridging a delay, are both solved by a larger learning rate.
options.why: No learning rate solves a delay. Credit across time is still open after error-driven learning.

options.text: No limitation at all is repaired until the rule is given a teacher that already holds the correct answer for each moment.
options.why: Error-driven learning does repair one, indifference to outcomes, with no teacher needed.

items.stem: Blocking shows that a summed error can divide credit among cues. Why does that not solve credit across a sequence of actions?

options.text: It divides credit among cues present at once; when an animal acts there is nothing yet to compare against, and later the act is over.
options.why: Correct. Nothing in a single error term divides credit among things that happened at different moments.

options.text: It divides credit among cues of the same sense alone, and the actions in a sequence use different muscles and draw on different senses.
options.why: Blocking is not limited to one sense. The difficulty is time, not modality.

options.text: It divides credit only when the learning rate is low, and sequences of actions happen too quickly for a low rate to work.
options.why: The learning rate does not decide whether credit can reach across moments.

options.text: It divides credit only for punishments, and sequences of actions are usually followed by rewards rather than punishments.
options.why: Blocking works with food, a reward. The limitation is about time.

items.stem: What two things does tier-four learning require, in the chapter's statement of the problem?

options.text: A record of what was done that persists until the news comes in, and a way of apportioning that news across everything recorded.
options.why: Correct. These are the two halves the rest of the section addresses.

options.text: A teacher that holds the right sequence of actions, and a learning rate low enough to ignore the accidental ones made along the way.
options.why: Nothing in tier four needs a teacher, and a low learning rate does not apportion credit.

options.text: A link between two events in the world, and a running count of how often each has occurred in the animal's experience so far.
options.why: Those belong to tiers two and one, which involve no delay between an action and its outcome.

options.text: A verdict on each action as it happens, and a way of adding the verdicts together once the whole sequence has finished.
options.why: A verdict on each action as it happens is exactly what is missing when the outcome arrives late.

items.stem: What does discounting mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Counting an outcome for less the further in the future it lies, by applying a factor slightly below one for each step of delay.
options.why: Correct. The factor is γ, and it answers the question of how far ahead to care.

options.text: Using one of a system's own estimates as the target for another, rather than waiting for the true outcome to arrive.
options.why: That is bootstrapping, a way of learning before the outcome, not of weighting it.

options.text: A fading mark left on whatever was recently active, so that a signal arriving later can still find the connections that were involved.
options.why: That is an eligibility trace, which marks connections rather than weighting outcomes.

options.text: A small number setting how much of the available change a rule takes on any one occasion it is applied.
options.why: That is the learning rate, which scales changes, not the value of delayed outcomes.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Counting an outcome for less the further in the future it lies, by applying a factor slightly below one for every step of delay".

options.text: discounting
options.why: Correct. It is the chapter's answer to how far ahead to care.

options.text: bootstrapping
options.why: Bootstrapping uses an estimate as a target; it does not weight by delay.

options.text: learning rate
options.why: The learning rate scales how much each occasion changes a weight.

options.text: eligibility trace
options.why: An eligibility trace is a fading mark on connections, not a weight on outcomes.

items.stem: With a discount factor γ = 0.9, roughly how much does an outcome ten steps away count compared with the same outcome delivered now?

options.text: About a third as much.
options.why: Correct. 0.9 applied ten times is about 0.35.

options.text: About nine-tenths as much.
options.why: That is one step of discounting, not ten; the factor is applied again at every step.

options.text: About a tenth as much.
options.why: That subtracts 0.09 per step rather than multiplying by 0.9 each step.

options.text: Almost nothing at all.
options.why: That is closer to an outcome a hundred steps away.

items.stem: With γ = 0.5, how much does an outcome of size 1 count if it arrives three steps from now?

options.text: One eighth.
options.why: Correct. The factor is applied once per step: 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125.

options.text: One half.
options.why: That is one step of discounting, applied once instead of three times.

options.text: One and a half.
options.why: That multiplies by the number of steps rather than applying the factor at each one.

options.text: Almost exactly one.
options.why: That would be a factor very close to one, not 0.5.

items.stem: What happens to a learner's behavior when its discount factor γ is raised, and when it is lowered?

options.text: Raised, distant outcomes weigh more; lowered, what is close at hand governs the choice.
options.why: Correct. The factor sets how far ahead the learner cares.

options.text: Raised, the learner learns faster; lowered, it learns more slowly and more carefully.
options.why: Speed of learning is the learning rate's job, not γ's.

options.text: Raised, the learner explores more; lowered, it sticks with the first adequate option.
options.why: That describes exploration against exploitation, a different trade-off.

options.text: Raised, the learner cares only about the next step; lowered, it cares equally about every future step.
options.why: That reverses the effect of the factor: a higher γ makes the far future count more, not less.

items.stem: What does bootstrapping mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Using one of a system's own estimates as the target for another, rather than waiting for the true outcome.
options.why: Correct. The family of rules built on it is temporal-difference learning.

options.text: Counting an outcome for less the further in the future it lies, applying a factor below one for each step of delay.
options.why: That is discounting, which weights outcomes by delay rather than supplying a target.

options.text: Cutting back an early overabundance of connections, with activity deciding which connections survive.
options.why: That is pruning, a developmental process with nothing to do with estimates.

options.text: Changing a weight in proportion to the difference between a target output supplied from outside and the output produced.
options.why: That is the delta rule with a supplied target, not the use of one's own estimate as a target.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Using one of a system's own estimates as the target for another, rather than waiting for the true outcome to arrive".

options.text: bootstrapping
options.why: Correct. It sounds like cheating and works because the chain is anchored.

options.text: discounting
options.why: Discounting weights outcomes by delay; it does not supply a target.

options.text: prediction learning
options.why: Prediction learning's target is the world's next input, not the system's own estimate.

options.text: gradient descent
options.why: Gradient descent is stepping down an error slope.

items.stem: What does temporal-difference learning mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A family of rules comparing each estimate with the system's own next one, so that value propagates backward along a sequence.
options.why: Correct. It is built on bootstrapping, and its errors are what a critic produces.

options.text: A family of rules that change a weight in proportion to how active two cells were at the same moment in time.
options.why: That is Hebbian learning, which needs simultaneity.

options.text: A rule in which the two cells' activity makes a synapse eligible to change and a third signal from elsewhere decides whether it does.
options.why: That is the three-factor rule, a physical arrangement.

options.text: The dependence of synaptic change on the order of two cells' spikes, within a window tens of milliseconds wide.
options.why: That is spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A family of rules that compare each estimate against the next estimate the system itself produces, so that value propagates backward along a sequence".

options.text: temporal-difference learning
options.why: Correct. Its errors are what a critic produces.

options.text: spike-timing-dependent plasticity
options.why: That is about spike order at a synapse, not estimates of value.

options.text: Hebb's rule
options.why: Hebb's rule compares nothing; it multiplies two activities present at once.

options.text: delta rule
options.why: The delta rule compares an output with a supplied target, not with the next estimate.

items.stem: How can a learner change a weight in response to an outcome that has not yet arrived?

options.text: By treating the gap between one moment's estimate of how things are going and the next moment's as an error.
options.why: Correct. That error can move a weight right then, with nothing left to wait for.

options.text: By waiting until the outcome arrives and then changing every weight that was active at any point before it.
options.why: That waits, and it credits everything, which is Hebb's second failure.

options.text: By asking a teacher at each moment what the eventual outcome will be, and learning from the teacher's answer.
options.why: No teacher is involved. The learner uses its own next estimate.

options.text: By setting the discount factor to one, so that the future outcome counts as though it had already arrived.
options.why: Discounting weights outcomes; it does not supply an error before the outcome.

items.stem: A rat learns a sequence: press the lever, approach the tray, nose in, eat. Under temporal-difference learning, how does value spread over repeated trials?

options.text: Backward: the moment just before food carries it first, then earlier ones, until the lever press carries most of it.
options.why: Correct. By then the food itself is no longer surprising.

options.text: Forward: the lever press carries it first, then each later step in turn, until the moment of eating carries most of it.
options.why: The first value appears next to the reward, not at the start of the chain.

options.text: All at once: every step in the sequence gains the same value on the first trial the food arrives.
options.why: That would be crediting everything equally, which is what a coincidence rule does.

options.text: Nowhere: value stays on the food itself and no earlier step ever comes to carry any of it.
options.why: Value does seep backward. That is how the lever press comes to matter.

items.stem: Treating an unreliable estimate as a target sounds like a recipe for learning nothing. Why does it work?

options.text: The chain is anchored: something real happens at the end, and every estimate connects to it through the links between.
options.why: Correct. The real outcome at the end is what keeps the estimates honest.

options.text: The estimates are never unreliable, since a nervous system only forms an estimate once it is already sure of the outcome.
options.why: Early estimates are poor, as the chapter says. The method works despite that.

options.text: A teacher checks each estimate against the right answer before the estimate is allowed to serve as a target.
options.why: No teacher is involved in temporal-difference learning.

options.text: The learning rate is set to zero for unreliable estimates, so only reliable ones are ever used as targets.
options.why: Nothing screens the estimates. The anchoring does the work.

items.stem: In the lever chamber, a rat presses the lever and later grooms before reaching the food. Why does temporal-difference learning come to credit the press and not the grooming?

options.text: The press changed the estimate of how things are going, since a pellet was now coming; grooming left the rat no better placed.
options.why: Correct. No change in the estimate means no error, and nothing to strengthen.

options.text: The press happened first, and temporal-difference learning always gives the most credit to the earliest action in any sequence.
options.why: Order alone does not decide it. An early action that changed nothing would gain nothing.

options.text: The press was followed by food more often than grooming was, and the rule counts how often each action preceded food.
options.why: Grooming preceded food too. What matters is the change in estimate, not the count.

options.text: The press is an action and grooming is a reflex, and temporal-difference learning can only strengthen actions.
options.why: Grooming is an action too. It fails to be credited because it changes nothing.

items.stem: Early in training, grooming on the way to the food may pick up some credit. What removes it, and how does grooming finally fare with discounting in force?

options.text: Experience, as the estimates before and after grooming converge; with discounting, grooming does slightly worse than nothing.
options.why: Correct. Grooming leaves the same outcome one step further away, so it is mildly penalized.

options.text: A teacher tells the rat that grooming is irrelevant; with discounting in force, grooming then ends up with exactly zero credit.
options.why: No teacher is needed. Experience alone makes the estimates converge.

options.text: The rat works out in advance that grooming is irrelevant; with discounting, grooming then gains a little credit.
options.why: The animal does not have to know in advance. That is the chapter's point.

options.text: Nothing removes it; with discounting, grooming keeps whatever credit it picked up early on in training.
options.why: Experience does remove it, as the estimates converge.

items.stem: An animal learns that a tone predicts a shock, until the tone alone produces fear. A light is then paired with the tone, never with a shock, and the light comes to be feared too. What does this show?

options.text: Animals bootstrap: a learned predictor, the tone, served as the teacher for the light.
options.why: Correct. That is exactly the assumption temporal-difference learning runs on.

options.text: Fear spreads to anything present during training, whether or not it predicts the shock.
options.why: The light was not present during shock training. It was taught by the tone.

options.text: The light was secretly paired with the shock, or it could not have come to produce fear.
options.why: The light was never paired with the shock. That is what makes the result telling.

options.text: The tone lost its fear, which moved over to the light because only one cue can hold it.
options.why: Nothing in the case says the tone lost its fear.

items.stem: What two jobs does the chapter say have been running together in learning from outcomes?

options.text: Choosing what to do, and judging how things are going; a system can be good at one and poor at the other.
options.why: Correct. Separating them is what an actor–critic architecture does.

options.text: Forming a link, and breaking one; a system has to do both at the same moment for any weight to change.
options.why: Forming and breaking links is not the pair the chapter separates here.

options.text: Sensing the world, and moving through it; a system has to do both before any learning can happen at all.
options.why: Sensing and moving are not the two jobs named. Choosing and judging are.

options.text: Predicting the next input, and discounting the future; a system has to do both to learn anything over time.
options.why: Those are two tools. The two jobs are choosing and judging.

items.stem: What does policy mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A mapping from situations to what to do in them, which a learner can adjust.
options.why: Correct. The actor holds one and adjusts it using the critic's errors.

options.text: An estimate of how well things will go from a given situation onward, held by a learner.
options.why: That is value, which the critic learns, rather than a rule for what to do.

options.text: A consequence that makes the response it followed more likely in that situation afterward.
options.why: That is a reinforcer, a consequence rather than a mapping.

options.text: A tendency to find one thing easier to learn than another, set before the learning begins.
options.why: That is inductive bias, a prior tilt in what is easy to learn, not a mapping to actions.

items.stem: What does value mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: An estimate of how well things will go from a given situation onward.
options.why: Correct. It is what the critic learns, as distinct from the actor's policy.

options.text: A mapping from situations to what to do in them, which the learner adjusts as outcomes come in.
options.why: That is a policy, which the actor holds, rather than an estimate of how things will go.

options.text: A signal reporting that an outcome was better or worse than predicted, broadcast widely through tissue.
options.why: That is a reward prediction error, a change in value, not value itself.

options.text: A consequence that makes the response it followed more likely in that situation afterward.
options.why: That is a reinforcer, an outcome rather than an estimate.

items.stem: What does actor–critic mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: An arrangement where a critic learns to predict how things will go and an actor adjusts its policy using the critic's errors.
options.why: Correct. The critic learns value; the actor learns behavior.

options.text: An arrangement where one cell strengthens its connection to another because the two are repeatedly active at the very same time.
options.why: That is Hebb's rule, which has no critic and no policy.

options.text: An arrangement where a teacher supplies the correct output and a learner adjusts toward it by the size of its error.
options.why: That is supervised learning with a teacher, not a critic predicting value.

options.text: An arrangement where two sets of synapses compete for a limited resource, so that strengthening one weakens the other.
options.why: That is synaptic competition, a physical mechanism with no critic in it.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "An arrangement that separates two jobs: a critic that learns to predict how well things will go from here, and an actor that holds a policy and adjusts it using the critic's errors".

options.text: actor–critic
options.why: Correct. Separating judging from choosing is its computational insight.

options.text: temporal-difference learning
options.why: Temporal-difference learning is the family of rules the critic uses, not the two-part arrangement.

options.text: three-factor rule
options.why: The three-factor rule is a synaptic arrangement, not a division of labor between judging and choosing.

options.text: model-based
options.why: Model-based choice runs a model of what leads to what.

items.stem: In an actor–critic arrangement, things go better than the critic expected. What happens to whatever the actor just did?

options.text: It becomes more likely in that situation afterward.
options.why: Correct. The critic's positive error adjusts the actor's policy toward that action.

options.text: It becomes less likely, since the critic's prediction was wrong.
options.why: A wrong prediction on the good side strengthens the action, not weakens it.

options.text: It stays the same, since only the critic's estimate changes.
options.why: Both change: the critic revises its estimate and the actor its policy.

options.text: It is repeated at once, whatever the situation happens to be.
options.why: The action becomes more likely in that situation, not everywhere and immediately.

items.stem: Why does the chapter call separating actor from critic a computational insight before an algorithmic one?

options.text: An animal that cannot yet act well can still be improving at telling good situations from bad ones, and that is not wasted.
options.why: Correct. It is a claim about what problem gets solved, not only about how.

options.text: It explains which brain structures carry each job, so it belongs to the level of physical parts rather than procedures.
options.why: Systems-level anatomy is left to a later module. The insight is about what is being solved.

options.text: It shows that an animal must learn to act well before it can begin to judge situations, since judging depends on acting first.
options.why: The reverse: judging can improve before acting does.

options.text: It proves that value and behavior are the same thing, since the critic and the actor always learn together.
options.why: They are different things learned by different parts. That is why they can be separated.

items.stem: What does eligibility trace mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A fading mark left on whatever was recently active, so a signal arriving later can find the connections involved.
options.why: Correct. A connection stays a candidate for a while and then stops being one.

options.text: A factor slightly below one applied once for every step of delay, so a distant outcome counts for less.
options.why: That is discounting, which weights outcomes rather than marking connections.

options.text: A lasting strengthening of a synapse, produced when the two cells it joins are repeatedly active together at the same moment.
options.why: That is long-term potentiation, a physical change rather than a temporary mark.

options.text: An estimate of how well things will go from a given situation onward, revised moment by moment.
options.why: That is value, an estimate of how things will go, not a mark on connections.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A fading mark left on whatever was recently active, so that a signal arriving later can find the connections that were involved".

options.text: eligibility trace
options.why: Correct. It is the algorithmic proposal for marking candidates.

options.text: discounting
options.why: Discounting weights outcomes by delay rather than marking any connection.

options.text: long-term potentiation
options.why: Long-term potentiation is a lasting strengthening, not a fading mark.

options.text: value
options.why: Value is an estimate of how well things will go.

items.stem: Propagating value backward through time leaves half of credit assignment unexplained. Which half does an eligibility trace address?

options.text: Marking which connections were involved, so that a signal arriving later finds the right ones.
options.why: Correct. Value tells how good a moment was; the trace tells which connections to change.

options.text: Deciding how much a delayed outcome should count for, so that distant rewards weigh less than near ones.
options.why: That is discounting, which settles how much a delayed outcome counts, not which connections it should reach.

options.text: Supplying the correct output for each connection, so that the right one can be adjusted.
options.why: That would be a teacher, which the trace is not.

options.text: Predicting the next input, so that each connection can compare its own output with it.
options.why: That is prediction learning's requirement, not the trace's job.

items.stem: What kind of claim is an eligibility trace, according to the chapter?

options.text: A proposal about a procedure; whether anything in a nervous system behaves like one is a separate question.
options.why: Correct. It sits at the algorithmic level, and the physical question is taken up on its own terms.

options.text: A claim about tissue, since a fading chemical mark at the synapse has been directly observed doing this job.
options.why: The chapter is careful to keep the procedure apart from any physical claim.

options.text: A computational claim about why animals need to bridge delays, rather than about any procedure at all.
options.why: The trace is a procedure for bridging delays, not the statement of why they matter.

options.text: A claim about behavior, since an animal with a trace can be seen repeating actions that were recently active.
options.why: The trace is a proposal about how connections are marked, not an observation of behavior.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how temporal-difference learning comes to credit a rat's lever press but not its grooming on the way to the food, and why learning from its own estimates does not lead it astray.
items.answer: Temporal-difference learning compares each estimate of how well things are going with the next estimate, and treats the difference as an error that can change a weight immediately. Pressing the lever changes the estimate, because a pellet is now on its way, so the press is strengthened. Grooming leaves the rat no better placed, so the estimates before and after it are the same, and with no error nothing is strengthened. Early on the estimates are poor and grooming may pick up credit, but experience removes it as the estimates converge. This works because the chain is anchored: something real happens at the end, and every estimate is linked to it.
rubric: Describes the error as the difference between successive estimates.
Explains that the press changes the estimate and grooming does not.
Notes early spurious credit is removed by experience as estimates converge.
Explains anchoring: a real outcome at the end ties every estimate to reality.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe the actor–critic arrangement and explain why separating the two parts is useful to a learning animal.
items.answer: The arrangement separates two jobs, judging how things are going and choosing what to do. The critic learns value, a prediction of how well things will go from here, and its prediction errors are temporal-difference errors. The actor holds a policy, a mapping from situations to actions, and adjusts it using the critic's errors, so an action that turns out better than expected becomes more likely in that situation. Separating them is useful because an animal that cannot yet act well can still be improving at telling good situations from bad ones, and that improvement is not wasted.
rubric: Names the critic as learning value and producing prediction errors.
Names the actor as holding a policy adjusted by the critic's errors.
Says a better-than-expected outcome makes the action more likely.
Explains that judging can improve before acting does, and is not wasted.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what discounting is, work out roughly how much an outcome ten steps away counts at γ = 0.9, and say what raising or lowering γ does to behavior.
items.answer: Discounting counts an outcome for less the further in the future it lies, by applying a factor γ slightly below one for each step of delay. At γ = 0.9, an outcome ten steps away counts for 0.9 multiplied by itself ten times, about a third of the same outcome now. Raising γ makes distant outcomes weigh more heavily, and lowering it makes behavior governed by what is close at hand.
rubric: Defines discounting as a factor below one applied per step of delay.
Computes roughly a third for ten steps at 0.9.
Says raising γ makes distant outcomes count more.
Says lowering γ makes nearby outcomes dominate.

items.stem: In the lab's corridor, the animal crosses the marker, then the turn, then the approach, and then reaches food. In what order did the three stretches of floor gain value across trials?

options.text: The approach first, then the turn, then the marker.
options.why: Correct. Value seeps backward from the food along the chain.

options.text: The marker first, then the turn, then the approach.
options.why: That is the order the animal crosses them, not the order they gained value.

options.text: All three together on the first trial.
options.why: Value appeared next to the food first and worked backward.

options.text: The turn first, then the approach and the marker together.
options.why: The stretch nearest the food gained value first.

items.stem: In the corridor, the size of the surprise at the food was tracked over about thirty trials. What happened to it, and why?

options.text: It shrank from its full size on the first trial, because the prediction came to anticipate the food; the food did not change.
options.why: Correct. It matches the dopamine pattern: a fully predicted outcome produces less and less surprise.

options.text: It grew over the trials, because each trial added value to the food itself and made the food more and more rewarding to the animal.
options.why: The food was the same every trial. What grew was the prediction, not the surprise.

options.text: It stayed at its full size throughout, because the food was delivered on every single trial.
options.why: Delivery alone does not keep the surprise high; prediction shrinks it.

options.text: It fell to zero on the second trial, because one trial is enough to predict the food exactly.
options.why: It fell gradually over many trials, as value worked back along the chain.

items.stem: In the corridor, the eligibility trace window was set to zero. What happened to the chain of values and to the surprise at the food?

options.text: Nothing in the chain gained value, and the surprise at the food stayed at its full size.
options.why: Correct. By the time the news arrived, no connection was still marked as a candidate.

options.text: The chain filled faster than usual, since without a trace the news reached every connection at once.
options.why: Without a trace, the news reached no connection at all.

options.text: The chain filled as usual, since value propagation does not depend on the trace.
options.why: With the window at zero, nothing filled.

options.text: The surprise at the food vanished, since without a trace nothing surprising could be registered.
options.why: The surprise stayed at full size, because nothing learned to predict the food.

items.stem: In the corridor, a passing vibration washed through on every trial before the food. What did the rule do with the vibration's weight?

options.text: It stayed near zero, because the vibration did not change the estimate of how well things were going.
options.why: Correct. It is the grooming rat of the chapter: active before food, and credited with nothing.

options.text: It grew as much as the marker's, since the vibration was active before the food arrived on every single trial.
options.why: That is what the Coincidence rule would do. This rule credits only what changes the estimate.

options.text: It grew larger than the marker's, since the vibration came closest in time to the food.
options.why: Closeness in time is not what this rule rewards.

options.text: It went strongly negative, since the vibration was treated as a sign that food was coming late.
options.why: The vibration's weight stayed near zero rather than being pushed down.

items.stem: In the corridor, the discount factor was set first to 0.5 and then to 0.99. How far back along the chain did value get in each case?

options.text: At 0.5 it never reached the marker; at 0.99 the marker ended up holding more than the approach.
options.why: Correct. A low discount makes distant outcomes count for little; a high one lets them count almost fully.

options.text: At 0.5 the marker held the most; at 0.99 value stayed at the approach and went no further.
options.why: That reverses the two settings: the higher discount carried value further back, not the lower.

options.text: At both settings value reached the marker equally, since the discount only affects the food itself.
options.why: The discount changes how much a distant outcome counts at each earlier point.

options.text: At neither setting did value leave the food, since the discount factor stops value propagating.
options.why: Value propagated at both settings; the discount decided how far back it got.

pools.title: Machines, Habits, Extinction, and What Cannot Be Learned
pools.covers: reading §5.2.9, §5.2.10, §5.2.11, §5.2.12 · lecture 5.2 slides same_rules_in_machines, habits_and_goals, extinction_is_not_unlearning, what_cannot_be_learned · lab (the extinction closer)

items.stem: What was ADALINE?

options.text: A physical adaptive circuit built in 1960 that ran the delta rule, adjusting resistances as its weights.
options.why: Correct. Widrow and Hoff's rule was a machine's learning rule before it was matched to animal learning.

options.text: A 1951 machine of vacuum tubes and clutches built to model a rat finding its way through a maze.
options.why: That describes SNARC, an earlier machine with a different rule.

options.text: A checkers program of the 1950s that compared each position's evaluation with one from a few moves later.
options.why: That describes Samuel's checkers program, an early temporal-difference learner.

options.text: A game-playing system given only the rules of a game, which learned by playing millions of games against itself.
options.why: That describes AlphaZero, which pairs a critic with an actor.

items.stem: SNARC, built in 1951, strengthened whatever connections had recently been active whenever the machine did well. It improved a little and then stopped. Why?

options.text: It treated connections that mattered and ones that merely happened to be on alike, so it hit the credit assignment problem.
options.why: Correct. The instinct was right but not enough; the problem appeared in a machine long before it had an answer.

options.text: It had only forty units, and a machine that small cannot learn anything further once its first few connections have been set.
options.why: Size is not the chapter's explanation. The rule itself could not tell useful connections from incidental ones.

options.text: It strengthened connections when it did badly instead of well, so its successes weakened the very wiring that had produced them.
options.why: The rule strengthened connections when it did well, which is the right instinct.

options.text: It had no way to be told what the right move was, and every learning machine needs a teacher to improve at all.
options.why: Later machines improved without a teacher. SNARC's problem was apportioning credit.

items.stem: Arthur Samuel's checkers program adjusted each position's evaluation toward the evaluation it reached a few moves later. What kind of learning was that?

options.text: Temporal-difference learning, two decades before the name.
options.why: Correct. The program came to play better than Samuel did.

options.text: Supervised learning, with Samuel as the teacher.
options.why: Samuel supplied no correct evaluations. The program used its own later estimates.

options.text: Hebbian learning, strengthening whichever moves co-occurred.
options.why: The program compared estimates across time, which Hebb's rule never does.

options.text: Prediction learning of the opponent's next move alone.
options.why: The target was its own later evaluation of the position, not the opponent's move.

items.stem: How does AlphaZero learn, according to the chapter?

options.text: Given only the rules, it plays itself; a critic estimates positions and an actor proposes moves.
options.why: Correct. The estimates are trained on game outcomes, and the moves on the estimates.

options.text: Given a record of expert human games, it learns to predict the move a strong player would make next.
options.why: AlphaZero is given no record of human play and no opening book.

options.text: Given a teacher that scores every move, it adjusts its moves toward the teacher's highest-scoring choice.
options.why: No teacher scores its moves. It learns from its own games.

options.text: Given the rules and a large library of openings, it strengthens whichever moves occurred together most often.
options.why: It has no opening library, and co-occurrence is not how it learns.

items.stem: At what level does the chapter claim AlphaZero resembles an animal?

options.text: The procedure alone: nothing about its weights, training schedule or hardware resembles a nervous system.
options.why: Correct. The chapter makes that distance wider rather than narrower when it reaches the physical level.

options.text: The hardware: its chips process information in parallel the same way a brain's neurons do.
options.why: The chapter explicitly denies any resemblance in hardware.

options.text: The whole system: it resembles an animal at every level, which is why it can learn games as animals learn tasks.
options.why: The claim is limited to the procedure, on purpose.

options.text: The training schedule: it learns in stages that match the critical periods of a developing animal.
options.why: Its training schedule is one of the things the chapter says does not resemble a nervous system.

items.stem: What does the chapter say is genuinely shared between AlphaZero and a learning animal?

options.text: The shape of the rule, arrived at twice: by people asking what a rat is doing, and by people making a machine improve.
options.why: Correct. The shared object is the procedure.

options.text: The number of connections, since both have to reach a certain size before learning from self-play becomes possible at all.
options.why: Nothing about size is claimed as shared; the chapter's claim is about the rule.

options.text: The kind of experience, since both learn only from the outcomes of games they have played against themselves.
options.why: An animal does not learn only from self-play. The shared thing is the rule's shape.

options.text: The physical signal, since both carry their errors in a chemical that is released across many connections at once.
options.why: AlphaZero carries no chemical. The chapter keeps the resemblance at the level of procedure.

items.stem: What does model-free mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Choosing an action by repeating what has worked in that situation before, with no model of where the action leads.
options.why: Correct. It is what a policy adjusted by reinforcement amounts to.

options.text: Choosing an action by running a model of what leads to what, and selecting on the basis of where the model ends up.
options.why: That is model-based choice, which consults where an action leads.

options.text: Choosing an action by asking a source that already holds the correct answer, and doing what that source specifies.
options.why: That describes learning from a teacher, not a way of choosing without a model.

options.text: Choosing an action by sampling one that might be better and might be worse, rather than the one known to be decent.
options.why: That is exploration, one side of a trade-off, not the definition of model-free choice.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Choosing an action by running a model of what leads to what, and selecting on the basis of where the model ends up".

options.text: model-based
options.why: Correct. Changing the value of an outcome changes the model's verdict at once.

options.text: model-free
options.why: Model-free choice repeats what has worked, with no model of consequences.

options.text: actor–critic
options.why: An actor–critic arrangement divides judging from choosing; its actor repeats what the critic's errors favor, with no model of consequences.

options.text: policy
options.why: A policy is a mapping from situations to actions, which model-free choice relies on.

items.stem: A rat trained to press a lever for a particular food is then, away from the lever, made sick on that food until it refuses it. Back at the lever, what should a model-based rat and a model-free rat each do?

options.text: The model-based rat stops pressing at once; the model-free rat keeps pressing, since nothing about the bar it presses changed.
options.why: Correct. The model says the lever leads to food it no longer wants; repeating what worked consults no model.

options.text: The model-based rat keeps pressing, since its model was built before the food was devalued and has not been consulted or rerun since.
options.why: A model-based chooser consults the model at the moment of choice, and the model now ends in unwanted food.

options.text: The model-free rat stops pressing at once, since it has learned that the food now makes it sick.
options.why: The sickness was paired with the food, not the lever. A model-free rat has no model linking the two.

options.text: Both rats stop pressing at once, since any rat that refuses a food will also refuse to work for it.
options.why: That is the model-based prediction only. The experiment exists because the two can come apart.

items.stem: Two rats learn to press a lever for a food, one with modest training and one with extended training. After the food is devalued, which rat keeps pressing, and what is its behavior called?

options.text: The extensively trained rat keeps pressing; its behavior has become a habit.
options.why: Correct. Modest training leaves pressing goal-directed; extended training makes it insensitive to devaluation.

options.text: The modestly trained rat keeps pressing; its behavior has not yet become goal-directed.
options.why: The reverse: modest training leaves the pressing sensitive to devaluation.

options.text: Both keep pressing; any behavior that was once reinforced continues after devaluation.
options.why: Which result appears depends on how much training came first.

options.text: Neither keeps pressing; devaluation removes the reason to press for either of them.
options.why: The extensively trained rat does keep pressing. That is the habit.

items.stem: What does goal-directed mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Choosing by consulting a model of what an action leads to, so changing the outcome's value changes the choice at once.
options.why: Correct. In the devaluation experiment it is the pressing that stops.

options.text: A behavior chosen by repeating what has worked before, which continues even after its outcome has been made undesirable.
options.why: That is a habit, the pressing that continues.

options.text: A mapping from situations to what to do in them, adjusted by the errors of a part that predicts outcomes.
options.why: That is a policy, which a model-free chooser relies on.

options.text: An estimate of how well things will go from a given situation onward, revised moment by moment.
options.why: That is value, an estimate rather than a way of choosing an action.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A behavior chosen by repeating what has worked before, which continues even after the outcome it once produced has been made undesirable".

options.text: habit
options.why: Correct. Extended training produces it, and devaluation does not stop it.

options.text: goal-directed
options.why: Goal-directed behavior stops when the outcome is devalued.

options.text: extinction
options.why: Extinction is a learned response fading when its outcome stops.

options.text: reinforcer
options.why: A reinforcer is a consequence, not a behavior.

items.stem: Someone who has changed jobs keeps driving the old route to their former workplace. How does the lecture ask us to understand a habit like that?

options.text: Not as a goal forgotten, but as a different way of choosing, one that runs on after the goal has moved.
options.why: Correct. The habit repeats what has worked here; it does not consult where the route now leads.

options.text: As a goal that has been forgotten, so reminding the driver of the new job would be enough to end it at once.
options.why: The lecture rejects the forgotten-goal reading. A habit does not consult the goal at all.

options.text: As a failure of learning, since a nervous system working properly would never keep a response that no longer pays.
options.why: The lecture treats habit as a normal way of choosing, not as a malfunction.

options.text: As a sign that the new job has not yet been learned, since habits only persist while nothing better is known.
options.why: The driver knows the new job. The habit runs regardless, because it does not consult that knowledge.

items.stem: What does extinction mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: The fading of a learned response when the outcome stops arriving, as new learning that competes with the original association.
options.why: Correct. It adds learning rather than removing it.

options.text: The fading of a learned response when the outcome stops arriving, as the weight decays back to where it started before training.
options.why: That is the tidy story the chapter says is wrong.

options.text: A decline in a response to a stimulus repeated without consequence, restored at once by a novel stimulus.
options.why: That is habituation, which involves no previously learned link.

options.text: The finding that a cue paired with an outcome goes unlearned when another cue already predicts that outcome.
options.why: That is blocking, a failure to learn rather than a fading of what was learned.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The return of an extinguished response after a delay, with no further training of any kind".

options.text: spontaneous recovery
options.why: Correct. Time alone brings the response back.

options.text: renewal effect
options.why: The renewal effect depends on a change of place, not on time.

options.text: reinstatement
options.why: Reinstatement follows a single unpaired delivery of the outcome.

options.text: conditioned response
options.why: A conditioned response is what a conditioned stimulus comes to produce, not its return after extinction.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The return of an extinguished response when the animal is tested somewhere other than where extinction took place".

options.text: renewal effect
options.why: Correct. The new learning was largely about the context.

options.text: spontaneous recovery
options.why: Spontaneous recovery depends on the passage of time, not a change of place.

options.text: reinstatement
options.why: Reinstatement follows one delivery of the outcome on its own.

options.text: blocking
options.why: Blocking is a failure to learn about a redundant cue.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The return of an extinguished response after the outcome has been delivered once on its own, unpaired".

options.text: reinstatement
options.why: Correct. One unannounced outcome is enough.

options.text: spontaneous recovery
options.why: Spontaneous recovery needs only time, with no outcome delivered.

options.text: renewal effect
options.why: The renewal effect needs a change of context.

options.text: conditioned response
options.why: A conditioned response is what a conditioned stimulus comes to produce, not a return after extinction.

items.stem: A dog's fear of a buzzer is extinguished during sessions at a clinic. At home, the buzzer frightens it again. Which finding is this?

options.text: The renewal effect.
options.why: Correct. Testing somewhere other than where extinction took place brings the response back.

options.text: Spontaneous recovery.
options.why: Spontaneous recovery is about time passing, and here what changed is the place.

options.text: Reinstatement.
options.why: Reinstatement follows a lone delivery of the feared outcome, which did not happen here.

options.text: Sensitization.
options.why: Sensitization is a general rise in responsiveness, not the return of one extinguished response.

items.stem: A rat's fear of a tone has been extinguished. Weeks later, with no training of any kind, the fear returns. In a second rat, a single unannounced shock, with no tone, brings its extinguished fear back. Which findings are these?

options.text: Spontaneous recovery in the first rat, and reinstatement in the second.
options.why: Correct. Time alone did the first; one unpaired outcome did the second.

options.text: Reinstatement in the first rat, and spontaneous recovery in the second.
options.why: The pairing is reversed. Reinstatement needs the outcome delivered, which only the second rat received.

options.text: The renewal effect in both rats, since each was tested after extinction had ended.
options.why: Renewal needs a change of place, which neither case involves.

options.text: Sensitization in both rats, since each became more responsive after something significant.
options.why: These are returns of one extinguished response, not a general rise in responsiveness.

items.stem: The tidy story says extinction returns a weight to roughly where it started. Why do the three findings show that story is wrong?

options.text: A weight that simply decayed could produce none of them; with nothing left, nothing could come back.
options.why: Correct. So extinction adds new learning rather than removing the old.

options.text: The three findings show the weight decays too slowly, so the tidy story is right about direction but wrong about speed.
options.why: Speed is not the issue. A decayed weight cannot bring a response back at all.

options.text: The three findings show the weight never changes during extinction, so the fading must be caused by fatigue.
options.why: Extinction is learning, not fatigue. The point is what kind of learning it is.

options.text: The three findings show the weight rises during extinction, so the response ought to grow stronger rather than fade.
options.why: The response does fade during extinction. The findings concern what survives underneath.

items.stem: What does an animal learn during extinction, according to the chapter?

options.text: A new fact, that the old association does not seem to hold in this context, with the original surviving under it.
options.why: Correct. Which fact governs depends on where the animal is and how long it has been.

options.text: That the old association was never true, so the original is erased and replaced by its opposite in every context.
options.why: The original is not erased. The new learning is tied to context.

options.text: That the cue now predicts a different outcome, which overwrites the old outcome in the same connection.
options.why: The chapter's account keeps the old association and adds a context-dependent exception.

options.text: Nothing new, since extinction is simply what happens to an association when it goes unused for long enough.
options.why: Extinction is new learning, not the result of an association going unused.

items.stem: What does extinction require of any procedure for updating a weight?

options.text: It cannot just put the weight back: something must hold the association and its contradiction together, and arbitrate.
options.why: Correct. The chapter calls this a real complication.

options.text: It must run with a higher learning rate than acquisition did, so that the weight comes back down faster than it rose.
options.why: Speed does not address the requirement. Both facts have to be kept.

options.text: It must be able to make a weight negative, so that extinction can push the cue's weight below where it began.
options.why: A negative weight on the cue would still be one number. The requirement is to hold two facts at once.

options.text: It must switch off learning during extinction, so that the original association is not disturbed while the response fades.
options.why: Extinction is learning; switching learning off would not produce it.

items.stem: A person's fear of dogs is extinguished over several sessions in a therapist's office. What do the chapter and the lecture suggest about the fear in the weeks that follow?

options.text: It has not been deleted, so it may return with time, in a different place, or after one frightening encounter.
options.why: Correct. The lecture says this directly, and it is why the chapter calls extinction its most practically consequential result.

options.text: It has been deleted for good, since the sessions returned the fear to where it was before it was first learned.
options.why: That is the tidy story, which the three findings refute.

options.text: It will spread to other animals, since extinction of one fear always raises responsiveness to similar things.
options.why: Extinction does not spread fear. The concern is that the original fear can return.

options.text: It will return only if the person is shown the same dogs used in the office, since extinction is specific to cues.
options.why: The new learning is about context as much as cue, so a different place can bring the fear back.

items.stem: Pigeons trained to peck a key for food come to peck it as they peck grain, and raccoons trained to drop coins in a slot for food start rubbing the coins together. What does the chapter take these cases to show?

options.text: Reinforcement was arranged correctly, yet each animal drifted toward something more natural for its lineage.
options.why: Correct. The limit is not in the rule but in what the animal brings to it.

options.text: The reinforcement was arranged wrongly, since a correct schedule would have kept the trained movement exact.
options.why: The chapter says the reinforcement was arranged correctly in both cases.

options.text: The animals had forgotten the training, since extended training makes any learned movement fade over time.
options.why: Nothing was forgotten. The movement drifted toward the lineage's own way of handling food.

options.text: The animals were being clever, having worked out that the old movement would get them the food more quickly.
options.why: The drift is toward a less effective movement, and the chapter describes no working out.

items.stem: Which pairing does a rat learn most readily, according to the chapter?

options.text: A novel flavor with illness, across several hours, after one occasion.
options.why: Correct. A flavor with shock, or a noise with illness, is learned hardly at all.

options.text: A novel flavor with an electric shock, when the shock follows the flavor within a second.
options.why: However carefully that pairing is arranged, it is learned hardly at all.

options.text: A noise with illness, as long as the illness follows within a few hours of the noise.
options.why: A noise with illness is nearly hopeless for a rat.

options.text: Any of these equally, since the rules for learning treat every pair of events alike.
options.why: The rules may treat pairs alike on paper, but the animal does not.

items.stem: If the learning rules themselves have no preferences, where do a rat's preferences about what to link come from?

options.text: From the animal, whose leanings line up with the pairings its ancestors had reason to pick up.
options.why: Correct. The rules are general; what they are applied to in a real animal is not.

options.text: From the rules after all, since a rule that learns quickly about one pair must be slower about the others.
options.why: The chapter says the rules have no preferences. The animal supplies them.

options.text: From the experimenter, since a careful enough pairing can make any link as easy to learn as any other.
options.why: The chapter says a flavor with shock is learned hardly at all however carefully it is arranged.

options.text: From earlier training in the lab, since a rat learns each pairing faster once it has learned one of the same type.
options.why: Prior learning can shape what is easy, but the chapter traces these preferences to the lineage.

items.stem: What does inductive bias mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A tendency to find one thing easier to learn than another, set before the learning begins by lineage or by earlier learning.
options.why: Correct. It is why a rat links flavor with illness so much more easily than with shock.

options.text: A tendency to repeat what has worked before in a situation, even after the outcome it produced has been made undesirable to the animal.
options.why: That is a habit, a way of choosing rather than a tilt in what is easy to learn.

options.text: A trade-off between changing enough to learn something new and changing little enough to keep what was learned before.
options.why: That is stability versus plasticity, a trade-off every learner faces.

options.text: A move from "this region was active" to "the task involved the process that region does", which is often wrong.
options.why: That is reverse inference, a problem of interpreting brain data.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A tendency to find one thing easier to learn than another, established before the learning begins, whether by the animal's lineage or by what it has already learned".

options.text: inductive bias
options.why: Correct. Learning rules run on inputs already sorted by what a lineage needed.

options.text: habit
options.why: A habit is a behavior that persists after devaluation.

options.text: blocking
options.why: Blocking is a failure to learn a redundant cue.

options.text: stability versus plasticity
options.why: That is a trade-off every learner faces, not a tilt toward some pairings.

items.stem: A learning rule written on a page looks fully general. What does the chapter say about the same rule in a real animal?

options.text: It is applied to some pairings and not others, since its inputs are already sorted by what a lineage needed.
options.why: Correct. None of the rules is a blank slate operating on arbitrary inputs.

options.text: It is applied to every pairing equally, which is why animals of one species all learn the same things in the same way.
options.why: Animals do not learn every pairing equally. The flavor and noise cases show it.

options.text: It is applied to pairings the animal was taught by a parent and no others, since other pairings never reach it.
options.why: Nothing restricts learning to what a parent taught.

options.text: It is applied in the first weeks of life and then stops, since after that the animal's wiring is fixed for good.
options.why: The rule runs throughout life. The limit is on which pairings it is applied to.

items.stem: Four kinds of rule have been shown to work, in the sense that a system running one improves at something. What question does that leave open?

options.text: Whether nerve cells actually run any of these rules, which needs a "better than expected" signal reaching the right synapses.
options.why: Correct. That is the physical question the next level takes up.

options.text: Which of the four kinds is correct, since only one of them can be the rule that animals actually use.
options.why: The chapter does not treat the four as rivals for one slot. They suit different situations.

options.text: Whether the rules work in machines, since so far they have been shown to work in animals and nowhere else.
options.why: The rules were shown to work in machines, some before they were matched to animals.

options.text: Whether learning happens at all, since the rules so far have been stated without any supporting evidence from real, living animals.
options.why: The chapter has given plenty of animal evidence for learning. The open question is about mechanism.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, name the three findings that show extinction is not unlearning, and explain why a weight that had simply decayed could produce none of them.
items.answer: Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response after a delay with no further training. The renewal effect is its return when the animal is tested somewhere other than where extinction happened. Reinstatement is its return after the outcome is delivered once on its own. If extinction had simply put the weight back where it started, there would be nothing left to come back. Instead, extinction adds new learning, mostly about the context, and the original association survives underneath it.
rubric: Names and describes spontaneous recovery.
Names and describes the renewal effect.
Names and describes reinstatement.
Explains that a decayed weight leaves nothing to return, so extinction must be new learning.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe the reinforcer devaluation experiment and explain how it tells goal-directed behavior from a habit.
items.answer: A rat is trained to press a lever for a particular food. Then, away from the lever, that food is paired with illness until the rat refuses it, and the rat is returned to the lever. A rat choosing on a model of what the lever leads to should stop pressing, because the lever now leads to food it does not want. A rat repeating what has worked should keep pressing, because nothing about the lever changed. After modest training the pressing stops, so the behavior is goal-directed; after extended training it continues, so it has become a habit.
rubric: Describes training on the lever and devaluing the food away from it.
Predicts that model-based choice stops pressing.
Predicts that model-free choice keeps pressing.
Links modest training to goal-directed and extended training to habit.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what AlphaZero shares with a learning animal, according to the chapter, and where the resemblance stops.
items.answer: AlphaZero is given only a game's rules and learns by playing itself. One part estimates how good a position is, which is the critic, and another proposes moves, which is the actor, so it runs the same shape of rule the chapter describes for animals. That resemblance holds at the level of the procedure and nowhere else. Nothing about its weights, its training schedule or its hardware resembles a nervous system. What is shared is the shape of the rule, which was arrived at twice, once by people studying rats and once by people building machines.
rubric: Identifies the critic and actor in AlphaZero.
Limits the resemblance to the level of procedure.
Denies resemblance in weights, training schedule or hardware.
Notes the rule's shape was arrived at independently from animals and machines.

items.stem: In the lab's extinction dish, salt first marks the food, then marks nothing. After the response to salt faded, what did the weights show?

options.text: The salt weight was still well above zero, while the dish-one and session-one weights had gone negative.
options.why: Correct. The learning that made the response fade went into the context, and it was inhibitory.

options.text: The salt weight had returned to zero, and every other weight was unchanged.
options.why: That is the tidy story, and the weights refuted it.

options.text: The salt weight had gone negative, and the dish-one and session-one weights were unchanged from where they started.
options.why: The salt weight stayed positive; the context connections carried the new, negative learning.

options.text: Every weight, salt and context alike, was exactly as it had been before acquisition.
options.why: The salt weight kept much of what it had gained, and the context weights had changed.

items.stem: From one extinguished animal in the lab, the response to salt was checked after Move to the second dish, after Wait, and after Deliver one outcome. Which of these moved no weight at all, though the response came back anyway?

options.text: Move and Wait.
options.why: Correct. Both brought the response back by changing the context the weights applied in, not the weights.

options.text: Deliver one outcome and Wait.
options.why: Delivering the outcome did land a meal; the two that left every weight untouched were Move and Wait.

options.text: Move and Deliver one outcome.
options.why: Waiting also moved no weight; the weight trace stayed flat through it.

options.text: Only Move.
options.why: Waiting also changed no weight, yet the response came back partly.
