items.stem: After extinction in the lab, the response to salt had faded, yet the animal still headed toward salt when it sensed it. How can both be true?

options.text: The approach steers on the salt weight alone, which stayed high; the fading ran through context cells that never steer.
options.why: Correct. What extinguished was the verdict to salt, not the salt weight that drives approach.

options.text: The animal had not actually been extinguished, so the fading of the response on the scorecard was only a display error.
options.why: The response did fade. It faded in a way that did not touch the approach.

options.text: The animal was steering on almond odor, which had quietly taken over from salt during extinction.
options.why: Almond odor played no part in this dish's extinction.

options.text: The approach is set by a neuromodulator, which extinction cannot reach.
options.why: The lab's account is about which weights steer, not about a modulator.

pools.title: What Physically Changes: Synapses, the NMDA Receptor, and Timing
pools.covers: reading §5.3.1, §5.3.2, §5.3.3, §5.3.4 · lecture 5.3 slides title, where_the_account_stops, ltp_and_ltd, nmda_and_gate, timing

items.stem: At the algorithmic level a weight is a number in a rule. What is it at the implementational level?

options.text: A physical arrangement, the strength of a connection, and something physical has to move when it changes.
options.why: Correct. That strength is also one of Module 3's answers to how identical spikes carry different information.

options.text: A pattern of spikes in the receiving cell, which stores the number by firing at a rate equal to its value.
options.why: A weight is not a firing rate. It is the strength of the connection the spikes cross.

options.text: A gene in the receiving cell's nucleus, whose expression level is the number the rule would otherwise write down.
options.why: Genes can be involved in making changes last, but the weight itself is the connection's strength.

options.text: An abstraction with no physical counterpart, since only the rule, and never the tissue, can hold a number.
options.why: The chapter's whole point at this level is that something physical has to change.

items.stem: Where does the chapter's physical account of learning stop, and why?

options.text: At the synapse and the cell; whole brain structures for kinds of learning come later, and synaptic learning came first.
options.why: Correct. Where those structures are, and why an animal has separate ones, is Module 6's question.

options.text: At the brain structures for each kind of learning, since learning cannot be explained below the level of a whole structure.
options.why: The account stops below that level, at the synapse and cell, on purpose.

options.text: At the gene, since every lasting change a synapse makes is ultimately written in the cell's DNA.
options.why: Nothing in the account goes down to genes as the stopping point. It stops at synapse and cell.

options.text: At the whole animal's behavior, since the physical level can only be studied by watching what an animal does.
options.why: Behavior is the computational side. The physical account is about synapses and cells.

items.stem: What single principle does the chapter say lies underneath every physical mechanism of learning it describes?

options.text: A lasting change that is a function of activity; what varies is where it is made and what regulates it.
options.why: Correct. The loci and the regulators vary; the principle does not.

options.text: A signal broadcast from elsewhere that reports how things went, which every mechanism of learning must receive.
options.why: A broadcast signal is one regulator, not the principle beneath all of them.

options.text: A new synapse formed wherever two cells fire together, since learning always means growing new connections.
options.why: Forming connections is one place a change can be made, not the principle.

options.text: A decrease in firing whenever a stimulus is repeated, since learning at bottom means responding less to the familiar.
options.why: That describes habituation, one kind of learning, not the underlying principle.

items.stem: According to the chapter, in which three places can a lasting change be made?

options.text: The strength of a synapse, how readily a cell fires at all, and whether a connection is there in the first place.
options.why: Correct. These are the three loci, the places where a lasting change can be made.

options.text: A broadcast signal, a fading mark on recent activity, and mechanisms that keep the arrangement from running away.
options.why: Those are the three regulators, not the loci.

options.text: The sensory cells, the interneurons, and the motor cells, since those are the three kinds of cell in a circuit.
options.why: The loci are kinds of change, not kinds of cell.

options.text: The gene, the protein, and the ion, since those are the three physical scales at which a cell can change.
options.why: These are levels of chemistry, not the chapter's three places where a lasting change is made.

items.stem: According to the chapter, in which three ways can a lasting change be regulated?

options.text: By a signal broadcast from elsewhere, by a fading mark on what was recently active, and by mechanisms that stop runaway.
options.why: Correct. These are the three regulators, each deciding whether and where a change is made.

options.text: By the strength of a synapse, by how readily a cell fires, and by whether a connection exists at all.
options.why: Those are the three places a change is made, the loci.

options.text: By the learning rate, by the discount factor, and by the eligibility window, since those three settings govern every rule.
options.why: Those are parameters of rules in the algorithmic account, not the physical regulators listed.

options.text: By hunger, by fatigue, and by sleep, since those three states decide whether any learning happens.
options.why: None of these is named as a regulator in the chapter's frame.

items.stem: The lecture says every physical mechanism of learning is one entry from each of two lists of three: a place the change is made, and what regulates it. Which pairing is set up correctly?

options.text: Place: the strength of a synapse. Regulator: a signal broadcast from elsewhere.
options.why: Correct. That pairing is the three-factor rule's arrangement.

options.text: Place: a signal broadcast from elsewhere. Regulator: the strength of a synapse.
options.why: This swaps the lists. A broadcast signal regulates; synaptic strength is where change is made.

options.text: Place: a fading mark on recent activity. Regulator: whether a connection exists.
options.why: A fading mark is a regulator, and whether a connection exists is a place.

options.text: Place: mechanisms that prevent runaway. Regulator: how readily a cell fires.
options.why: Preventing runaway is a regulator, and how readily a cell fires is a place.

items.stem: What does long-term potentiation mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A lasting strengthening of a synapse, produced when the two cells it joins are repeatedly active together.
options.why: Correct. It lasts for hours or longer, and it is the physical side of strengthening.

options.text: A lasting weakening of a synapse, produced when the sending cell is repeatedly active while the receiving cell is not.
options.why: That is long-term depression, the weakening that pairs with it.

options.text: A learning rule that changes a weight in proportion to how active two cells were at the same time.
options.why: That is Hebb's rule, stated as a procedure rather than as a physical change.

options.text: The formation of new synapses, which early in life produces far more connections than will survive.
options.why: That is synaptogenesis, the growth of new synapses rather than the strengthening of an existing one.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A lasting weakening of a synapse, produced when the sending cell is repeatedly active while the receiving cell is not".

options.text: long-term depression
options.why: Correct. It is what lets a weight move downward.

options.text: long-term potentiation
options.why: Long-term potentiation is the strengthening, when both cells are active together.

options.text: pruning
options.why: Pruning removes connections altogether, during development.

options.text: habituation
options.why: Habituation is a behavioral decline to a repeated stimulus, not a synaptic change.

items.stem: At one synapse, the sending cell fires again and again while the receiving cell stays quiet. What happens to the synapse?

options.text: It weakens, which is long-term depression.
options.why: Correct. The sending cell's activity without the receiver's weakens the connection.

options.text: It strengthens, which is long-term potentiation.
options.why: Strengthening needs the two cells active together.

options.text: It stays exactly as it was, since only joint activity changes a synapse.
options.why: Activity on one side alone can change a synapse; here it weakens it.

options.text: It is removed entirely, since unused connections are pruned at once.
options.why: Pruning is a developmental process; this synapse weakens rather than vanishing.

items.stem: Physically, what changes when a synapse is potentiated or depressed?

options.text: How much an arriving spike accomplishes: transmitter released on one side and receptors to catch it on the other.
options.why: Correct. More of each in potentiation, less of each in depression.

options.text: How fast spikes travel down the sending cell's axon, which sets how soon the receiving cell responds.
options.why: Conduction speed along the axon is not what these changes alter.

options.text: How many spikes the sending cell fires, since a potentiated cell fires more often than a depressed one does.
options.why: The sending cell's rate is not the change. The synapse's effect per spike is.

options.text: How large each spike is, since a potentiated synapse carries a bigger spike than a depressed synapse ever carries.
options.why: Spikes are all-or-nothing in size. What changes is what each spike accomplishes at the synapse.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say the pair, potentiation and depression together, matters more than either one?

options.text: A synapse that could only strengthen would be a one-way ratchet, Hebb's rule's limit; depression lets a weight move both ways.
options.why: Correct. Depression is what turns a coincidence rule into one that can subtract.

options.text: Either one alone would make a synapse unstable, since strengthening and weakening each depend on the other to switch them off again.
options.why: The point is not mutual switching off. It is that a weight needs to be able to move in both directions.

options.text: Potentiation happens in vertebrates and depression in invertebrates, so only together do they cover every animal.
options.why: Both occur widely. The pair matters because of direction, not distribution.

options.text: Each needs the other's chemistry to work, so a synapse lacking either one cannot change at all.
options.why: The chapter's reason is about what a one-directional synapse cannot do, not about shared chemistry.

items.stem: What does NMDA receptor mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A receptor that opens only when transmitter is bound and the receiving cell is already depolarized.
options.why: Correct. It responds to two conditions at once and to neither alone.

options.text: A receptor that opens whenever transmitter is bound to it, whatever state the receiving cell happens to be in.
options.why: That is what the NMDA receptor does not do; a magnesium ion blocks it unless the cell is depolarized.

options.text: A signal reporting that an outcome was better or worse than predicted, broadcast widely rather than to particular cells.
options.why: That is a reward prediction error, a signal rather than a receptor.

options.text: A fading mark left on whatever was recently active, so that a signal arriving later can find the connections involved.
options.why: That is an eligibility trace, a proposed mark rather than a receptor.

items.stem: Transmitter from the sending cell binds to an NMDA receptor, but the receiving cell is at rest and not depolarized. What happens?

options.text: Nothing: a magnesium ion still plugs the channel, so no calcium enters.
options.why: Correct. Transmitter alone does nothing while the plug is in place.

options.text: The channel opens partway, letting in half the calcium that full depolarization would allow.
options.why: The receptor behaves as an AND gate. With one condition missing, the channel stays shut.

options.text: The channel opens fully, since bound transmitter is all an NMDA receptor needs to open.
options.why: Bound transmitter is only one of the two conditions.

options.text: The receiving cell depolarizes as a result, which then expels the magnesium ion a moment later.
options.why: Nothing here depolarizes the cell. Without depolarization the plug stays.

items.stem: A receiving cell is strongly depolarized, but no transmitter has been released onto its NMDA receptors. What happens?

options.text: Nothing opens, since no transmitter is bound; only both conditions together let calcium in.
options.why: Correct. Depolarization alone does nothing, because nothing is bound.

options.text: The channels open, since depolarization expels the magnesium plug and that is all they need.
options.why: Expelling the plug is one condition. Transmitter must also be bound.

options.text: Calcium leaks in slowly, since a depolarized cell draws calcium through any channel.
options.why: The NMDA receptor stays shut without bound transmitter.

options.text: The synapse weakens, since depolarization without transmitter is the signal for depression.
options.why: That is not what the chapter describes; nothing happens at the receptor.

items.stem: Module 4 treated AND as an operation a threshold unit computes. How is the NMDA receptor's AND different?

options.text: It is built from a protein, a magnesium ion and a voltage: a truth table made of chemistry.
options.why: Correct. The same logical operation, physically realized in a receptor.

options.text: It computes OR rather than AND, since either condition is enough to let some calcium into the cell.
options.why: Either condition alone lets nothing in. It is AND.

options.text: It is set by a threshold like Module 4's unit, since the receptor opens once enough transmitter has bound.
options.why: What opens it is two conditions together, not an amount of transmitter crossing a threshold.

options.text: It is not an AND at all, since a receptor cannot compute and only a network of units can.
options.why: The chapter calls it a truth table built out of chemistry, and in this case the name is the mechanism.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Responding only when two things occur together, and to neither of them alone".

options.text: coincidence detection
options.why: Correct. It is what the NMDA receptor does.

options.text: contingency
options.why: A contingency is a relationship in the world, not a way of responding.

options.text: classical conditioning
options.why: Classical conditioning is learning a link between events, not the act of responding to them together.

options.text: synaptic competition
options.why: Synaptic competition is a contest among synapses for a shared resource.

items.stem: The chapter says that for the NMDA receptor, "coincidence detection" is not a description of the mechanism from a distance. What does it mean?

options.text: Here the name and the physical process coincide: the receptor literally responds to two conditions at once.
options.why: Correct. Elsewhere a name is laid over a mechanism; here it is the mechanism.

options.text: The name is inaccurate, since the receptor merely detects calcium rather than any coincidence between two separate events.
options.why: The receptor detects two conditions together, which is exactly coincidence.

options.text: The name belongs to the algorithmic level only, so it cannot be applied to a receptor at all.
options.why: The chapter's point is that the name applies at the physical level too, directly.

options.text: The name describes what the whole animal does, and the receptor only contributes a small part of it.
options.why: The name is claimed for the receptor itself, not only for the animal.

items.stem: The sending cell fires 10 milliseconds before the receiving cell fires, again and again. What happens to the synapse?

options.text: It strengthens.
options.why: Correct. Sender first, within the window, strengthens.

options.text: It weakens.
options.why: Weakening follows when the sending cell fires just after the receiving cell.

options.text: It stays the same.
options.why: Ten milliseconds is well within the window where order matters.

options.text: It is pruned.
options.why: Pruning is developmental and is not what spike order does.

items.stem: At two synapses, the sending cell fires 10 milliseconds after the receiving cell at the first, and 200 milliseconds before it at the second. What happens at each?

options.text: The first weakens; the second changes very little, being far outside the window.
options.why: Correct. Order matters within a few tens of milliseconds, and little happens beyond that.

options.text: The first strengthens; the second strengthens even more, since the sending cell fired well before.
options.why: Firing after weakens, and 200 milliseconds is outside the window in either direction.

options.text: Both weaken, since in neither case did the two cells fire at exactly the same moment.
options.why: Exact simultaneity is not required. Order within the window decides.

options.text: Both strengthen, since the two cells were active within a fraction of a second of each other.
options.why: A fraction of a second is too long for the second synapse, and the first has the wrong order.

items.stem: What does spike-timing-dependent plasticity mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: The dependence of synaptic change on the order of two cells' spikes, within a window tens of milliseconds wide.
options.why: Correct. Sender first strengthens; sender second weakens.

options.text: A lasting strengthening of a synapse, produced when the two cells it joins are repeatedly active together.
options.why: That is long-term potentiation, which says nothing about order.

options.text: A fading mark left on whatever was recently active, so that a signal arriving later can find the right connections.
options.why: That is an eligibility trace, which lasts far longer than a few tens of milliseconds.

options.text: A window of development during which experience has an outsized and lasting effect on how a system is wired.
options.why: That is a critical period, measured in months or years rather than milliseconds.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The dependence of synaptic change on the order of two cells' spikes: the sending cell firing first strengthens the synapse, the reverse weakens it, within a window tens of milliseconds wide".

options.text: spike-timing-dependent plasticity
options.why: Correct. It carries order at a single synapse.

options.text: long-term potentiation
options.why: Long-term potentiation is only the strengthening, without the dependence on order.

options.text: temporal-difference learning
options.why: Temporal-difference learning compares estimates across time at the algorithmic level.

options.text: eligibility trace
options.why: An eligibility trace is a fading mark on connections, not a rule about spike order.

items.stem: A rule that responds to co-occurrence cannot tell a cause from a coincidence. How does spike timing at a synapse partly answer that objection?

options.text: A cell that helped fire another fired first; a merely coincident one is as likely to fire just after.
options.why: Correct. Some of the difference between causing and accompanying is carried in milliseconds of order.

options.text: A cell that caused another to fire does so more strongly, so causes are picked out by the size of the spike.
options.why: Spikes do not grow with causal importance. Order is what differs.

options.text: A coincident cell fires at a different rate from a causal one, so the synapse can tell them apart by rate alone.
options.why: The chapter's answer is about order, not rate.

options.text: A synapse checks with other synapses on the cell to see whether the input was needed to fire it at all.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter's account involves synapses checking with one another.

items.stem: The chapter said earlier that an association across time must record which event came first, as with a rustle before a predator and a carcass after one. What does spike timing contribute to keeping that promise?

options.text: A synapse registers order itself, strengthening when the sender fires ahead and weakening when it fires behind.
options.why: Correct. The lecture calls it that record, at a single synapse.

options.text: A synapse registers the delay between two events however long it is, so a rustle minutes before a predator can be linked.
options.why: The window is a few tens of milliseconds. Longer delays need other machinery.

options.text: A synapse registers which event mattered more, strengthening only for the more dangerous of two events.
options.why: Spike timing registers order, not importance.

options.text: A synapse registers nothing about order; the promise is kept instead by the brain structures of a later module.
options.why: Order is registered at the synapse, which is exactly the point.

items.stem: The lecture lists the AND gates the course has met: Module 4's threshold unit, the cnidarian's gated stinging cell, and the NMDA receptor. What do all three have in common?

options.text: Each responds only when two conditions hold together, and to neither of them alone.
options.why: Correct. The same logical operation, realized three different ways.

options.text: Each is learned during the animal's life, so none of them is present until experience builds it.
options.why: Module 4's threshold unit was fixed in advance, and the receptor is a molecule; neither is learned.

options.text: Each responds whenever either condition holds, so a single signal is enough to set it off.
options.why: That is OR. All three need both conditions.

options.text: Each is found only in vertebrates, since logical operations need a centralized brain to carry them out.
options.why: The stinging cell belongs to a cnidarian. Logical operations are not a vertebrate privilege.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how the NMDA receptor works as an AND gate, and why the chapter says the name "coincidence detection" is the mechanism here rather than a description of it.
items.answer: The NMDA receptor opens only when two conditions hold at once. Transmitter from the sending cell must be bound to it, and the receiving cell must already be depolarized enough to expel a magnesium ion that plugs the channel. Transmitter alone does nothing because the plug stays in, and depolarization alone does nothing because nothing is bound. With both, the channel opens and calcium enters, setting the lasting change in motion. That is a truth table made of chemistry. Elsewhere a computational name describes a mechanism from a distance, but here the receptor literally responds to two things together, so the name and the mechanism coincide.
rubric: States both conditions: bound transmitter and prior depolarization.
Explains that the magnesium plug is what depolarization removes.
Says either alone does nothing and both let calcium in.
Explains that here the computational name is the physical mechanism.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe spike-timing-dependent plasticity and explain how it lets a synapse carry some of the difference between a cause and a coincidence.
items.answer: If the sending cell fires shortly before the receiving cell, the synapse strengthens; if it fires shortly after, the synapse weakens. Order matters only within a window a few tens of milliseconds wide. A plain co-occurrence rule cannot tell a cause from a coincidence, since both look like two things happening together. But a cell that helped fire another must have fired first, while a cell that merely happened to be active is as likely to have fired just after as just before. So the synapse, by being sensitive to order, strengthens causes more reliably than coincidences.
rubric: States the direction rule: sender first strengthens, sender second weakens.
Gives the window as a few tens of milliseconds.
Notes that co-occurrence alone cannot separate cause from coincidence.
Explains that a causal input fires first while a coincidental one may fire after.

items.stem: In a few sentences, define long-term potentiation and long-term depression, and explain why having both answers a limitation of Hebb's rule.
items.answer: Long-term potentiation is a lasting strengthening of a synapse when its two cells are repeatedly active together. Long-term depression is a lasting weakening when the sending cell is repeatedly active while the receiving cell stays quiet. Hebb's rule in its basic form can only add, so a synapse running it would be a one-way ratchet. Long-term depression means a real coincidence-driven synapse can move its weight in both directions.
rubric: Defines long-term potentiation as strengthening from joint activity.
Defines long-term depression as weakening when only the sender is active.
Identifies Hebb's rule's limit as only being able to add.
Explains that depression lets the weight move both ways.

pools.title: Runaway and Its Bounds, Aplysia, and the Three-Factor Rule
pools.covers: reading §5.3.5, §5.3.6, §5.3.7 · lecture 5.3 slides runaway_and_bounds, aplysia, three_factor_rule, dopamine_prediction_error · lab (the bounds)

items.stem: Why would a Hebbian synapse, left to itself, run away?

options.text: Strengthening makes the receiver fire more readily, making the pairing more reliable, which strengthens it further.
options.why: Correct. It is a positive feedback loop, and Module 3 said such loops run to completion.

options.text: Strengthening uses up the transmitter in the sending cell, so the synapse has to strengthen further to make up for it.
options.why: Nothing in the account runs out. The loop feeds on itself.

options.text: Strengthening makes the sending cell fire less often, so each spike has to count for more to keep the pairing going.
options.why: A stronger synapse makes the receiver fire more readily, not the sender less often.

options.text: Strengthening is triggered by a broadcast signal that never switches off once a reward has been delivered to the animal.
options.why: A basic Hebbian synapse needs no broadcast signal. The runaway comes from the pair itself.

items.stem: If nothing bounded Hebbian strengthening, what would a nervous system end up like?

options.text: Every useful connection saturated and every cell responding to everything, which makes the cells useless.
options.why: Correct. A cell that responds to everything tells the rest of the system nothing.

options.text: Every connection weakened to nothing and every cell silent, since strengthening would use up what synapses need.
options.why: Unbounded strengthening saturates connections rather than silencing them.

options.text: Every cell tuned more sharply to one stimulus, since strengthening would make each cell pickier over time.
options.why: Runaway strengthening makes cells less selective, not more.

options.text: Every connection exactly as it began, since strengthening and weakening would balance out on their own.
options.why: Without bounds, nothing balances the strengthening. That is why bounds are needed.

items.stem: What two things bound Hebbian strengthening, according to the chapter?

options.text: Long-term depression, which weakens a synapse directly, and synaptic competition for a limited, shared resource.
options.why: Correct. The second is the answer to the question about weakening left open by Hebb's rule.

options.text: The learning rate, which keeps each step small, and discounting, which makes every later step count for a little less.
options.why: Those belong to rules at the algorithmic level. The chapter names two physical bounds.

options.text: Habituation, which reduces a repeated response, and sensitization, which raises responses after a shock.
options.why: These are tier-one kinds of learning, not bounds on strengthening.

options.text: A broadcast reward signal, which stops strengthening after success, and fatigue, which stops it after heavy use.
options.why: Neither is named as a bound on runaway strengthening.

items.stem: What does synaptic competition mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Synapses onto one cell competing for a limited shared resource, so strengthening some weakens others.
options.why: Correct. It is one of the two bounds on runaway strengthening.

options.text: A lasting weakening of a synapse, produced when the sending cell is active while the receiving cell is not.
options.why: That is long-term depression, which weakens a synapse directly rather than through its neighbors.

options.text: The cutting back of an early overabundance of connections, with activity deciding which ones survive.
options.why: That is pruning, which removes connections during development.

options.text: Mechanisms that hold total activity and total synaptic strength within a range, bounding what plasticity does.
options.why: That is homeostatic plasticity, a related but broader set of mechanisms.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Rivalry among the synapses onto one cell for a limited shared resource, so that strengthening some of them weakens others".

options.text: synaptic competition
options.why: Correct. It weakens a synapse as a consequence of strengthening its neighbors.

options.text: long-term depression
options.why: Long-term depression weakens a synapse directly, not by way of its neighbors.

options.text: homeostatic plasticity
options.why: Homeostatic plasticity holds total activity within a range, a broader idea.

options.text: competitive exclusion
options.why: Competitive exclusion is a term from ecology for species competing over a niche; this course uses it for nothing at the synapse.

items.stem: One input to a set of cells stops carrying useful signal, while the other inputs to the same cells stay active. With synaptic competition in force, what happens to the quiet input?

options.text: It loses ground it already held, because the busy neighbors keep claiming the shared resource.
options.why: Correct. The lecture ties this to the deprived eye, which loses connections it had.

options.text: It keeps the ground it already held but gains no more, since an idle synapse is simply left alone.
options.why: Without competition that would be right. Competition means it loses what it had.

options.text: It gains ground, since an input that goes quiet frees up resources for itself.
options.why: Resources go to the active inputs, not the quiet one.

options.text: It is protected from change altogether, since only synapses carrying signal can be changed.
options.why: Competition acts on the quiet input precisely because the others are active.

items.stem: A student repeats a common claim: Hebbian learning has no way to weaken a connection. What does the chapter say?

options.text: The claim is false: one mechanism weakens a synapse directly, and another weakens it as neighbors strengthen.
options.why: Correct. Long-term depression and synaptic competition both weaken.

options.text: The claim is true, and that is why a separate learning system is needed to weaken any connection in the brain.
options.why: The chapter says outright that the claim is false.

options.text: The claim is true of synapses but false of whole cells, which can lower how readily they fire.
options.why: Synapses themselves can weaken, by two mechanisms.

options.text: The claim is false, but only because a broadcast reward signal can reverse every Hebbian change.
options.why: A modulator can reverse a change, but the two mechanisms named here work without one.

items.stem: Why has Aplysia, a sea slug, been so useful for tracing learning to synapses?

options.text: It has only about twenty thousand neurons, many large enough to see without a microscope and to record from singly.
options.why: Correct. Its gill-withdrawal reflex could then be traced cell by cell.

options.text: It has more neurons than any vertebrate, so every kind of learning can be found somewhere or other in its nervous system.
options.why: It has far fewer neurons than a vertebrate. Size of cells, not number, is the advantage.

options.text: It has no synapses at all, so its learning must happen inside single cells and is easier to measure there.
options.why: Its learning was traced to particular synapses.

options.text: It learns just one thing, so any change found in its nervous system must be the change behind that learning.
options.why: Its one reflex carries three kinds of learning.

items.stem: After a shock to its tail, an Aplysia withdraws its gill more vigorously in response to almost anything. Which kind of learning is this?

options.text: Sensitization.
options.why: Correct. The same reflex also shows habituation and classical conditioning, each traced to particular synapses between identified cells.

options.text: Habituation.
options.why: Habituation would be a weaker response to a touch repeated without consequence.

options.text: Classical conditioning.
options.why: Classical conditioning needs a touch paired with the shock, and this response is to almost anything.

options.text: Extinction.
options.why: Extinction is the fading of a learned response, not a general rise.

items.stem: What produces sensitization in Aplysia's gill-withdrawal reflex?

options.text: A third cell releasing serotonin onto the connection between the reflex cells, changing the sender's transmitter release.
options.why: Correct. Neither cell in the reflex pathway changes on its own.

options.text: A change inside the sensory cell itself, which becomes more excitable after a shock without any signal from other nearby cells.
options.why: The chapter says the change is not inside either of the two cells in the pathway.

options.text: A change inside the motor cell, which grows more receptors after a shock and so responds to any input more strongly.
options.why: The change is driven from outside the pair, by a third cell.

options.text: A new synapse growing between the siphon and the gill, bypassing the original reflex pathway entirely.
options.why: No new pathway is formed. A third cell modulates the existing connection.

items.stem: What is the broader significance of the third cell in Aplysia's sensitization?

options.text: A signal from outside the pair changed what the pair does, found first in an invertebrate.
options.why: Correct. It is the three-factor idea, before it is named.

options.text: It shows that learning requires a brain, since the third cell sits in Aplysia's central ganglion.
options.why: The point is about a signal from outside a pair, not about brains.

options.text: It shows that serotonin is the only chemical involved in learning, since it is the one released here.
options.why: One example does not make serotonin the only signal; dopamine is named later as another.

options.text: It shows that sensitization is not really learning, since a third cell rather than the reflex itself changed.
options.why: Sensitization is learning by the chapter's definition. The third cell shows how it is regulated.

items.stem: What does three-factor rule mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Two cells' activity makes a synapse eligible; a signal from elsewhere settles whether, and which way, it changes.
options.why: Correct. The division of labor is the point.

options.text: A rule changing a weight in proportion to how active two cells were at once, needing nothing beyond those two cells.
options.why: That is Hebb's rule, which has only two factors.

options.text: A rule changing a weight in proportion to target minus actual output, scaled by the input the weight carries.
options.why: That is the delta rule, stated as a procedure.

options.text: A rule in which a synapse changes according to the order of two cells' spikes, within tens of milliseconds.
options.why: That is spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A rule in which presynaptic and postsynaptic activity together make a synapse eligible to change, and a third signal from elsewhere settles whether it changes, and in which direction".

options.text: three-factor rule
options.why: Correct. Dopamine is one of the third factors.

options.text: Hebb's rule
options.why: Hebb's rule uses only the two cells, with no third signal.

options.text: temporal-difference learning
options.why: Temporal-difference learning is a family of rules comparing estimates; the three-factor rule is the synaptic arrangement that could carry its error.

options.text: actor–critic
options.why: Actor–critic divides judging from choosing; it is not the synaptic arrangement.

items.stem: In the three-factor rule, what does the local pair of cells settle, and what does the third factor settle?

options.text: The pair settles which synapses are eligible; the third factor, whether and which way they change.
options.why: Correct. Eligibility is local; the decision comes from elsewhere.

options.text: The pair settles the direction of the change; the third factor settles only how large the change is.
options.why: The third factor can reverse the sign, not merely scale the size.

options.text: The pair settles whether a change happens; the third factor settles which synapses the change reaches.
options.why: The roles are reversed. The pair marks candidates; the third factor decides.

options.text: The pair settles nothing without the third factor; the third factor settles eligibility and direction together.
options.why: The pair does settle something on its own: which synapses are eligible.

items.stem: In one preparation, the same pairing of sending and receiving activity strengthens a synapse when one modulatory receptor is engaged, and weakens it when another is. What does that show about the third factor?

options.text: It is not a volume knob on a change already decided; it can reverse the sign of the change.
options.why: Correct. The obvious guess, that it only scales the change, is wrong.

options.text: It scales the size of a change that the pair of cells has already decided on, and does nothing more.
options.why: If it only scaled the size, the same pairing could not produce opposite changes.

options.text: It does nothing on its own, and the direction is set entirely by the timing of the two cells' spikes.
options.why: The pairing was held the same, so timing cannot explain the difference.

options.text: It works only in invertebrates, since vertebrate synapses always strengthen when their cells fire together.
options.why: The chapter does not restrict sign reversal to invertebrates.

items.stem: A coincidence detector on its own is Hebbian and has no term for how things went. What turns the same detector into a reward learner?

options.text: A signal arriving when an outcome beat expectation, with the detection itself unaltered.
options.why: Correct. This is the bridge from Hebb's limits to learning from outcomes.

options.text: A second coincidence detector wired alongside it, so that two detectors together can compare outcomes.
options.why: The chapter's bridge is a broadcast signal, not a second detector.

options.text: A higher learning rate, so that each coincidence changes the synapse more when a reward is present.
options.why: The learning rate scales changes but carries no information about how things went.

options.text: A longer timing window, so that the detector can include the reward among the events it counts as coincident.
options.why: Widening the window does not supply a verdict on how things went.

items.stem: What does reward prediction error mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A signal reporting an outcome as better or worse than predicted, broadcast widely.
options.why: Correct. Dopaminergic cells carry one, released across a wide stretch of tissue.

options.text: The gap between what was expected and what occurred, as it appears inside Rescorla and Wagner's rule.
options.why: That is prediction error in general. A reward prediction error is a broadcast signal about how things went.

options.text: A consequence that makes the response it followed more likely in that situation afterward.
options.why: That is a reinforcer, a consequence in the world rather than a signal inside the animal.

options.text: An estimate of how well things will go from a given situation onward, revised as the situation changes.
options.why: That is value; the reward prediction error reports a change against it.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A signal reporting that an outcome was better or worse than predicted, broadcast widely rather than addressed to particular cells".

options.text: reward prediction error
options.why: Correct. It is the verdict of reinforcement learning, made physical.

options.text: prediction error
options.why: Prediction error is the general gap between expected and actual, which need not be broadcast or about reward.

options.text: eligibility trace
options.why: An eligibility trace marks connections; it does not report outcomes.

options.text: temporal-difference learning
options.why: Temporal-difference learning is a family of rules; the broadcast signal described is what such a rule's error can look like in tissue.

items.stem: A monkey has learned that a light is always followed by juice. The light comes on and the juice arrives exactly as usual. What do its dopaminergic cells do when the juice arrives?

options.text: Nothing different: they stay at baseline, since the outcome matched the prediction.
options.why: Correct. No prediction error, and so no change from baseline.

options.text: They fire well above baseline, since juice is a reward and dopamine cells fire whenever a reward arrives.
options.why: That treats dopamine as a reward signal. It reports the difference from prediction.

options.text: They fall below baseline, since a reward that is fully expected is treated as a disappointment.
options.why: Falling below baseline happens when an outcome is worse than predicted.

options.text: They fire above baseline at a lower rate than at first, since the juice is still good but no longer as good.
options.why: Once fully predicted, the outcome produces no change at all.

items.stem: The same monkey sees the light, but this time no juice arrives. What do its dopaminergic cells do at the moment the juice would have come?

options.text: Fall below baseline, since the outcome was worse than predicted.
options.why: Correct. An omitted reward is a negative prediction error.

options.text: Stay at baseline, since nothing happened and dopamine cells respond only to events that occur.
options.why: The absence of an expected reward is itself worse than predicted.

options.text: Fire above baseline, since the light was seen and it has become a stand-in for the reward.
options.why: Any response to the light itself would come when the light appears, not at the missed juice.

options.text: Fire above baseline at first and then fall, since the cells check twice before reporting a loss.
options.why: The chapter describes a fall below baseline, nothing more elaborate.

items.stem: Module 4 gave dopamine a role in wanting and pursuit, which it kept separate from liking. How does this chapter's account of dopamine relate to that?

options.text: It adds a reward prediction error as the rest of the story, without taking back the role in pursuit.
options.why: Correct. The chapter says Module 4 held the rest back, and here is the rest. Neither account makes dopamine a signal of pleasure.

options.text: It replaces Module 4's account, showing that dopamine is really the pleasure an animal feels when a reward arrives.
options.why: Neither module makes dopamine a pleasure signal, and a fully predicted reward produces no change at all.

options.text: It shows Module 4's account was wrong, since a cell reporting prediction error cannot also play a part in pursuit.
options.why: The chapter presents the prediction-error role as an addition, not a correction.

options.text: It applies only to the worm, where dopamine reports prediction error, while Module 4's account applies to vertebrates.
options.why: The prediction-error recordings were made in vertebrates, largely primates.

items.stem: The chapter calls the reward prediction error the one broadcast number of reinforcement learning, made physical. What does that mean?

options.text: The verdict on how things went, a single quantity, is carried by cells whose signal spreads widely.
options.why: Correct. It is not addressed to particular connections, which is why something else must mark them.

options.text: The target supervised learning needs, the correct output, is carried by cells that deliver it to each connection that erred.
options.why: Dopamine reports better or worse than predicted, not the correct output.

options.text: The next input prediction learning needs is carried by cells that release it just before the input arrives.
options.why: Dopamine does not carry the next input; it reports how things went.

options.text: The co-activity Hebbian learning needs is carried by cells that fire whenever two other cells fire together.
options.why: Hebbian learning needs nothing broadcast at all.

items.stem: A student argues that because dopamine is found in worms, the worm's learning must run on a dopamine reward prediction error. What does the chapter say?

options.text: The recordings were made in vertebrates, largely primates; how far down the tree it goes is a separate question.
options.why: Correct. The evidence comes from animals that arrived long after the mechanism did.

options.text: The student is right, since any molecule found in two different animals must be doing the same job in both of them.
options.why: Module 4 already cautioned that conserved molecules need not do identical jobs, and this chapter keeps the question open.

options.text: The student is wrong, since the chapter shows that worms use serotonin rather than dopamine for all their learning.
options.why: The chapter makes no such claim about worms.

options.text: The student is wrong, since the chapter shows reward prediction errors exist in primates and nowhere else.
options.why: The chapter does not say they exist only in primates. It says the evidence comes largely from them.

items.stem: The lecture says the dopamine result mattered so much because the signal is also something else the module has met. What?

options.text: The temporal-difference error of the critic: a quantity from an algorithm, found in cells.
options.why: Correct. An algorithm built for machines and a recording from cells arrived at the same quantity.

options.text: The eligibility trace of each connection, so the cells mark which synapses were recently active.
options.why: Dopamine is a broadcast signal, not a local mark on each connection.

options.text: The learning rate of every synapse, so the cells set how much each occasion changes a weight.
options.why: The dopamine signal reports how things went, not a fixed step size.

options.text: The value of each situation, so the cells hold an estimate of how well things will go from here.
options.why: Value is what the critic estimates; dopamine reports the error in that estimate.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the three-factor rule, including what the third factor can do that a volume knob could not, and how the rule turns a Hebbian coincidence detector into a reward learner.
items.answer: The three-factor rule uses presynaptic activity, postsynaptic activity, and a third signal broadcast from elsewhere. The local pair settles which synapses are eligible to change, and the third factor settles whether they change and in which direction. It is not a volume knob, because the same pairing can produce strengthening or weakening depending on which modulatory receptor is engaged, so the third factor can reverse the sign of the change. A coincidence detector on its own is Hebbian and has no term for how things went. Add a signal that arrives when things went better than expected, and the same detector becomes a reward learner without any change to the detection itself.
rubric: Names the three factors.
Assigns eligibility to the pair and the decision to the third factor.
States that the third factor can reverse the sign, not just scale.
Explains how adding a better-than-expected signal makes a reward learner.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe how dopaminergic cells respond to outcomes better than, worse than, and exactly as predicted, say how this fits with Module 4's account of dopamine, and state the limit on the evidence.
items.answer: Dopaminergic cells fire above baseline when an outcome is better than predicted, fall below baseline when it is worse, and do not change when it arrives exactly as predicted. That is a reward prediction error. Module 4 gave dopamine a role in wanting and pursuit and held the rest back, so this is an addition to that account rather than a replacement. The recordings were made in vertebrates, largely primates, so how far down the animal tree the arrangement extends is a separate question.
rubric: Gives all three responses: above, below, unchanged.
Names the pattern a reward prediction error.
Presents it as adding to Module 4's wanting-and-pursuit role, not replacing it.
States that the evidence comes largely from primates and does not settle the rest of the tree.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why a Hebbian synapse would run away if left alone, and name the two things that bound it.
items.answer: Strengthening a synapse makes the receiving cell fire more readily, which makes the pairing more reliable, which strengthens the synapse further. That positive feedback would leave every useful connection saturated and every cell responding to everything. Long-term depression bounds it by weakening a synapse directly. Synaptic competition bounds it because synapses onto one cell share a limited resource, so strengthening some weakens others. So the claim that Hebbian learning cannot weaken a connection is false.
rubric: Describes the positive feedback loop.
Says the unbounded result is saturated connections and cells responding to everything.
Names long-term depression as one bound.
Names synaptic competition, with the shared resource, as the other.

items.stem: In the lab's salt dish at a high learning rate with both bounds off, the salt weight pinned at its ceiling. What did the weight trace do once Weakening was switched on?

options.text: It went down as well as up, and no longer sat pinned at the ceiling.
options.why: Correct. A direct weakening mechanism keeps the weight from running to saturation.

options.text: It stayed pinned at the ceiling, since weakening only acts on weights that are already low.
options.why: With Weakening on, the trace moved in both directions and left the ceiling.

options.text: It fell to zero and stayed there, since weakening removes whatever strengthening builds.
options.why: Weakening bounded the weight; it did not erase it.

options.text: It rose past the ceiling, since weakening frees room for more strengthening.
options.why: Nothing in the lab pushed the weight above its ceiling.

items.stem: In the salt dish with Competition switched on, the salt weight leveled off on its own. With almond odor then added at every site as a second cue, how did the two weights end up?

options.text: They shared the amount one cue had held alone, each settling at about half of it.
options.why: Correct. What a connection needs in order to grow is limited and shared, so two cues split it.

options.text: Each reached the level salt had reached alone, so adding a cue doubled the total strength.
options.why: Competition holds the total fixed. Adding a cue splits it rather than adding to it.

options.text: Salt kept its full level and almond stayed at zero, since salt had arrived first.
options.why: Under competition the two cues divided the resource; neither kept it all.

options.text: Both ran to the ceiling, since competition only acts when one cue is present.
options.why: Competition acts precisely when several inputs share one cell's resource.

pools.title: The Trace Made Physical, and Learning's Schedule
pools.covers: reading §5.3.8, §5.3.9 · lecture 5.3 slides trace_made_physical, learning_has_a_schedule, what_the_evidence_supports

items.stem: What physical counterpart to the eligibility trace does the chapter describe?

options.text: A just-active synapse left in an altered state fading over seconds; a modulatory signal inside that window makes the change last.
options.why: Correct. A signal arriving after the window has closed does nothing.

options.text: A just-active synapse that grows a new branch within seconds, which a later signal then prunes or keeps.
options.why: Nothing grows here. The synapse is left in a temporary altered state.

options.text: A just-active synapse that stays permanently marked, so that any later signal, however late, can still find it.
options.why: The mark fades over seconds. A late signal finds nothing.

options.text: A just-active synapse that releases its own reward signal, so no signal from anywhere else is ever needed to make the change last.
options.why: The lasting change needs a neuromodulatory signal from elsewhere, arriving in time.

items.stem: Two synapses are active together once. A modulatory signal reaches the first a second later, and the second only after half a minute. What happens at each?

options.text: The one reached within a second changes lastingly, inside the fading window; the other does not.
options.why: Correct. The window lasts seconds, and a signal after it has closed does nothing.

options.text: Both change lastingly, since both synapses were active and both received the signal in the end.
options.why: Timing matters. The altered state has faded before the second signal arrives.

options.text: Neither changes, since a modulatory signal has to arrive at the same instant as the activity to have any effect.
options.why: The point of the altered state is that a signal can arrive a little later and still count.

options.text: The second changes more, since a longer wait lets the altered state build up before the signal arrives.
options.why: The altered state decays; it does not build up.

items.stem: An algorithmic proposal, the eligibility trace, turns out to have a physical counterpart. What does that convergence show, according to the chapter?

options.text: That what the algorithm needed is the sort of thing a synapse can be, not that the algorithm is correct.
options.why: Correct. The chapter is careful to keep the two claims apart.

options.text: That the algorithm is correct, since finding its parts in tissue is the strongest test an algorithm can pass.
options.why: The chapter says outright that the convergence does not show the algorithm is correct.

options.text: That the physical account came first, and the algorithm was only ever a description of what synapses already do.
options.why: The algorithm was invented to solve a timing problem, before its counterpart was found.

options.text: That the algorithm is wrong, since a physical process that fades cannot be the same as an idealized mark.
options.why: The convergence supports the algorithm's plausibility; it does not refute it.

items.stem: What kind of signal does a climbing fiber in the cerebellum carry, according to the chapter?

options.text: An error signal for one output cell in particular: one source, one target cell, one instruction.
options.why: Correct. It specifies a different output item by item, the teacher case.

options.text: A single number broadcast widely, reporting whether things went better or worse than expected.
options.why: That is the reward prediction error. The climbing fiber is addressed to one cell.

options.text: A fading mark on recently active synapses, so that a later broadcast signal can find them.
options.why: That is the eligibility trace's job, not the climbing fiber's.

options.text: A running count of how often a stimulus has occurred, so that the cell can stop responding to it.
options.why: That is a tier-one requirement, and not what the climbing fiber carries.

items.stem: Of the four kinds of learning, which does the cerebellum's climbing-fiber arrangement correspond to, and why is that notable?

options.text: Supervised learning, the teacher case, which the chapter called the hardest for a nervous system to arrange.
options.why: Correct. Here is a structure arranged around exactly that signal.

options.text: Reinforcement learning, the verdict case, since the fiber reports whether the whole animal did well.
options.why: The fiber's signal is addressed to one cell and specifies its error, not one broadcast verdict.

options.text: Hebbian learning, the unsupervised case, since the fiber and the output cell fire together.
options.why: The fiber carries an instruction, which is exactly what Hebbian learning lacks.

options.text: Prediction learning, the self-supervised case, since the fiber carries the next input that the world delivers to it.
options.why: The fiber is a specific error signal for a cell, not the world's next input.

items.stem: What does synaptogenesis mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: The formation of new synapses, which early in life produces far more connections than will survive.
options.why: Correct. Pruning follows, cutting the surplus back by activity.

options.text: The cutting back of an early overabundance of connections, with activity deciding which ones survive.
options.why: That is pruning, which comes after the proliferation.

options.text: A lasting strengthening of a synapse, produced when the two cells it joins are repeatedly active together.
options.why: That is long-term potentiation, a change to an existing synapse.

options.text: The property of nervous tissue that allows a connection, or a cell, to undergo a lasting change.
options.why: That is plasticity, the general property rather than one process.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "The cutting back of an early overabundance of connections, with activity deciding which ones survive".

options.text: pruning
options.why: Correct. The competitive rule does the deciding.

options.text: synaptogenesis
options.why: Synaptogenesis is the proliferation that comes first.

options.text: long-term depression
options.why: Long-term depression weakens a synapse; it does not remove it.

options.text: extinction
options.why: Extinction is a learned response fading when its outcome stops.

items.stem: What decides which connections survive pruning, and what does that mean for a young nervous system?

options.text: The competitive rule, running while the animal is being built; it is settling which connections will exist to have weights.
options.why: Correct. Early on it is not merely adjusting weights.

options.text: A genetic list of which connections to keep, so that pruning is fixed in advance and experience plays no part in deciding what survives.
options.why: The chapter says activity decides which connections last.

options.text: A broadcast reward signal, so that connections active during rewarding moments are the ones kept.
options.why: The deciding rule is competition, not a reward signal.

options.text: The age of each connection, so that the oldest connections are kept and the newest are removed first.
options.why: Age is not the criterion. Activity, through competition, decides.

items.stem: What does critical period mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A window when experience has an outsized, lasting effect on how part of a nervous system is wired, and whose closing is active.
options.why: Correct. The closing is an active process, not a running-down.

options.text: A window after which no further learning of any kind is possible, because the nervous system has become fixed for the rest of life.
options.why: That is the overstatement the chapter rejects. A window that closes does not end learning.

options.text: The seconds after a synapse is active, during which a modulatory signal can make a change last.
options.why: That is the physical eligibility trace, on a scale of seconds rather than a period of development.

options.text: The period of early life in which synapses are formed in great profusion, before any are cut back.
options.why: That is synaptogenesis, the proliferation itself.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "A window during which experience has an outsized and lasting effect on how part of a nervous system ends up wired, and whose closing is an active process rather than a gradual running-down".

options.text: critical period
options.why: Correct. The deprived eye and infant speech sounds are the chapter's cases.

options.text: stability versus plasticity
options.why: That is the general trade-off a schedule of plasticity manages.

options.text: synaptogenesis
options.why: Synaptogenesis is the formation of new synapses.

options.text: eligibility trace
options.why: An eligibility trace lasts seconds and marks synapses.

items.stem: One eye of a young animal is closed early in life and later reopened; the same is done to an adult. What happens in each case?

options.text: The young animal's closed eye ends up with less cortical territory and does not recover it; the adult barely changes.
options.why: Correct. The inputs from the two eyes compete for territory, and early experience settles the outcome.

options.text: Both animals' closed eyes lose territory for good, since closing an eye always costs it cortical territory at any age at all.
options.why: The adult shows very little effect. That difference is what makes this a critical period.

options.text: The young animal's closed eye recovers fully once reopened; the adult's eye loses territory for good.
options.why: The pattern is the reverse: the young animal's loss persists and the adult is barely affected.

options.text: Neither animal is affected, since territory in visual cortex is fixed before birth.
options.why: Territory is settled by competition after birth, which is why early deprivation matters.

items.stem: The lecture stresses that the deprived eye's territory is lost ground, not merely ground not gained. Why does that distinction matter?

options.text: It shows competition at work: an input that stops carrying signal loses territory it already held.
options.why: Correct. The same principle that bounds runaway strengthening decides the territory.

options.text: It shows the eye itself was damaged by closing, since nothing but damage could remove territory once it was held.
options.why: Nothing says the eye was damaged. The territory was lost to the competing eye.

options.text: It shows the lost territory was never really the closed eye's, since territory is assigned at birth.
options.why: The territory had been held before deprivation. That is the point.

options.text: It shows that the open eye stopped growing, since territory can only be gained by a growing input.
options.why: The open eye gains territory; the closed eye loses it.

items.stem: What happens to human infants' ability to hear distinctions between speech sounds that their language does not use?

options.text: Much of it is lost across the first year, as the contrasts that occur come to organize how speech sounds are heard.
options.why: Correct. It is the chapter's second case of a critical period.

options.text: It grows across the first year, as exposure to many speech sounds sharpens every distinction that the infant can hear.
options.why: The distinctions an infant's language does not use are the ones that fade.

options.text: It is absent at birth and appears only in children raised hearing two languages.
options.why: Infants start out able to hear distinctions their language does not use.

options.text: It stays the same throughout life, since hearing speech sounds depends on the ear rather than on wiring.
options.why: The change is in how speech sounds are heard, which is a matter of wiring.

items.stem: The chapter says the closing of a critical period is an active process rather than a gradual running-down. What follows from that?

options.text: Plasticity has a schedule, not merely a rate, since the change in it is itself driven by the system.
options.why: Correct. A running-down would be a rate; an active closing is a schedule.

options.text: Nothing can be learned after a window closes, since the system has actively switched learning off.
options.why: A closed window changes what later learning works with. It does not end learning.

options.text: The closing can be prevented by extra stimulation, since an active process can be kept running by input.
options.why: The chapter says extra stimulation during a window is not supported as producing a better capacity.

options.text: The closing happens at the same age for every capacity, since one active process closes all windows at once.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter says every window closes at once.

items.stem: Which claim about early experience does the chapter say the evidence supports?

options.text: Experience in infancy has effects on some capacities that are large, specific, and difficult to reverse afterward.
options.why: Correct. The deprived eye and infant speech sounds are the clearest cases.

options.text: Development is a series of windows that slam shut, after which the capacity involved cannot be changed by anything.
options.why: The chapter lists this as not supported; adults go on learning.

options.text: Missing a window means the capacity it governs is gone for good, however much is tried afterward.
options.why: This is also on the not-supported list; recovery is usually partial, not nothing.

options.text: Extra stimulation during a window produces a better capacity later than ordinary experience does.
options.why: The chapter lists this as not supported, despite how often it is claimed.

items.stem: A company sells a program of intensive sounds and images for babies, promising to "use the critical period" to build a better brain. What do the chapter and the lecture say about the claim behind it?

options.text: It rests on an idea the evidence does not support: that extra stimulation during a window yields a stronger capacity later.
options.why: Correct. The lecture notes this claim is behind a great deal of marketing aimed at parents.

options.text: It is well supported, since critical periods are real windows when experience has an outsized and lasting effect on the brain's wiring.
options.why: An outsized effect of ordinary experience is not evidence that extra stimulation adds anything.

options.text: It is well supported for vision but not for hearing, since only the eye has been shown to have a window.
options.why: Both vision and speech sounds have windows. The unsupported part is the benefit of extra stimulation.

options.text: It cannot be judged, since critical periods have only ever been studied in animals and never in humans.
options.why: Infant speech perception is a human case the chapter discusses.

items.stem: A forty-year-old begins learning Japanese. What does the chapter's account of critical periods imply about this?

options.text: Learning is still possible; a closed window changes what later learning works with, but does not end it.
options.why: Correct. Adults learn second languages, and recovery from early deprivation is usually partial.

options.text: Learning is impossible, since the window for speech sounds closed in the first year of life.
options.why: The chapter says adults learn second languages.

options.text: Learning will be just as easy as for an infant, since these windows apply to vision and not to language.
options.why: The window for speech sounds is one of the chapter's two cases, so it does make a difference.

options.text: Learning is possible only for grammar, since the window that closed covers every aspect of language.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter splits language that way. The point is that learning continues.

items.stem: A learner, the chapter argued, needs a setting between changing with every experience and changing with none, and probably a schedule that moves it. Do nervous systems have one?

options.text: Yes, built from mechanisms already described: profuse early connections, pruning, and critical periods.
options.why: Correct. The schedule is made out of competition and the timing of plasticity.

options.text: No, since a nervous system keeps one fixed setting for life and relies on the learning rate alone.
options.why: The chapter says nervous systems have such a schedule.

options.text: Yes, but in vertebrates alone, since invertebrate nervous systems are too small to change their settings.
options.why: The chapter does not restrict the schedule to vertebrates.

options.text: No, since the schedule described is a feature of machine learning that animals do not share.
options.why: The schedule described is biological: synaptogenesis, pruning, critical periods.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, say what the evidence on critical periods supports, name the popular claims that go beyond it, and state the chapter's summary of what a closing window does.
items.answer: The evidence supports that early experience has effects on some capacities that are large, specific, and difficult to reverse, as with the deprived eye and infants' loss of speech-sound distinctions. It does not support the idea that development is a series of windows that slam shut, that missing one means a capacity is gone for good, or that extra stimulation during a window produces a better capacity later. Adults learn second languages, and recovery from early deprivation is usually partial. A window that closes changes what later learning has to work with; it does not end learning.
rubric: States the supported claim: large, specific, hard-to-reverse effects.
Names at least two of the three unsupported claims.
Mentions adult learning or partial recovery as counterevidence.
Gives the summary: a closing window changes later learning's material, not its possibility.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe the physical counterpart of the eligibility trace, and explain what finding it shows and what it leaves open.
items.answer: A synapse that has just been active is left in an altered state that decays over seconds. If a neuromodulatory signal arrives inside that window, the altered state becomes a lasting change; if it arrives after, nothing happens. So an algorithmic proposal invented to solve a timing problem turns out to have a physical counterpart. That does not show the algorithm is correct. It shows that what the algorithm needed is the sort of thing a synapse can be.
rubric: Describes the altered state decaying over seconds.
Says a signal inside the window makes the change last and one after does not.
Says the finding does not prove the algorithm correct.
Says it shows the needed component is physically possible at a synapse.

pools.title: Several Loci, Several Regulators, and Learning and Memory
pools.covers: reading §5.3.10, §5.3.11 · lecture 5.3 slides several_loci_several_regulators, is_it_a_memory, latent_learning

items.stem: Besides the strength of a synapse, what else can a nervous system change lastingly, according to the chapter?

options.text: How readily a cell fires at all, and whether a connection exists in the first place.
options.why: Correct. With synaptic strength, these are the three places a lasting change can be made.

options.text: The speed of each spike along its axon, and the size of each spike, which can grow with repeated use.
options.why: Neither conduction speed nor spike size is among the chapter's three places of change.

options.text: The number of neurons in the brain, which grows throughout life in step with the amount learned.
options.why: The chapter's loci concern synapses, cell excitability and connections, not the number of cells.

options.text: The genes a cell carries, which are rewritten whenever the animal learns something new.
options.why: Genes are not rewritten by learning. They are not among the three loci.

items.stem: What does intrinsic excitability mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: How readily a cell fires at all, lastingly changeable so the same input carries it further than before.
options.why: Correct. It is a lasting change to a cell rather than to one of its synapses.

options.text: A lasting strengthening of a synapse, produced when the two cells it joins are repeatedly active together.
options.why: That is long-term potentiation, a change to one synapse rather than to the cell.

options.text: Mechanisms that hold total activity and total synaptic strength within a range, bounding other plasticity.
options.why: That is homeostatic plasticity, a regulator rather than a locus.

options.text: A rise in responsiveness to stimuli generally, following something significant that has just happened to the animal.
options.why: That is sensitization, a behavioral change rather than a property of a single cell.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "How readily a cell fires at all, which can itself be lastingly changed, so that the same arriving input carries the cell further than it did before".

options.text: intrinsic excitability
options.why: Correct. It is the second of the three loci.

options.text: long-term potentiation
options.why: Long-term potentiation changes a synapse, not the cell's own readiness to fire.

options.text: sensitization
options.why: Sensitization is a behavioral rise in responsiveness.

options.text: plasticity
options.why: Plasticity is the general property; intrinsic excitability is one thing it can change.

items.stem: After training, a cell fires in response to an input that used to leave it below threshold, although none of the synapses carrying that input has changed. Which locus of change is this?

options.text: Intrinsic excitability: the cell itself is now easier to drive.
options.why: Correct. The same arriving input now carries the cell further.

options.text: Synaptic strength: the input's synapses must have strengthened.
options.why: The case rules this out; none of the synapses changed.

options.text: Whether a connection exists: a new synapse must have formed.
options.why: No new connection is described. The cell's own readiness changed.

options.text: Homeostatic plasticity: the cell has been held within a range.
options.why: Homeostatic plasticity is a regulator, not a place where change is made.

items.stem: The chapter's third locus of lasting change is whether a connection exists at all. What settles it during development?

options.text: Competition, which decides which of an early profusion of connections survive pruning.
options.why: Correct. The same competitive rule that bounds strengthening does this job while the animal is built.

options.text: A broadcast reward signal, which keeps whichever connections were active during rewarding moments.
options.why: Pruning is decided by competition, not by a reward signal.

options.text: Intrinsic excitability, which removes connections from any cell that fires too readily.
options.why: Excitability is a separate locus; it does not remove connections.

options.text: A fixed genetic program that decides every connection in advance, with no role for activity.
options.why: Activity decides which connections last, through competition.

items.stem: What does homeostatic plasticity mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Mechanisms holding total activity and synaptic strength within a range, bounding other plasticity.
options.why: Correct. With competition, it is the third regulator.

options.text: A window during which experience has an outsized and lasting effect on how part of a nervous system is wired.
options.why: That is a critical period, a window in development rather than a bounding mechanism.

options.text: How readily a cell fires at all, which can be lastingly changed so the same input carries it further.
options.why: That is intrinsic excitability, a locus rather than a regulator.

options.text: A fading mark left on whatever was recently active, so a signal arriving later can find the right connections.
options.why: That is an eligibility trace, a different regulator.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Mechanisms that hold total activity and total synaptic strength within a range, bounding what other kinds of plasticity would otherwise drive to an extreme".

options.text: homeostatic plasticity
options.why: Correct. It keeps the totals from running off.

options.text: synaptic competition
options.why: Synaptic competition is a contest for a shared resource, which works alongside homeostatic plasticity.

options.text: long-term depression
options.why: Long-term depression weakens one synapse; it is not a mechanism for holding totals.

options.text: stability versus plasticity
options.why: That is the trade-off every learner faces, not the mechanism that bounds totals.

items.stem: In the chapter's frame of three regulators, which one settles which synapses are still candidates when a signal from elsewhere arrives?

options.text: The eligibility trace.
options.why: Correct. The modulatory signal gates the change; homeostasis and competition bound the result.

options.text: The modulatory signal.
options.why: The modulatory signal gates the change and can set its direction; it does not mark candidates.

options.text: Homeostatic plasticity.
options.why: Homeostatic plasticity bounds totals rather than marking which synapses are eligible.

options.text: Intrinsic excitability.
options.why: Intrinsic excitability is a place where change is made, not a regulator.

items.stem: Having listed three places a change can be made and three regulators, the chapter says the answer "tidies" the physical account rather than complicating it. Why?

options.text: Every mechanism is one principle, a lasting effect of activity, at some locus with some regulator.
options.why: Correct. One principle, at several loci, with several regulators.

options.text: Every mechanism described turns out to be a version of long-term potentiation, so the other terms can be dropped.
options.why: The loci and regulators are genuinely different; they are unified by a principle, not reduced to one mechanism.

options.text: Every mechanism described belongs to a different kind of animal, so the account sorts them by group.
options.why: The frame sorts mechanisms by locus and regulator, not by animal.

options.text: Every mechanism described is found in the cerebellum, so the account locates learning in one structure.
options.why: The account stops at the synapse and the cell, and makes no such claim about structures.
