items.stem: Some say Hebbian plasticity is the only real learning, and everything else is just modulation of it. How does the chapter treat that claim?

options.text: As a disagreement about which word to use, since nobody disputes the pieces; naming questions are not findings.
options.why: Correct. Whether to call gating, traces and excitability learning or its regulation is a choice of words.

options.text: As a finding that settles the matter, since only Hebbian plasticity changes a synapse's strength directly.
options.why: The chapter does not treat it as settled by evidence; it treats it as a naming question.

options.text: As a false claim, since the chapter shows that modulation is the only real learning and Hebbian change is secondary.
options.why: The chapter does not invert the claim. It dissolves it.

options.text: As an open empirical question, to be settled by recordings from vertebrates of the kind that established dopamine's role.
options.why: No recording could settle a question about which word to use.

items.stem: What hedge does the chapter attach to its account of where lasting change is held?

options.text: It is where evidence now sits, not proof; storage in molecules inside cells is a live minority view.
options.why: Correct. The Further Reading points to it.

options.text: It is certain, since every lasting change has been directly observed at a synapse or in a cell's excitability.
options.why: The chapter explicitly declines to claim certainty.

options.text: It is out of date, since most researchers now think lasting changes are held in the genes rather than the synapses.
options.why: The chapter calls the molecular view a live minority argument, not the majority view.

options.text: It applies only to invertebrates, since vertebrate learning is held in brain structures rather than synapses.
options.why: The account stops at the synapse and cell for all animals; structures are a separate question.

items.stem: A synapse has changed and stayed changed. In what sense is that a memory, and why does the chapter set that sense aside?

options.text: Any persisting change from experience fits, but then bent metal remembers too; a word covering everything distinguishes nothing.
options.why: Correct. The chapter looks for the distinction that does work.

options.text: It is a memory only if the animal is aware of it, and the chapter sets the sense aside because awareness cannot be measured in animals.
options.why: Awareness is not the chapter's criterion, and it plays no part in the argument.

options.text: It is a memory if it lasts for years and not otherwise, and the chapter sets the sense aside because most synaptic changes are brief.
options.why: Duration is not the issue. The ordinary sense is too broad, not too strict.

options.text: It is a memory in every sense, and the chapter sets nothing aside, treating all learning and all memory as one thing.
options.why: The chapter distinguishes dispositions from records precisely because they are not one thing.

items.stem: What is the distinction between kinds of lasting change that the chapter says does real work?

options.text: When the use of what is stored is settled: as it is laid down, or later at retrieval.
options.why: Correct. That separates a disposition from a record.

options.text: How long what is stored lasts: minutes, days, or a lifetime.
options.why: Duration is not the distinction the chapter draws.

options.text: Where what is stored is held: in a synapse, in a cell, or in a whole brain structure.
options.why: Location is a different question. The distinction concerns when the use is settled.

options.text: Whether what is stored is conscious: noticed by the animal, or not.
options.why: Consciousness plays no part in the chapter's distinction.

items.stem: What does disposition mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: A lasting change whose use is settled as it is laid down, fixing what the animal is now likelier to do.
options.why: Correct. Learning as the chapter describes it produces dispositions.

options.text: Something kept without its use being settled, so what it is for is decided later, when it is retrieved.
options.why: That is a record, the uncommitted kind of lasting change.

options.text: A tendency to find one thing easier to learn than another, set before the learning begins.
options.why: That is an inductive bias, a prior tilt in what is easy to learn.

options.text: A behavior chosen by repeating what has worked before, which continues after its outcome has been devalued.
options.why: That is a habit, one kind of behavior rather than the general kind of lasting change.

items.stem: Which term does this course use for the following? "Something kept without its use being settled, so that what it is for is decided later, at the moment it is retrieved".

options.text: record
options.why: Correct. A record's use is settled when it is retrieved, unlike a disposition's; records are taken up in Module 10.

options.text: disposition
options.why: A disposition is committed when it is laid down.

options.text: eligibility trace
options.why: An eligibility trace is a fading mark, not a kept thing awaiting later use.

options.text: value
options.why: Value is an estimate of how well things will go.

items.stem: A worm's food-odor connection has strengthened over many meals, so it now turns toward the odor more readily. Is that a disposition or a record, in the chapter's terms?

options.text: A disposition: what the change does was fixed as it was laid down.
options.why: Correct. Learning as the chapter describes it produces dispositions.

options.text: A record: the worm has kept its meals for later use.
options.why: Nothing about particular meals was kept; only a tendency.

options.text: Both: the change is a disposition now and a record later.
options.why: A change committed at encoding is not later uncommitted.

options.text: Neither: a strengthened connection is not a lasting change at all.
options.why: A strengthened connection that persists is exactly a lasting change.

items.stem: Why does the vocabulary of encoding, storage and retrieval sound strange when applied to a sea anemone that has habituated to a frond?

options.text: Nothing is retrieved: the change acts whenever the touch recurs, and retrieval belongs to uncommitted records.
options.why: Correct. The three-part decomposition belongs to records, not dispositions.

options.text: Anemones have no brain, and the vocabulary of retrieval can only be applied to animals with one.
options.why: The chapter's reason is about commitment, not brains.

options.text: Habituation is not learning, so no vocabulary of storage applies to it in the first place.
options.why: Habituation is learning by the chapter's definition.

options.text: The anemone's change is too brief to be stored, since habituation fades within seconds of the last touch it feels.
options.why: The chapter treats habituation as a lasting change. The strangeness is about retrieval.

items.stem: An animal's weights have been shaped by hundreds of meals. What can those weights tell an observer, and what can they never tell?

options.text: What tends to happen, but never what happened on a particular occasion, since no occasion was kept.
options.why: Correct. A weight is a residue; an animal whose learning is all dispositional cannot revisit an occasion.

options.text: What happened on each occasion, but never what tends to happen, since each meal is stored separately.
options.why: That reverses it. The weights hold a tendency, not a list of events.

options.text: Both what tends to happen and what happened, since each meal left its own trace in the weight.
options.why: Each meal changed the weight, but the weight keeps only the sum of those changes.

options.text: Neither, since weights hold nothing about the world and only reflect the animal's genes.
options.why: Weights shaped by experience do reflect something about the world: what tends to happen.

items.stem: A bell and a light are paired with each other, with nothing following either. Later the light alone is paired with food. The animal now responds to the bell too. Why is this a hard case for purely dispositional learning?

options.text: When the bell and the light were linked, no use for the link had yet been settled.
options.why: Correct. A disposition is committed when laid down; this link was not.

options.text: The bell was paired with food directly at some point, or the animal could not respond to it the way it now does.
options.why: The bell was never paired with food. That is what makes the result striking.

options.text: The animal must have habituated to the bell, which is why it now responds more strongly to it.
options.why: Habituation lowers a response; here a new response appears.

options.text: The light was blocked by the bell, so all the learning about food went to the bell instead.
options.why: Blocking concerns cues present together with the outcome; here the bell was never there with food.

items.stem: Rats wander a maze with no food and seem to learn nothing. When food is then placed in the maze, they reach it about as efficiently as rats rewarded from the start. What does this show?

options.text: Something was picked up while they wandered that was not yet committed to any use.
options.why: Correct. It is latent learning, and it is where a disposition stops being enough.

options.text: The rats had learned nothing at all, and simply got lucky once food appeared in the maze.
options.why: Reaching food about as efficiently as trained rats is not luck.

options.text: The rats had been secretly rewarded by exploring, so they were learning to find food all along.
options.why: The point is that what they picked up was not tied to food when they picked it up.

options.text: The food itself taught them the maze instantly, since a strong enough reward is learned in one trial.
options.why: One trial of food does not explain matching rats trained from the start. Something was already kept.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say latent learning is where a disposition stops being enough?

options.text: Something was kept that was not yet committed to any action, and a later process had to put it to work.
options.why: Correct. That later process, and the records it uses, are Module 10's.

options.text: The rats' dispositions were too weak, and needed food to strengthen them before they could act on them.
options.why: The problem is not weakness. What was kept was not committed to any action at all.

options.text: The rats had dispositions for every route, and needed food to choose among them by chance.
options.why: Nothing in the account has the rats holding every route as separate dispositions.

options.text: The rats had no dispositions at all while wandering, since learning without reward is impossible.
options.why: Learning without reward is exactly what latent learning shows is possible.

items.stem: How do a disposition and a record differ in whether they need a separate retrieval step?

options.text: A disposition needs none, acting when its situation recurs; a record needs one, deciding its use.
options.why: Correct. The retrieval step is where a record's use gets settled.

options.text: A disposition needs one before it can act; a record needs none, and acts whenever its situation recurs.
options.why: That reverses them. A disposition acts on its own; a record has to be retrieved.

options.text: Both need one, since nothing kept in a nervous system can act until it has been retrieved.
options.why: A disposition acts directly. That is what being committed at encoding means.

options.text: Neither needs one, since in both cases what is kept acts on its own when the situation recurs.
options.why: A record's use is not settled until it is retrieved, so it does need the step.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the difference between a disposition and a record, say which one learning as the chapter describes it produces, and explain why latent learning is a hard case.
items.answer: The difference is when the use of what is stored gets settled. A disposition is committed when it is laid down: the change itself fixes what the animal is now more likely to do. A record is kept without its use being settled, and what it is for is decided later, when it is retrieved. Learning as the chapter describes it produces dispositions. Latent learning is a hard case because rats wandering a maze with no food picked up something that was not committed to any use; when food appeared, they put it to work. So something was kept that was not a disposition to act.
rubric: Frames the difference as when the use of the stored thing is settled.
Defines a disposition as committed at encoding.
Defines a record as uncommitted, with use settled at retrieval.
Says learning here produces dispositions and explains why latent learning exceeds them.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how the chapter handles the claim that Hebbian plasticity is the only real kind of learning and everything else is modulation of it.
items.answer: The chapter treats it as a disagreement about words rather than about what happens. Nobody disputes that a coincidence-sensitive change in synaptic strength exists, that neuromodulators gate it, that traces settle what it lands on, or that changes in excitability and in connectivity go along with it. Whether to call the gating, the traces and the other changes learning or the regulation of learning is a naming question. Naming questions are not findings.
rubric: Says the chapter treats the claim as a matter of naming.
Lists at least two of the undisputed pieces.
Says whether to call them learning or regulation is a choice of words.
States that naming questions are not findings.

pools.title: One Mechanism, Several Jobs, and What the Chapter Concludes
pools.covers: reading §5.3.12, §5.C (the unnumbered Close) · lecture 5.3 slides one_mechanism_several_jobs, what_separates_the_four, where_marr_strains

items.stem: Is the machinery of coincidence detection, gating and competition a learning-specific device?

options.text: No. The same parts also wire a developing brain, tune sensory maps and support memory.
options.why: Correct. Nothing in the frame is dedicated to learning in particular.

options.text: Yes. It is found only in synapses that take part in learning, and other synapses are built differently.
options.why: The chapter's point is that the same parts serve several jobs.

options.text: Yes. It evolved for learning alone, and its uses in development and memory appeared much later as side effects.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim that learning came first; it says the parts are shared.

options.text: No. It serves development only, and learning uses a separate set of mechanisms entirely.
options.why: Learning uses exactly these mechanisms, and so do development and memory.

items.stem: Module 1 taught multiple realizability. What does the chapter call the case of one mechanism doing several jobs?

options.text: Its converse: one implementation serving many functions, rather than the other way round.
options.why: Correct. The two run in opposite directions between levels.

options.text: A special case of it: one function running on many different implementations, all of them built from synapses.
options.why: Multiple realizability runs from one function to many implementations. This case runs the other way.

options.text: A counterexample to it: showing that each function has exactly one implementation after all.
options.why: Nothing here shows one function has only one implementation.

options.text: Its equivalent: the same claim stated in the vocabulary of the physical level instead.
options.why: The chapter presents it as the converse, not the same claim restated.

items.stem: A researcher finds NMDA-dependent plasticity active in a brain region during a task, and concludes the task must involve learning. What does the chapter say about this inference?

options.text: It is unsafe: when one mechanism does several jobs, finding it active does not show which one.
options.why: Correct. That is reverse inference, named in Module 2.

options.text: It is sound, since NMDA-dependent plasticity is the mechanism of learning and appears nowhere else.
options.why: The same mechanism also wires development and tunes sensory maps.

options.text: It is sound as long as the region is active only during that task and never during rest or during any other task.
options.why: Selectivity of activity helps, but the same mechanism still serves several jobs.

options.text: It is unsafe only because NMDA receptors are too small to measure reliably in a living brain.
options.why: Measurement is not the issue. The issue is that a mechanism does not fix a job.

items.stem: What does reverse inference mean, as this course uses the term?

options.text: Inferring from "this region was active during the task" that the task involved that region's process.
options.why: Correct. Regions are not dedicated to single processes, so how much an activation licenses depends on how selectively the region responds.

options.text: Using one of a system's own estimates as the target for another, rather than waiting for the true outcome.
options.why: That is bootstrapping, a learning procedure rather than an inference about brain data.

options.text: Moving from a behavior to the rule that must have produced it, which is how algorithms are discovered.
options.why: That describes a general scientific move, not the specific inference from brain activity to process.

options.text: Working backward from an outcome to the earlier actions that earned it, and crediting them.
options.why: That is credit assignment, a problem a learner faces, not an inference from activation to process.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say the overlap between learning, development and memory is not an embarrassment for its account?

options.text: A principle general enough for several loci and regulators, committed to no task, is what gets reused.
options.why: Correct. It is what two earlier modules would have predicted.

options.text: The overlap is only apparent, since careful study shows each job uses its own separate synapses.
options.why: The chapter accepts the overlap as real and says it was to be expected.

options.text: The overlap shows the account is incomplete, but the missing pieces are expected to be found in Module 6.
options.why: The chapter does not treat the overlap as a gap to be filled later.

options.text: The overlap is found only in vertebrates, so it does not affect the chapter's account of learning in invertebrates at all.
options.why: Nothing restricts the overlap to vertebrates.

items.stem: The four kinds of learning all change a weight. What does the chapter conclude separates them?

options.text: How much of the world must reach the connection before it moves, and who supplies any answer.
options.why: Correct. That is the through-line of the whole module.

options.text: Which weights each one changes: those of sensory cells, those of interneurons, or those of the motor cells that move the body.
options.why: All four can change any weight. What differs is what the change depends on.

options.text: How large a change each one makes on a single occasion, from very small to very large.
options.why: Step size is set by a learning rate, which any kind can have.

options.text: Which animals each one is found in, from cnidarians up to primates.
options.why: The kinds are separated by information, not by animal group.

items.stem: A weight change can depend on the two cells alone, on the world's next input, on an answer held by some source, or on one number about how things went. Which is hardest for an animal to arrange?

options.text: What a teacher would supply: the response that should have been made.
options.why: Correct. The order runs backward from the one most people expect.

options.text: The two cells alone, since they have to be recorded at the same moment.
options.why: The two cells' activity is already at the connection. It is the easiest.

options.text: The world's next input, since it has to be predicted in advance.
options.why: The world delivers the next input unasked; holding a prediction is not hard.

options.text: One number about how things went, since a body cannot compute one.
options.why: A body produces such numbers easily: a full stomach, a pain signal.

items.stem: The chapter concludes that one synapse, given the right third factor, implements all of it. What does that mean?

options.text: The same synapse can carry any of the four kinds of learning, depending on which signal from elsewhere reaches it.
options.why: Correct. The coincidence detection stays the same; the third factor makes the difference.

options.text: One special synapse in each brain carries all four kinds, while every other synapse in that brain carries only Hebbian learning.
options.why: The claim is about what a synapse can do, not about one special synapse.

options.text: A single synapse can store all four kinds of learning at once, holding four separate weights side by side.
options.why: A synapse has one strength. What varies is what the change depends on.

options.text: The four kinds reduce to one, since a synapse cannot tell which kind of signal is reaching it.
options.why: The four kinds remain distinct; one synapse can serve each, given the right signal.

items.stem: What is the chapter's test for when vocabulary about goals and errors is earned?

options.text: It is earned exactly where something in the mechanism plays the part the word names.
options.why: Correct. It is the lesson the chapter says travels furthest.

options.text: It is earned whenever a system's behavior looks well fitted to its surroundings.
options.why: Looking fitted is exactly what tempts the mistake; selection and Hebb's rule both produce it.

options.text: It is earned whenever the system is complex enough that no simpler description is available.
options.why: Complexity is not the test. What the mechanism contains is.

options.text: It is earned whenever the system is an animal, and never when it is a machine.
options.why: The test applies to mechanisms, animal or machine alike.

items.stem: A student describes Hebbian wiring as having been designed to capture which things go together. Which mistake from Module 2 does the chapter say this repeats?

options.text: Reading design into the peppered moth's coloring, when differential survival left it behind.
options.why: Correct. Hebb's rule holds no goal and registers no miss, just as selection has none.

options.text: Assuming homology whenever two species share a trait, when the trait may have arisen twice.
options.why: That is a real Module 2 error, but not the one the chapter pairs with Hebb's rule.

options.text: Treating the tree of life as a ladder, when every living lineage has in fact been evolving for exactly as long as ours.
options.why: That is a different Module 2 warning, about ranking animals.

options.text: Moving from brain activity to a process, when regions are not dedicated to single processes.
options.why: That is reverse inference, which concerns interpreting brain data.

items.stem: Why do the words "expected" and "error" describe error-driven learning rather than decorate it?

options.text: The rule holds an expectation and computes a difference, so the mechanism plays the parts named.
options.why: Correct. That passes the chapter's test for when such words are earned.

options.text: The rule was invented by engineers, whose vocabulary is always literal rather than figurative.
options.why: Who invented a rule does not settle whether a word fits it.

options.text: The rule produces behavior that looks purposeful to an observer, and purposeful-looking behavior is what earns such words.
options.why: Looking purposeful is not the test; Hebbian wiring looks fitted too.

options.text: The rule is found in humans, and words from human experience fit whatever humans do.
options.why: The rule is found in rats and circuits too. The test is about the mechanism.

items.stem: The lecture suggests applying the test for goal-and-error vocabulary outside the course. A headline says a gene "wants" to be passed on. What does the test ask?

options.text: Whether anything in the mechanism plays the part of a want; if not, the word only decorates.
options.why: Correct. The lecture names this kind of headline, and a claim that an AI system "believes" something, as places to use it.

options.text: Whether the gene is in fact passed on often, since a gene that spreads can be said to want to spread.
options.why: Spreading is an outcome. The test asks what plays the part the word names.

options.text: Whether the headline was written by a scientist, since experts may use intentional words freely.
options.why: Who writes the words does not change what the mechanism contains.

options.text: Whether the gene is in an animal with a brain, since only a brain can want anything at all, and a gene has no brain of its own.
options.why: The test is not about brains. It is about whether anything in the mechanism plays the part.

items.stem: The chapter says Marr's three levels have no slot for evidence. What does it mean?

options.text: Findings like blocking are claims at no level, yet they decide between proposals at every level.
options.why: Correct. A scheme that classifies explanations is silent about what adjudicates them.

options.text: Evidence belongs only at the implementational level, so claims at the other two levels cannot be tested at all.
options.why: Findings test proposals at every level, not just one.

options.text: Evidence belongs only at the computational level, since only behavior can be observed directly.
options.why: Recordings from cells are evidence too. Findings do not sit at any one level.

options.text: The levels are so general that no evidence could ever bear on any of them.
options.why: Evidence does bear on them; the point is that it has no level of its own.

items.stem: At which of Marr's three levels does the blocking result sit, according to the chapter?

options.text: It is a finding rather than a claim at any level, and it decides between proposals at every level.
options.why: Correct. The same goes for devaluation, renewal and instinctive drift.

options.text: The computational level, since it concerns what problem the rat is solving when it learns about a cue.
options.why: The chapter declines to place it at any level.

options.text: The algorithmic level, since it concerns the rule the rat follows.
options.why: Blocking bears on the rule, but it is a finding, not an algorithmic claim.

options.text: The implementational level, since it was measured in a real animal.
options.why: Being measured in an animal does not make a result implementational.

items.stem: The chapter says the levels were not independently specifiable in this module. What case shows this?

options.text: Temporal-difference learning was accepted largely because dopamine recordings behaved as its error term said.
options.why: Correct. The evidence for the algorithm came from the implementation.

options.text: The delta rule was accepted for animals because it had been built into a working machine first, years before anyone applied it to a rat.
options.why: That history is real, but the chapter's case is about evidence from the implementation.

options.text: Hebb's rule was accepted because it matched the computational problem, without any evidence from cells.
options.why: That is not the chapter's example, and Hebb's rule was not the one accepted from below.

options.text: The adaptive landscape was accepted because biologists drew it before any population was measured.
options.why: The adaptive landscape is a picture, not an algorithm supported from below.

items.stem: The chapter says the mapping between levels is loose downward as well as upward. What was found at the implementational level that shows this?

options.text: A general principle, at several loci with several regulators, that does not pick out the function above it.
options.why: Correct. The physical account is too general to say which job is being done.

options.text: A mechanism dedicated to each of the four kinds of learning, each in its own separate part of the brain.
options.why: Nothing dedicated turned up; that is the point.

options.text: No physical change at all, since learning turned out to have no implementation below the algorithm.
options.why: Plenty of physical change was found; it is simply general-purpose.

options.text: A single molecule responsible for all learning, which fixes every function above it without any ambiguity about the job.
options.why: The chapter found a principle at several loci, not one molecule that settles every function.

items.stem: Having named three places Marr's levels strained, does the chapter conclude that the levels fail?

options.text: No. They separated why change, by what rule, and in what material, which let the families be compared.
options.why: Correct. A framework is a tool with a shape, and knowing where it strains is part of using it.

options.text: Yes. The three strains show the levels should be replaced by a scheme with a place for evidence.
options.why: The chapter says the levels did their work; it does not call for replacing them.

options.text: Yes. The levels only work for vision, and learning is a case they were never meant to cover.
options.why: The chapter used the levels throughout and says they did the work.

options.text: No. The strains are only apparent, and a careful reading shows the levels were never really strained at all.
options.why: The chapter treats the strains as real, while still concluding the levels did their work.

items.stem: The chapter concludes that the learning machinery it has described is general-purpose and undifferentiated. What limitation does that bring?

options.text: Reusable everywhere, it is specialized for nothing, and cannot do two incompatible things at once.
options.why: Correct. Efficient, and limited, which is what motivates specialists.

options.text: It cannot learn anything new, since general-purpose machinery can only repeat what selection has built into it.
options.why: The machinery learns. Its limit is that nothing in it is specialized.

options.text: It works in small animals and no others, since a large brain cannot use the same rule in every synapse.
options.why: Size raises the question of specialists; it does not stop the rule running.

options.text: It cannot bridge any delay, since general-purpose synapses register just the events that coincide.
options.why: Delay is bridged by traces and temporal-difference learning. The limit concerns specialization.

items.stem: Everything in the chapter's account is general-purpose: the same rule in the same tissue wherever there are synapses. What question does that limitation raise?

options.text: What happens when an animal is large enough to build specialists: the question asked of circuits, one level up.
options.why: Correct. A principle reusable everywhere is specialized for nothing, so the next question is what building specialists would gain.

options.text: What a single unit cannot learn however well it is trained: a limit on one unit's capacity, asked again of learning.
options.why: That thread is left open too, but it concerns one unit's limits, not what general-purpose machinery cannot do.

options.text: How kept traces are put to use later on: the question of states that outlast their cause, asked again.
options.why: Kept traces are a separate open thread. The limit of general-purpose machinery is that it is specialized for nothing.

options.text: How an animal chooses by consulting a model of the world: the question of approach and avoidance, asked again.
options.why: Choosing by a model is a separate open thread. General-purpose machinery raises the question of specialists.

items.stem: Which pair of descriptions passes the chapter's test for goal-and-error vocabulary?

options.text: "The delta-rule unit corrected its error"; "the Hebbian synapse strengthened because both cells fired together".
options.why: Correct. The first uses error words where an error is computed; the second avoids them where none is.

options.text: "The Hebbian synapse corrected its error"; "the delta-rule unit strengthened because both cells fired together".
options.why: This swaps them. Hebb's rule computes no error, and the delta rule does not work on co-activity.

options.text: "The Hebbian synapse learned what the tone means"; "the delta-rule unit corrected its error".
options.why: The first credits Hebb's rule with understanding a meaning, which nothing in it plays the part of.

options.text: "Evolution corrected the worm's error about copper"; "the delta-rule unit corrected its error".
options.why: Nothing in a population computes an error, so the first fails the test.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, name the three ways Marr's levels strained in this module and say whether the chapter concludes that the levels fail.
items.answer: First, the levels have no slot for evidence: blocking, devaluation, renewal and instinctive drift are findings, not claims at any level, yet they decide between proposals at every level. Second, the levels were not independently specifiable: temporal-difference learning was accepted largely because dopamine recordings behaved as its error term predicted, so evidence for the algorithm came from the implementation. Third, the mapping is loose downward: the physical level turned up a general principle at several loci, which does not pick out the function above it. The levels do not fail, since they separated why, by what rule, and in what material, which made comparing the families possible.
rubric: Names the missing slot for evidence, with an example finding.
Names the dopamine case showing the levels were not independent.
Names the loose downward mapping from a general principle.
States that the levels still did their work.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, state the chapter's test for when words about goals and errors are earned, and apply it to Hebb's rule, the delta rule, and one case from outside biology of your choosing.
items.answer: The test is that goal and error vocabulary earns its place exactly where something in the mechanism plays the part the word names. Hebb's rule holds no goal and registers no miss, so describing its wiring as designed repeats the peppered-moth mistake. The delta rule holds an expectation and computes a difference from it, so saying it was wrong and corrected itself describes the mechanism. For a case outside biology, a headline saying a phone app "wants" to know where its user is fails the test unless something in the app actually plays the part of wanting; otherwise the word decorates rather than describes.
rubric: States the test in terms of what the mechanism contains.
Applies it negatively to Hebb's rule.
Applies it positively to the delta rule.
Applies it sensibly to a new case, saying what would have to be in the mechanism.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how one mechanism doing several jobs is the converse of multiple realizability, and why it makes reverse inference unsafe.
items.answer: Multiple realizability, from Module 1, is one function running on many possible implementations. Here the direction is reversed: one implementation, coincidence detection, gating and competition, serves many functions, including learning, wiring a developing brain, tuning sensory maps and supporting memory. Because the same mechanism does several jobs, finding it present or a structure active does not establish which job is being done. That is why the reverse inference from mechanism to job is unsafe.
rubric: States multiple realizability as one function, many implementations.
States the converse as one implementation, many functions, with examples.
Says finding the mechanism does not establish the job.
Connects this to reverse inference.
